game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 13 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 1, 4 cards worth 2, 3 cards worth 3, 1 card worth 5, 1 card worth 11, 3 cards worth 14. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
On the bid side, a bid of 7 gives the best expected edge. On the ask side, every ask I tested loses money, so I won't quote one.

**Fair value.** The 13 cards sum to 76, so one card averages about 5.85 and three cards average about 17.5. The outcome splits by how many high cards (11 or 14) are dealt:

| High cards dealt | Probability | Typical sum |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | about 29% | about 7.7 |
| 1 | about 50% | about 18.4 |
| 2 | about 19% | about 29 |
| 3 | about 1.4% | about 40 |

**Bid side.** A bid of 7 only loses to informed sellers when the sum is 6 or less. That happens only when no high card is dealt, and the expected cost is about 0.05.

Noise traders sell to me about 4% of the time, each time about 10.5 below fair. That is worth about +0.21. The net expected edge is about +0.16, the best of the bids I checked.

**Ask side.**
- An ask around 22–26 sits in the gap between one high card and two. It loses more to informed buyers when two or three high cards are dealt than it gains from noise traders, for a net of about −0.05 or worse.
- A very high ask comes out at roughly zero.

{"bid": 7, "ask": null}

The 13-card deck sums to 76, so the average card is about 5.85. The expected 3-card sum is about 17.5.

**Shape of the distribution.** It is split into clusters by how many high cards (the 11 and the three 14s) are dealt:
- **No high cards:** about 29%, average sum about 7.7.
- **One high card:** about 50%, average sum about 17.9.
- **Two high cards:** about 19%, average sum about 28.
- **Three high cards:** about 1%, sum about 38.

**Quote 1.** My bid of 7 got no trade. Only about 8% of hands sum below 7, so this moves fair value up only slightly, to roughly 17.6.

**Choosing the quotes.** Informed traders hurt me badly whenever my quote sits inside one of the outer clusters. I set each side by weighing the expected gain from noise traders, whose valuations are 17.6 plus noise with standard deviation 6, against the expected loss to informed traders:
- **Bid at 12:** slightly negative, about −0.63 + 0.49.
- **Bid at 10:** roughly break-even. Bidding 9 moves further below the no-high-card hands, so it is safer.
- **Ask at 24:** slightly positive, about −0.42 + 0.45.
- **Ask at 26:** better, about −0.22 + 0.34, because it sits above most two-high-card sums.

So I quote wide around fair value: bid 9, ask 26.

{"bid": 9, "ask": 26}

Card 1 is a 3, so the expected settlement is about 15.2. The other two cards sum to either a low value (about 42%), a middle value (about 48%) or a high value (about 9%).

- **Bid 8:** Noise traders will sometimes sell to me well below fair value. Informed traders only sell when both remaining cards are small, so this bid has a small positive edge of about +0.3.
- **Ask 22:** Informed traders only buy when the remaining cards include a 14 and a 5, or two big cards. The noise-trader edge outweighs that, at about +0.1.

{"bid": 8, "ask": 22}

The fair value is about 15.3. At this price the main risk is informed traders, because the possible totals are bimodal: low around 6–11, middle around 15–22, and high at 28 or 31.

**Fair value**
- After card 1 = 3, the 12 cards left sum to 73. Two more cards are expected to add about 12.17, giving an unconditional fair value of about 15.17.
- No one traded at 8 / 22 in quote 3. An informed trader stays out only if the total is between 8 and 22. That makes middle totals a little more likely and moves the fair value up to about 15.33.

**Ask**
I compared what noise buyers pay me with what informed buyers take from me:

| Ask | Net expected edge |
|---|---|
| 19 | +0.12 |
| 21 | about +0.26 |
| 22 | about +0.27 |
| 24 | +0.19 |

At 22, informed traders only buy when the total is 28 or 31, which is about 9% likely after the no-trade update. I'll ask 22.

**Bid**

| Bid | Net expected edge |
|---|---|
| 7 | about +0.33 |
| 8 | about +0.35 |
| 9 | about +0.28 |

At 8, informed traders only sell when the total is 6 or 7, and those cases cost me little. Bids above 9 run into the large group of low totals. I'll bid 8.

{"bid": 8, "ask": 22}

With cards 1 and 2 revealed (3 and 2), the sum so far is 5. The settlement is 5 plus the value of the last card.

**What the last card can be**
The 11 cards left in the deck are: one 1, three 2s, two 3s, one 5, one 11 and three 14s. That gives these possible settlement values:

| Settlement | 6 | 7 | 8 | 10 | 16 | 19 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 1/11 | 3/11 | 2/11 | 1/11 | 1/11 | 3/11 |

The public fair value is 5 + 71/11 ≈ 11.45.

**Choosing the ask**
An informed trader only buys if the settlement is strictly above my ask. At an ask of 19.0, no settlement value is above 19, so informed traders never buy and I only face noise traders.
- A noise trader buys with probability P(N(11.45, 6) > 19) ≈ 0.104.
- When one does, I make about 7.55 on average.
- That is worth about 0.5 × 0.104 × 7.55 ≈ +0.39 per quote.

Lower asks attract more noise buyers but give away value to informed buyers:
- At 17, the expected profit is about +0.22.
- At 15.9, it is about +0.08.

**Choosing the bid**
An informed trader only sells if the settlement is strictly below my bid. At a bid of 6.0, no settlement value is below 6, so informed traders never sell.
- A noise trader sells with probability about 0.18.
- When one does, I make about 5.45 on average.
- That is worth about +0.50 per quote.

The alternatives are slightly worse:
- At 7.0, I would lose to informed sellers when the settlement is 6, for a net of about +0.47.
- At 5.5, the expected profit is about +0.48.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 19.0}

Fair value is about **11.45**, and I quote **bid 6, ask 19**.

**Fair value.** Cards 1 and 2 add up to 5. Removing a 3 and a 2 leaves 11 cards:
- 1 card worth 1
- 3 cards worth 2
- 2 cards worth 3
- 1 card worth 5
- 1 card worth 11
- 3 cards worth 14

These total 71, so card 3 is worth 71/11 ≈ 6.45 on average. Fair value is 5 + 6.45 ≈ 11.45.

The possible settlement values are:

| Value | 6 | 7 | 8 | 10 | 16 | 19 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 1/11 | 3/11 | 2/11 | 1/11 | 1/11 | 3/11 |

**Ask side.** The expected profit of a sale is half the informed trader's loss plus half the noise trader's gain.
- At ask 19, the informed trader never buys, because no value is above 19. The noise trader buys with probability P(N > 19) ≈ 0.104, and each sale earns about 7.55. The expected profit is about 0.39.
- At ask 18, it is about 0.32, because the informed trader buys whenever the value is 19.
- At ask 20, it is about 0.33.
- So 19 is the best ask.

**Bid side.**
- At bid 6, the informed trader never sells, because no value is below 6. The noise trader sells with probability P(N < 6) ≈ 0.18, and each purchase earns about 5.45. The expected profit is about 0.50.
- At bid 6.5, it is about 0.48.
- At bid 7, it is about 0.47.
- So 6 is the best bid.

{"bid": 6, "ask": 19}

game.title: Card sum
game.description: A custom deck of 11 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 0, 3 cards worth 2, 4 cards worth 3, 3 cards worth 11. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the sum of the dealt cards' values.

info.raw:
Fair value is about 13.9. The deck's average card is 51/11 ≈ 4.64, so three cards are worth about 13.9 in expectation.

The settlement value depends mainly on how many 11s are dealt:

| Number of 11s | Probability | Typical sum |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 34% | 4–9 |
| 1 | 51% | 13–17 |
| 2 | 15% | 22–25 |
| 3 | under 1% | 33 |

**Ask side.** An informed buyer only takes an ask of 18 or more when two or more 11s are dealt. That loses about 4–7 per trade, but only in roughly 15% of cases. Noise traders buying above fair value add profit. Weighing the two, expected profit is highest at an ask near 20, about +0.4 per quote.

**Bid side.** An informed seller only takes a low bid when no 11s are dealt and the sum is below the bid. A bid of 8 limits that adverse selection while still catching noise sellers. That gives about +0.55 per quote.

{"bid": 8, "ask": 20}

The prior expected sum is 3 × 51/11 ≈ 13.9. The value distribution is lumpy, depending on how many 11s are dealt:
- **No 11s:** sum is 9 or less.
- **One 11:** sum is 13 to 17.
- **Two 11s:** sum is 22 to 25.
- **Three 11s:** sum is 33.

**Updating on the buy at 20.** An informed trader buys at 20 only if the value is above 20, which needs at least two 11s. The prior chance of that is about 15%. After the buy at 20, it rises to about 43%. The posterior fair value is about 17.5.

**Ask.** The informed-trader values above 20 cluster at 22, 24 and 25. An ask at 24.9 only loses to informed buyers in the 25 and 33 cases. It still earns a large margin of about 7.4 from noise buyers. Expected edge is about +0.5 per quote, better than asking lower.

**Bid.** Every sum without an 11 is 9 or less, and every sum with one 11 is at least 13. A bid around 10.5 only loses to informed sellers when no 11 was dealt. It also collects a margin of about 7 from noise sellers. Expected edge is about +0.3.

{"bid": 10.5, "ask": 24.9}

Card 1 = 11, so the other two cards come from 10 cards: one 0, three 2s, four 3s and two 11s. With no other information, the fair value would be 11 + 2 × 4 = 19.

The two stage-1 trades change this. Counterparties bought at 20 and then at 24.9. An informed trader only buys above the true value, so these trades are much more likely when the settlement is above 24.9. I estimate each trade's likelihood as the informed share plus the noise share. For the noise share I used the public fair value at the time: about 13.9 for the first trade and roughly 16.5 for the second. Weighting the 45 possible pairs of remaining cards by those likelihoods gives roughly:

| Settlement | Posterior probability |
|---|---|
| 25 (11 + 11 + 3) | about 73% |
| 33 (three 11s) | about 9% |
| 22 or 24 | about 10% |
| 17 or less | about 8% |

The public fair value is therefore about 24.8.

**Quote choice:** I am short 2 and can sell one more unit. I quote around 24.8 and leave 25 strictly inside the spread. That way an informed trader in the most likely case (settlement 25) does not trade. My ask is only exposed to the 33 case. My bid only trades with informed sellers in the low cases, and those trades are profitable for me. Noise traders centred near 24.8 give me edge on both sides.

{"bid": 23, "ask": 26.5}

Card 1 is 11, and I estimate fair value at about 23.7. I'll quote 22.5 / 25.4.

**What can settle.** The ten unseen cards are one 0, three 2s, four 3s and two 11s. So the settlement value (11 plus two more cards) can only be 13–17, 22, 24, 25 or 33. The card reveal alone puts the expected value at 19.

**What the trades say.**
- In stage 1, buyers took my asks at 20 and 24.9. An informed trader only does that if the value is above the price, so this is strong evidence the total is high.
- At quote 3, someone sold to me at 23. That is mild evidence the total is low.

**Fair value.** Updating the possible totals on these three trades gives two clusters. Most of the weight is on 25 (about 62%), with some on 33. The rest is mainly on 13–17, plus small amounts on 22 and 24. The expected value comes out at about 23.7.

**Quote.**
- I put the ask just above 25. Informed buyers holding a 25 total then don't trade with me; only a 33 total would.
- I put the bid at 22.5. That stays below 22, 24 and 25, so an informed seller only hits it when the total is in the low cluster.
- The spread is roughly centred on fair value, which is also where noise traders are centred. I'm short 1, so another sale would only take me to −2, which is still allowed.

{"bid": 22.5, "ask": 25.4}

**Fair value.** The two revealed cards sum to 11 + 3 = 14. Nine cards remain: one 0, three 2s, three 3s and two 11s.

| Third card | Probability | Settlement |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 1/9 | 14 |
| 2 | 3/9 | 16 |
| 3 | 3/9 | 17 |
| 11 | 2/9 | 25 |

The expected third card is 37/9 ≈ 4.11, so public fair value is about 18.11. Noise traders value the contract at 18.11 plus noise with standard deviation 6.2.

**Ask.** An informed trader only buys if the value is 25.
- At an ask of 24, the expected edge is about 0.58.
- At an ask of 25, the expected edge is about 0.60. Informed traders never buy here, because a value of 25 is not above 25.

So I set the ask at 25. A sale would take me to −3, which is allowed.

**Bid.** An informed trader sells only if the value is below my bid.
- A bid of 16 gives about 0.43.
- A bid of 14 gives about 0.68, and informed traders never sell, since no value is below 14.
- A bid of 13 also gives about 0.68.

The best bid is around 13.5.

{"bid": 13.5, "ask": 25}

With card 1 = 11 and card 2 = 3, the dealt sum so far is 14. Nine cards remain for card 3: one 0, three 2s, three 3s and two 11s. The settlement can only be 14, 16, 17 or 25. Its expected value is 14 + 37/9 ≈ 18.1, which I take as the public fair value.

**Ask side**
- At an ask of 25, an informed trader never buys, because even the best outcome (25) is not above my ask.
- A noise trader buys about 13% of the time, and each such sale earns me about 6.9.
- That gives an expected profit of about 0.60.
- Lower asks catch more noise buyers but start losing to informed buyers when the value is 25. Higher asks lose too many noise buyers.

**Bid side**
- At a bid at or below 14, an informed trader never sells to me, because the lowest possible value is 14.
- At a bid of 13.5, a noise trader sells to me about 23% of the time, and each purchase earns me about 4.6.
- That gives an expected profit of about 0.68, which is close to the best available.

Both sides are allowed: selling would take me to -3 and buying to -1.

{"bid": 13.5, "ask": 25}

game.title: Dice/cards product
game.description:
Two dice are rolled independently.
- Die 1 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
- Die 2 (6 faces, each equally likely): 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6.
game.contract: The contract settles at the product of the two dice.

info.raw:
The contract's expected value is 3.5 × 3.5 = **12.25**, and its standard deviation is about 8.9. Noise traders' valuations are spread 13 around fair value, so a wide spread still gets plenty of noise trades.

I tested a half-spread of about 7 to 8 points:
- **Noise traders:** expected profit is about 1.7 per side.
- **Informed traders:** expected loss is small because the payoff is lopsided. Selling at 20 loses only on products of 24, 25, 30 or 36, which together have about an 11% chance (4/36 for 20 and above). Buying at 4.5 loses only on products of 1 to 4, about 22% (8/36).

The product distribution is skewed to the right. Big values are rarer but further from 12.25, so I set the bid about 7.75 below fair and the ask about 7.75 above it.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 20}

Fair value is about 11.7. The unconditional mean is 12.25, and the no-trade at quote 1 shades it down slightly.

I picked each side by comparing expected profit from noise traders with expected loss to informed traders:
- **Ask:** an ask near 22 earns about 1.56 per quote, which is the best of the levels I checked.
- **Bid:** a bid between 2 and 3 earns about 1.75 per quote. Below about 4, informed traders rarely sell, because a product below the bid is unlikely.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 22}

With die 1 revealed as 6, the contract settles at 6 times die 2. That is equally likely to be 6, 12, 18, 24, 30 or 36, so the fair value is 21.

For an ask at price a, I estimated expected profit as two parts:
- **Noise traders (80%):** they buy when 21 plus noise (standard deviation 13) is above a. I earn a − 21 on those trades.
- **Informed traders (20%):** they buy only when the true value is above a, and I lose that value minus a.

| Ask | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 24.1 | 0.41 |
| 26 | 0.93 |
| 28 | 1.32 |
| 30.1 | 1.57 |
| 31.5 | 1.61 |
| 32 | 1.62 |
| 33 | 1.61 |

Expected profit peaks at an ask of about 32. The values are symmetric around 21, so the matching bid is about 10.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 32}

The contract settles at 6 × die 2, which is one of {6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36}. Before any trading, the expected value is 21.

**Updating on the quote-3 trade.** A counterparty sold to me at 10.
- An informed trader would only sell at 10 if the value is 6.
- At that point the public fair value was 21. A noise trader sells at 10 with probability Φ(−11/13) ≈ 0.20.
- So the chance of that sell is about 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.20 ≈ 0.359 if the value is 6. For any other value it is about 0.8 × 0.20 ≈ 0.159.

info.raw:
Settlement can only be 0, 10 or 20, so I quote just inside the outcomes informed traders would exploit and earn the spread from noise traders.

**Fair value**
- Die 1 shows at least 7 (7, 8, 10, 12) with probability 4/6 = 2/3.
- Die 2 shows at least 7 (8, 9) with probability 3/10 + 1/5 = 1/2.
- Expected value = 10 × (2/3 + 1/2) ≈ 11.67.
- The distribution is P(0) = 1/6, P(10) = 1/2, P(20) = 1/3.

**Ask side**
- For an ask a between 10 and 20, only an informed trader who knows the value is 20 will buy.
- Expected profit = 0.65 × P(noise > a − 11.67) × (a − 11.67) − 0.35 × (1/3) × (20 − a).
- This rises to about 1.09 at a = 19.9, its highest point.

**Bid side**
- For a bid b between 0 and 10, only an informed trader who knows the value is 0 will sell.
- Expected profit = 0.65 × P(noise < b − 11.67) × (11.67 − b) − 0.35 × (1/6) × b.
- This is about 0.93 for b between 1 and 2, its highest range.

**Inventory**
- One unit of position stays well inside the ±5 limit.
- So inventory risk is minor, and I keep both sides wide.

Fair value has moved slightly down after the first quote, and my best quotes sit just outside the outcomes informed traders would trade on.

- Die 2 shows at least 7 with probability 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5.
- So P(0) = 1/6, P(10) = 1/2, P(20) = 1/3.
- The expected value is 10 × (2/3 + 1/2) ≈ 11.67.

**What the no-trade at quote 1 tells us.** The quote was bid 2, ask 19.9.
- An informed trader with value 0 would have sold at 2.
- An informed trader with value 20 would have bought at 19.9.
- Only an informed trader with value 10 would not trade.
- A noise trader does not trade with probability of about 0.628.

Updating on this, the probabilities become about P(0) = 0.117, P(10) = 0.650, P(20) = 0.233. Public fair value is now about 11.17.

**Ask side.**
- At 20.1, informed buyers never trade. My expected profit from noise buyers is about +1.08.

info.raw:
Fair value is about 3.55, and the settlement value can only be 1, 3, 9 or 14.

**Distribution of the minimum** (3 cards from 12, out of C(12,3) = 220 hands):

| Minimum | Hands | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 55 | 0.25 |
| 3 | 130 | 0.59 |
| 9 | 31 | 0.14 |
| 14 | 4 | 0.018 |

The expected value is 780/220 ≈ 3.55.

**Bid.** At 1.0, an informed trader never sells to me. It would need a value below 1, and the lowest possible value is exactly 1. A noise trader sells with probability of about 18%, and each such trade earns about 2.55. That gives an expected edge of about +0.23, the best of the bids I checked. Raising the bid toward 3 lets informed traders holding a 1 hit me, which costs more than it gains.

**Ask.** Any ask below 9 gets lifted by informed traders whenever the value is 9 or 14, which is expensive. An ask of about 9 is roughly break-even to slightly positive, at about +0.03. An ask of 8 is about zero.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

Pricing the contract (minimum of 3 cards dealt from 12):
- P(min = 1) = 0.25
- P(min = 3) ≈ 0.59
- P(min = 9) ≈ 0.14
- P(min = 14) ≈ 0.018

The fair value is about 3.5. The no-trade at quote 1 only rules out an informed trader holding a 14, which moves the fair value down only slightly.

**Bid at 1.** An informed trader never sells to me there, because the lowest possible value is 1 and they sell only if their value is strictly below my bid. Noise traders sell often enough that 1 is about the most profitable bid. Raising it to around 2.9 brings in informed sellers holding a 1, which costs about 0.24 against roughly 0.13 gained from noise traders, so it loses money overall.

**Ask at 9.** At this price only an informed trader holding a 14 (about 1.8% chance) buys from me. Noise traders who buy above 9 roughly cover that loss. A lower ask, such as 7 or 8, brings in informed buyers holding a 9, and that costs more than the extra noise trades earn.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 9}

Fair value is about 4.27. My bid is 1 and my ask is 9, because an informed trader would trade against me at any price strictly between the possible settlement values.

**Fair value given card 1 = 9**

The 11 remaining cards are one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s. Two of them are dealt. The settlement is the smallest of 9 and those two cards.

| Settlement | When it happens | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | The 1 is dealt | 2/11 |
| 3 | No 1 is dealt, but at least one 3 is | 6/11 |
| 9 | Both dealt cards are 9 or 14 | 3/11 |

This gives an expected value of 47/11, about 4.27.

**Choosing the quotes**

- **Ask:** If I ask below 9, every informed trader holding a 9-outcome buys from me and I lose money. At 9 exactly, informed traders don't buy, because they only buy when their valuation is above the ask. Noise traders still buy about 4.6% of the time, gaining me about 4.73 per trade. Asking higher than 9 earns less overall.
- **Bid:** Any bid above 1 lets informed traders holding a 1-outcome sell to me at a loss to me. At 1 exactly, informed traders don't sell. Noise traders still sell about 12% of the time, gaining me about 3.27 per trade. This bid has the highest expected profit of the ones I checked, between 1 and 3.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 9}

Card 1 is a 9, so the settlement can only be 1, 3 or 9. It depends on the two cards still hidden, drawn from the 11 left: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s.

**Settlement odds**
- There are C(11,2) = 55 equally likely pairs.
- Min = 1 if either card is the 1: 10/55.
- Min = 9 if both cards are 9s or 14s: C(6,2) = 15/55.
- Min = 3 in every other case: 30/55.
- Fair value = (10·1 + 30·3 + 15·9)/55 ≈ 4.27.

**Bid**
- Any bid above 1 gets hit by informed traders whenever the settlement is 1.
- That costs (b−1) × 0.5 × 10/55 per unit of bid above 1.
- Noise traders have valuations around 4.27 with standard deviation 2.8. Their extra fills from a higher bid don't make up for that loss.
- Expected profit per quote is about 0.20 at a bid of 1.0, 0.19 at 1.1, 0.15 at 2 and 0.02 at 3. So a bid of 1 is best.

**Ask**
- Any ask below 9 gets lifted by informed traders whenever the settlement is 9.
- That costs (9−a) × 0.5 × 15/55 per unit of ask below 9.
- Expected profit per quote is about 0.11 at an ask of 9, 0.07 at 8.5 and 0.03 at 8. So an ask of 9 is best.

{"bid": 1, "ask": 9}

The contract is now certain to settle at **1**:

- The deck has only one card worth 1, and card 2 is that card.
- Every other card is worth at least 3, so card 3 cannot be lower.
- So the minimum of the dealt cards is 1, and the public fair value is exactly 1.

**Who trades with me:**

- **Informed traders** value the contract at exactly 1. If my bid is below 1 and my ask is above 1, they never trade, so there is no adverse selection.
- **Noise traders** value it at 1 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 2.8. They are the only ones who will trade.

**Choosing the spread:** Each side earns its distance x from fair value times the chance a noise trader crosses it. With z = x/2.8, that profit is proportional to z·(1−Φ(z)), where Φ is the standard Normal cumulative distribution. This peaks at about z ≈ 0.75, so x ≈ 2.1 on each side.

That gives a bid of 1 − 2.1 = −1.1 and an ask of 1 + 2.1 = 3.1. This assumes the game accepts a negative bid.

{"bid": -1.1, "ask": 3.1}

The contract will settle at exactly 1. Card 2 is the deck's only 1-card, and no card is lower, so the minimum of the three dealt cards must be 1.

- **Informed traders:** they value the contract at exactly 1. They will not trade at any bid below 1 or ask above 1, so they cannot pick me off.
- **Noise traders:** they value it at 1 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 2.8. On each side, my expected profit is the distance from 1 times the chance the noise trader crosses that price.
- **Best distance:** for normal noise, that product is largest at about 0.75 × 2.8 ≈ 2.1 from fair value. That gives a bid of -1.1 and an ask of 3.1.
- **Position limit:** I am long 1, so buying one more unit takes me to +2. That is within the ±3 limit, and both sides are allowed.

   - Die 3 shows 9 (probability 0.1): the expected maximum is 9.75.
   - Die 3 shows 12 (probability 0.2): the result is 12.
3. **Fair value:** 0.6·8.125 + 0.1·8.375 + 0.1·9.75 + 0.2·12 ≈ 9.09.

Settlement is spread widely around that value, and 20% of counterparties are informed. I'll quote about ±1.3 around 9.09. That still lets me trade with a good share of noise traders, whose valuations have a standard deviation of 2.6.

|---|---|

| 6 | 2/16 |
| 7 | 2/16 |
| 8 | 6/16 |
| 12 | 4/16 |

- If die 3 shows 6 (probability 0.1), the expected value is 8.375.
- If die 3 shows 9 (probability 0.1), the expected value is 9.75.
- If die 3 shows 12 (probability 0.2), the value is 12.

Combining these: 0.6 × 8.125 + 0.1 × 8.375 + 0.1 × 9.75 + 0.2 × 12 ≈ **9.09**.

So I'm tightening slightly to 8.0 / 10.2. This should catch more noise traders while still giving some protection against informed ones.

| 14 | 4/220 ≈ 0.02 |

The expected value is about 3.55. The distribution is lumpy, with no values between 3 and 9. That shapes both sides of the quote.

**Bid side**
- If I bid at or above 3, informed sellers holding value 1 hit me often and cost about 2 points each time.
- If I bid exactly 1.0, informed traders never sell, because value 1 is not below 1.0.
- Noise traders still sell to me about 18% of the time, earning about 2.55 per trade.
- That gives an expected edge of about +0.23 per quote, roughly the best of the bids I checked.

**Ask side**
- An ask below about 8 loses money, because informed buyers holding value 9 or 14 outweigh the noise flow.
- At 9, only an informed buyer holding value 14 can hurt me.
- That leaves a small positive edge of about +0.025.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

The minimum of the 3 dealt cards has this distribution:

| Min value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 1 | 55/220 ≈ 0.25 |
| 3 | 130/220 ≈ 0.59 |
| 9 | 31/220 ≈ 0.14 |
| 14 | 4/220 ≈ 0.02 |

- Expected value ≈ 3.55.
- The 1/9 quote with no trade slightly lowers the chance of 14. Fair value is about 3.5.

**Bid:** If my bid is just above 1, an informed seller only hurts me when the true value is 1, and then only by about 0.1.
- Noise traders below about 1.1 sell to me at roughly 2.4 under fair value. That is a clear positive edge.
- A bid near 1.1 gives an expected edge of about +0.2 per quote. Bids of 1.5 or higher do worse because informed sellers at value 1 cost more.

**Ask:** Any ask below 9 lets informed buyers take me whenever the value is 9 (about 14%). That costs more than I earn from noise buyers.
- At 9, only a value of 14 hurts me, and that is rare.
- Noise traders who pay 9 or more give me a small positive edge.

{"bid": 1.1, "ask": 9}

The first card is a 9, so the contract can only settle at 1, 3 or 9 (14 is no longer possible). My quote is a bid of 0.6 and an ask of 9.0.

**Prior after the reveal.** The other two cards come from the remaining 11: one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s. That gives these probabilities for the minimum:
- 1: 10/55
- 3: 30/55
- 9: 15/55

**Effect of the trading history.** At quote 2 someone sold to me at 1.1.
- An informed trader sells there only if the value is 1.
- A noise trader sells there with about 19% probability.
- So that sale is fairly strong evidence that a 1 was dealt.

Updating on that sale and on the earlier no-trade:
- Settles at 1: about 0.58
- Settles at 3: about 0.28
- Settles at 9: about 0.14

That puts the public fair value at about 2.68.

**Ask.** Any ask below 9 gets bought by informed traders whenever the value is 9. Noise buyers rarely reach that high, so they don't make up for it. At 9.0 an informed trader holding a 9 does not buy, and I still collect the occasional noise buyer.

**Bid.** Any bid above 1 gets hit by informed traders whenever the value is 1, which happens 58% of the time. Bidding below 1 avoids that and still catches noise sellers. Expected profit from that side is highest at about 0.5–0.6.

{"bid": 0.6, "ask": 9.0}

Card 1 is a 9, so the settlement is min(9, card 2, card 3). The remaining 11 cards are one 1, four 3s, two 9s and four 14s.

**Settlement distribution and fair value**
- P(min = 1) = 1 − C(10,2)/C(11,2) = 10/55
- P(min = 3) = 30/55
- P(min = 9) = 15/55
- Fair value ≈ (10 + 90 + 135)/55 ≈ 4.27

The history adds almost nothing. The only trade happened before card 1 was revealed. At quote 3, no informed trader could have sold below 0.6 or bought above 9, and the noise trader simply didn't trade.

**Bid**
- At bid = 1.0, informed sellers never hit me, because 1 is not below 1.
- Noise traders sell with probability about 12%, and I gain about 3.27 each time. That is worth about +0.20 per quote.
- Raising the bid to the 1.5–3 range lets informed sellers hit me whenever the value is 1, which happens 18% of the time. The net edge falls to about +0.18 or less.
- So 1.0 is optimal.

**Ask**
- At ask = 9, informed traders never buy, because the value never exceeds 9.
- Noise traders buy with probability about 4.6%, and I gain about 4.73 each time. That is worth about +0.11 per quote.
- Lowering the ask to 8 exposes me to informed buyers when the value is 9, which happens 27% of the time. The edge falls to about +0.03.
- So I keep the ask at 9.

My inventory is +1, which is well within the limit, so it doesn't change the quote.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9}

The remaining 10 cards give a settlement value of 1, 3 or 9. The stage-1 sale at my 1.1 bid makes 1 more likely, so fair value is about 4.15. Quoting 1 / 9 means an informed counterparty never trades, and I still earn the edge from noise traders.

**Prior on the last card.** The deck is 12 cards, and 9 and 14 are already out. That leaves 1×1, 4×3, 2×9 and 3×14. The other two cards are 9 and 14, so:
- Card 3 = 1 gives settlement 1, probability 0.1.
- Card 3 = 3 gives settlement 3, probability 0.4.
- Card 3 = 9 or 14 gives settlement 9, probability 0.5.

That prior has an expected value of 5.8.

**Update from the trading history.** At quote 2 someone sold to me at 1.1.
- An informed seller only sells at 1.1 if the value is below 1.1, which means the value is 1.
- Before any reveal the public fair value was about 3.55. A noise trader values below 1.1 with probability about 0.19.
- So the chance of that sale is about 0.595 if the value is 1, and about 0.095 if it is 3 or 9.

The no-trade quotes 3 and 4 tell me nothing, because no informed counterparty would have traded at those prices. The updated probabilities are about 0.41 for 1, 0.26 for 3 and 0.33 for 9. That puts fair value at about 4.15.

**Ask.** Any ask below 9 gets bought by informed traders whenever the value is 9, which is a 33% chance. At ask 9 an informed trader never buys. A noise trader still buys about 4% of the time, gaining me about 4.85 each time. That is worth about +0.10 expected, which beats lower or higher asks.

**Bid.** Any bid above 1 gets hit by informed traders when the value is 1. At bid 1.0 an informed trader never sells. A noise trader sells about 13% of the time, gaining me about 3.15 each time. That is worth about +0.20 expected. A bid of 1.5 is worth only about +0.13 because of the informed losses.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

Bid 1.0 and ask 9.0, which keeps both sides just out of reach of informed traders while still catching noise trades.

**What the contract can settle at.** Cards 9 and 14 are revealed. The 10 cards left are one 1, four 3s, two 9s and three 14s. Settlement is min(9, card 3), so it can only be 1, 3 or 9. Before using the trade history, the probabilities are 0.1, 0.4 and 0.5, which gives an expected value of 5.8.

**What the history adds.** At quote 2 someone sold to me at 1.1.
- An informed trader would only do that if the minimum were 1, which means card 3 is the 1.
- A noise trader sells below 1.1 only about 15% of the time.
- So that sale is about 7.7 times more likely if card 3 is the 1.
- The quotes with no trade say almost nothing, because informed traders would not have traded at those prices whether the value was 1, 3 or 9.

After this update:
- P(1) ≈ 0.46
- P(3) ≈ 0.24
- P(9) ≈ 0.30
- Expected settlement value ≈ 3.9

**Ask.** Any ask below 9 is hit by informed traders when the value is 9, and that loss outweighs the noise flow. An ask of exactly 9 is not hit, because the rule requires a valuation strictly above the ask. Noise traders still buy there about 3% of the time at roughly +5 edge. Of the asks I checked, 9.0 had the highest expected profit.

**Bid.** Any bid above 1 is hit by informed traders when the value is 1. A bid of exactly 1.0 avoids that, and noise traders still sell there about 15% of the time at roughly +2.9 edge. Raising the bid to 1.5 brings in a little more noise flow but loses more to informed sellers.

game.title: Dice/cards max
game.description:
Three dice are rolled independently. Repeated numbers are separate faces.
- Die 1 (4 faces, each equally likely): 2, 4, 8, 8.
- Die 2 (4 faces, each equally likely): 4, 6, 7, 12.
- Die 3 (6 faces, loaded): 0 (prob 1/5), 1 (prob 1/5), 2 (prob 1/5), 6 (prob 1/10), 9 (prob 1/10), 12 (prob 1/5).
game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dice.

info.raw:
Expected settlement value is about 9.09, so I'm quoting roughly 1.3 either side of it.

**Dice 1 and 2.** The larger of dice 1 and 2 takes these values, out of 16 equally likely pairs:
- 4 in 2 of 16
- 6 in 2 of 16
- 7 in 2 of 16
- 8 in 6 of 16
- 12 in 4 of 16

Its expected value is 130/16 = 8.125.

**Adding die 3.** The expected maximum depends on die 3's roll:

| Die 3 | Probability | Expected max |
|---|---|---|
| 0, 1 or 2 | 0.6 | 8.125 (die 3 never matters) |
| 6 | 0.1 | 8.375 |
| 9 | 0.1 | 9.75 |
| 12 | 0.2 | 12 |

The overall expected value is about 9.09.

**Spread.** The settlement value is 12 with probability 0.4, so an informed buyer will lift any ask below 12. An informed seller will hit my bid if the value turns out to be 4, 6 or 7. Noise traders' valuations have a standard deviation of 2.6. A bid of 7.8 and an ask of 10.4 balances losses to informed traders against trades with noise traders.

{"bid": 7.8, "ask": 10.4}

Fair value is about 9.09, the expected maximum of the three dice. I'm quoting a bid of 7.0 and an ask of 11.6.

**Fair value.** The highest of dice 1 and 2 is:

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 4 | 1/8 |
| 6 | 1/8 |
| 7 | 1/8 |
| 8 | 3/8 |
| 12 | 1/4 |

Combining this with die 3 gives the expected settlement for each die 3 outcome:

| Die 3 | Probability | Expected settlement |
|---|---|---|
| 0, 1 or 2 | 0.6 | 8.125 |
| 6 | 0.1 | 8.375 |
| 9 | 0.1 | 9.75 |
| 12 | 0.2 | 12 |

So the fair value is about 9.09.

**Skew.** The settlement is 12 with probability 0.4. That means an informed counterparty buys at almost any ask below 12. The downside is milder: values of 7 or below occur with probability about 0.26, and the average loss to an informed seller there is small.

**Edge per quote.** These are expected profits per side, counting both noise and informed counterparties:
- **Ask:**
  - 10.4 gives about +0.20.
  - 11.5 to 11.8 gives about +0.30.
  - 12 gives about +0.31 from noise traders alone.
  
  I'm taking 11.6.
- **Bid:**
  - 8.0 gives about +0.18.
  - 7.0 gives about +0.29.
  - 6.5 gives about +0.28.
  
  I'm taking 7.0.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.6}

Die 3 is 6, so the payoff is the largest of die 1, die 2 and 6:
- If die 1 shows 2 or 4, the contract settles at 6, 6, 7 or 12. The average is 7.75.
- If die 1 shows 8, the contract settles at 8, 8, 8 or 12. The average is 9.
- That gives these settlement outcomes:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 6 | 1/4 |
| 7 | 1/8 |
| 8 | 3/8 |
| 12 | 1/4 |

- The fair value is 8.375.

**Ask side.** An informed buyer only lifts my ask when the value is 12. Netting the gain from noise traders against that loss gives the best expected profit at an ask of about 10.5–11. That is roughly +0.28 per arrival.

**Bid side.** The value cannot be below 6, so a bid near 6 risks almost nothing to informed sellers. Netting noise-trader profit against informed losses, the best bid is around 6.0–6.2. That is roughly +0.34 per arrival.

{"bid": 6.1, "ask": 10.7}

With die 3 revealed as 6, I'd quote a bid of 6.0 and an ask of 10.5, around a fair value of about 8.1.

**Settlement distribution.** The contract settles at max(die 1, die 2, 6).
- Die 1 counts as 6 (when it shows 2 or 4) or 8, each with probability 1/2.
- Die 2 counts as 6, 6, 7 or 12, each with probability 1/4.
- So the settlement is 6 with probability 2/8, 7 with 1/8, 8 with 3/8 and 12 with 2/8. The mean is 8.375.

**Update from quote 3.** Nobody traded at 6.1 / 10.7.
- An informed trader who knew the value was 12 would have bought at 10.7, so no trade makes 12 less likely.
- A noise trader would have done nothing with probability of about 0.62.
- After updating, the probabilities are about 0.27 for 6, 0.13 for 7, 0.40 for 8 and 0.19 for 12. The public fair value is about 8.1.

**Ask.** I compared expected profit at several ask prices, setting noise buyers against the informed trader who knows the value is 12.
- An ask of 10.0 earns about 0.28 per quote.
- An ask of 10.5 earns about 0.28.
- An ask of 11.0 earns about 0.27.
- I chose 10.5, which comes out marginally best.

**Bid.**
- At a bid of 6.0, an informed trader only sells if the value is below 6, which never happens. So I lose nothing to informed sellers.
- A noise trader sells with probability of about 0.21, so the expected profit is about 0.35.
- Bids of 6.5 or 7.0 earn less (about 0.32 and 0.24) because informed traders who know the value is 6 would sell to me.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 10.5}

The settlement value can now only be **8 or 12**, so I'm quoting a bid of **7.5** and an ask of **11.8** around a fair value of about **9.37**.

**Possible values.** Die 3 = 6 and die 1 = 8, so the contract settles at the larger of 8 and die 2. Die 2 is one of {4, 6, 7, 12}, so the value is 8 with probability 3/4 and 12 with probability 1/4.

**What the trading history says.**
- At quote 4, public fair value was about 8.4, before die 1 was revealed. Someone bought at 10.5.
  - If the value is 12, an informed counterparty buys there. Combined with a noise buy (about 21%), the chance of that trade is about 0.37.
  - If the value is 8, only a noise trader would buy, about 0.17.
- At quote 3, nobody traded at 6.1 / 10.7. That outcome is about 0.50 likely if the value is 12 and about 0.70 if it is 8.
- Updating the 1/4 prior with both observations gives P(value = 12) ≈ 0.34. Fair value ≈ 8 + 4 × 0.34 ≈ **9.37**.

**Choosing the quotes.** Noise traders value the contract at 9.37 plus noise with standard deviation 2.6.
- **Ask:** any ask below 12 loses to informed buyers when the value is 12. Balancing that loss against profit from noise buyers, expected profit is roughly flat and highest around 11.6–12. I chose 11.8.
- **Bid:** any bid at or above 8 lets informed sellers hit me when the value is 8. Noise-only profit is highest around 7.3–7.6, so I chose 7.5.

My position is -1, so either trade keeps me within the ±5 limit.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 11.8}

Bid 7.4 and ask 12.0; my estimate of fair value is about 9.36.

**Settlement.** Die 1 is 8 and die 3 is 6, so the contract settles at 12 if die 2 is 12. Otherwise it settles at 8. With no trading information, P(12) = 1/4.

**Updating on the trading history.**
- **Quote 4 (buy at 10.5):** Before die 1 was revealed, an informed buyer at 10.5 means die 2 = 12.
  - The public fair value then was 8.375, so the chance a noise trader values above 10.5 is about 0.207.
  - P(buy | 12) = 0.2 + 0.8×0.207 = 0.366.
  - P(buy | not 12) = 0.8×0.207 = 0.166.
  - This moves P(12) from 0.25 to about 0.42.
- **Quote 5 (no trade at 7.5 / 11.8):** At that point the fair value was about 9.70.
  - An informed trader would not trade if the value is 8. If the value is 12, it would have bought at 11.8.
  - The chance a noise trader's valuation falls between 7.5 and 11.8 is about 0.59.
  - P(no trade | 12) = 0.8×0.59 = 0.473.
  - P(no trade | 8) = 0.2 + 0.473 = 0.673.
  - This moves P(12) down to about 0.34, so fair value = 8 + 4×0.34 ≈ **9.36**.

**Choosing the ask.**
- Below 12, an informed buyer costs me (12 − ask) whenever the value is 12.
- At exactly 12, an informed buyer never trades, and expected profit from noise buyers is about 0.33.
- That is the best of the levels I checked: 11.0 gives about 0.28, 11.5 about 0.32, 11.8 about 0.33, and 12.2 about 0.31.

**Choosing the bid.**
- Above 8, an informed seller costs me whenever the value is 8, which is the likely outcome.
- Bids between 7.3 and 7.5 give expected profit of about 0.35. For comparison, 8.0 gives about 0.33 and 8.3 about 0.25.

**Position.** I am short 1, so either trade keeps me well within the ±5 limit.

{"bid": 7.4, "ask": 12.0}

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 8 cards is shuffled: 1 card worth 2, 2 cards worth 9, 4 cards worth 13, 1 card worth 14. 2 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
Pricing below assumes the noise traders' fair value is 8.68, the expected minimum computed here.

**Distribution of the settlement value**

The settlement value is the minimum of 2 cards dealt from {2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 13, 14}. There are C(8,2) = 28 equally likely pairs.

| Minimum | Pairs | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 7 (every pair containing the 2) | 25.0% |
| 9 | 11 (contains a 9, not the 2) | 39.3% |
| 13 | 10 (contains a 13, no 2 or 9) | 35.7% |
| 14 | 0 (only one 14 in the deck) | 0% |

The expected value is (7×2 + 11×9 + 10×13) / 28 = 243/28 ≈ 8.68.

**Choosing the quotes**

For each price I traded off expected profit from noise traders against expected losses to informed traders.

**Ask:**
- An ask just below 13 is lifted by informed traders whenever the value is 13.
- At 13.0 or higher, informed traders never buy.
- Expected profit is close to its maximum (about 0.86) for asks between about 13.3 and 13.5.

**Bid:**
- Any bid above 2 is hit by informed traders when the value is 2, which happens 25% of the time.
- The best trade-off is a bid near 3, with expected profit of about 0.79.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 13.4}

The 13.4 buy tells us nothing about the settlement value. The highest possible minimum is 13, so an informed trader would never buy at 13.4. That trade must have come from a noise trader, and the fair value stays at the prior.

**Settlement distribution.** The minimum of 2 cards drawn from {2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 13, 14} has 28 equally likely pairs:

| Minimum | Pairs | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 7 | 25% |
| 9 | 11 | 39% |
| 13 | 10 | 36% |

The expected value is 243/28 ≈ 8.68.

**Ask.** At 13 an informed trader never buys, because the value is never above 13. A noise trader buys with probability of about 25% and pays about 4.3 above fair. The expected gain is roughly 0.85 per quote. Lowering the ask toward about 12.5 earns slightly less, so 13 is the best choice.

**Bid.** An informed trader sells only when the value is 2, which happens 25% of the time. For bids between 2 and 9, the expected profit peaks with the bid near 3, at about 0.79.

{"bid": 3, "ask": 13}

Card 1 is 13, so the contract settles at min(13, card 2).

**Fair value.** Seven cards remain: one 2, two 9s, three 13s and one 14.
- The settlement is 2 with probability 1/7.
- It is 9 with probability 2/7.
- It is 13 with probability 4/7 (card 2 is 13 or 14).
- Expected value = (2 + 18 + 52)/7 ≈ 10.29.

**Ask.** The informed trader's highest possible value is 13. At any ask of 13 or above, the informed trader never buys, so only noise traders hit it. Expected profit per quote is 0.8 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 10.29):
- Ask 14 gives about 0.83.
- Ask 15 gives about 0.86 (the best).
- Ask 16 gives about 0.83.

**Bid.** Any bid of 9 or below means only an informed trader holding value 2 sells. That costs 0.2 × (1/7) × (bid − 2). The gain from noise traders is 0.8 × P(noise valuation < bid) × (10.29 − bid).
- Bid 6 gives net expected profit of about 0.74.
- Bid 5 gives about 0.76 (the best).
- Bid 4 gives about 0.74.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 15}

The fair value is about **10.29**. With card 1 = 13, the contract settles at 13 unless card 2 is lower. The 7 cards left are one 2, two 9s, three 13s and one 14. So the settlement is 2 with probability 1/7, 9 with probability 2/7 and 13 with probability 4/7. That gives 72/7 ≈ 10.29. Quote 3 had no trade, so the history adds nothing.

**Ask:** Any ask at or above 13 avoids losing to an informed trader, who only buys if the value is above my ask. Above 13, the expected edge from noise traders is about:
- 0.82 at an ask of 14
- 0.86 at an ask of 15
- 0.83 at an ask of 16

This peaks around **15**.

**Bid:** An informed trader only sells below 9 when the card is 2, which has probability 1/7. Each bid below is scored as expected noise-trader edge minus expected informed loss:
- At a bid of 5: noise edge ≈ 0.85, informed loss ≈ 0.09, net ≈ 0.76.
- At 4.5 and 5.5: net ≈ 0.76, so the curve is flat here.
- At 9: net ≈ 0.23, much worse.

I pick **5**.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 15}

info.raw:
Expected settlement value E[min] = (7·2 + 11·9 + 10·13)/28 ≈ 8.68.

**Bid side.** The informed trader only sells to me if the value is 2. That happens with probability 0.25. Noise traders have standard deviation 6.3. I compared expected profit across candidate bids:

| Bid | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|
| 3 | ≈ +0.79 (best) |
| 3.5 | ≈ +0.78 |
| 4 | ≈ +0.76 |

Expected profit is near its peak for any bid from 3 to 4, so I'll bid 3.2.

**Ask side.** No card worth more than 13 can be the minimum, since the minimum is at most 13. So an ask of 13 or above can never lose to an informed trader. Against noise traders, expected profit peaks around an ask of 13.5, at about +0.86 per quote.

{"bid": 3.2, "ask": 13.5}

I'm quoting a bid of 2.0 and an ask of 13.0. These are the prices that maximise expected profit against the expected mix of informed and noise traders.

**Fair value before trading.** The minimum of two cards from {2, 9, 9, 13, 13, 13, 13, 14} has this distribution over the 28 possible pairs:

| Minimum | Pairs | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 7 | 7/28 |
| 9 | 11 | 11/28 |
| 13 | 10 | 10/28 |

That gives an expected value of 243/28 ≈ 8.68.

**Update after the counterparty sold at 3.2.** A noise trader sells below 3.2 with probability about 0.19. An informed trader sells only if the value is 2.
- Chance of that sale if the value is 2: 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.19 ≈ 0.35.
- Chance of that sale otherwise: 0.8 × 0.19 ≈ 0.15.

This shifts the probabilities to about 0.43 for 2, 0.30 for 9 and 0.27 for 13. The fair value drops to about 7.04.

**Ask.** I compared the profit from noise buyers against the losses to informed buyers when the value is 13.
- At an ask of 13.0, expected profit is about 0.82, the highest of the asks I tried (10, 12, 12.5, 13, 13.5).
- At 13.0 an informed trader never buys, since the value is never above 13.

**Bid.** At a bid of 2.0, expected profit is about 0.86, the highest of the bids I tried.
- An informed trader holding a 2 does not sell, because its valuation is not below the bid.
- Raising the bid to 3 brings in more noise sellers, but the losses to informed sellers outweigh that gain.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 13.0}

Card 1 is a 2, the lowest card in the deck. So the minimum of the two dealt cards is certainly 2, and the contract settles at exactly 2. Everyone knows this, so the public fair value is 2.

- **Informed traders** value the contract at 2. They will not trade if my bid is below 2 and my ask is above 2.
- **Noise traders** value it at 2 + N(0, 6.3). Each trade earns my distance from 2.
- **Best distance:** expected profit on each side is x·(1−Φ(x/6.3)). This is largest at x ≈ 0.75·6.3 ≈ 4.7.
- **Quote:** that gives a bid of about −2.7 and an ask of about 6.7. My position stays well within the limits either way.

{"bid": -2.7, "ask": 6.7}

Card 1 is a 2, the lowest card in the deck, so the minimum is locked at 2. The settlement value is therefore known to be 2, and everyone can see it.

- **Informed traders** value the contract at exactly 2. They won't trade with me as long as my bid is below 2 and my ask is above 2.
- **Noise traders** value it at 2 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 6.3. All my profit comes from them.
- **Best spread:** I want to maximise x·(1−Φ(x/6.3)), where x is the distance from 2 to my quote. The optimum is at z ≈ 0.61, so x ≈ 3.86.
- **Quote:** that gives a bid of about −1.9 and an ask of about 5.9.
- **Position limits:** I'm at +1, so either fill keeps me well inside the ±5 range.

game.contract: The contract settles at the largest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:

| 3 | 3 | 1/1140 |

On the bid side, an informed seller appears when the maximum is 10 or less, about 32% of the time, and costs me about 1.5 per trade.

game.title: Dice/cards min
game.description: A custom deck of 22 cards is shuffled: 2 cards worth 2, 3 cards worth 3, 4 cards worth 4, 4 cards worth 5, 2 cards worth 12, 4 cards worth 13, 3 cards worth 15. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.
game.contract: The contract settles at the smallest of the dealt cards.

info.raw:
Fair value is the expected minimum of 3 cards drawn from the 22-card deck, which comes to about 3.77.

**Distribution of the minimum**

| Minimum | Probability |
|---|---|
| 2 | 0.26 |
| 3 | 0.30 |
| 4 | 0.256 |
| 5 | 0.131 |
| 12 or more | about 0.055 |

The distribution has a long right tail.

**Bid side**
- A bid at 1.9 sits below every possible settlement value, so informed traders never sell to me.
- Noise traders still sell there fairly often, which gives the best expected edge on that side (about 0.31 per quote).

**Ask side**
- Informed traders buy whenever the minimum is 5 or more, about 18.6% of the time. In those cases the average settlement value is about 7.2.
- Setting the ask around 5.6 balances the profit from noise traders against losses to informed traders (expected edge about 0.25 per quote).

{"bid": 1.9, "ask": 5.6}

Fair value is about 3.77. Here is the full distribution of the minimum card:

| Minimum | Probability |
|---|---|
| 2 | 0.26 |
| 3 | 0.30 |
| 4 | 0.26 |
| 5 | 0.13 |
| 12 | 0.03 |
| 13 | 0.02 |
| 15 | ~0 |

- **Bid:** If the bid sits just above 2, an informed seller only costs me a little, and only when the minimum is 2. A bid around 2.2 earns about 0.3 per quote from noise traders.
- **Ask:** I want to avoid the rare high values (12 or 13) that informed buyers would trade on. An ask around 5.5 balances the noise-trader edge (about 0.31) against the informed loss (about 0.075).

{"bid": 2.2, "ask": 5.5}

Given card 1 = 4, the remaining 21 cards are: 2×2, 3×3, 3×4, 4×5, 2×12, 4×13, 3×15. The settlement value is min(4, X, Y), where X and Y are two cards drawn from those 21. There are C(21,2) = 210 possible pairs.

- P(min = 2) = 1 − C(19,2)/210 = 39/210
- P(min = 3) = (C(19,2) − C(16,2))/210 = 51/210
- P(min = 4) = 120/210

Fair value = (78 + 153 + 480)/210 ≈ **3.39**

**Ask:** The settlement value can never be above 4, so the informed trader never buys at an ask of 4 or higher. That leaves only noise traders on this side. Expected profit per quote is (a − 3.39)·P(noise valuation > a). This peaks about 0.75σ above fair value, roughly 1.7 above, so the ask is about **5.1**.

**Bid:** Any bid above 2 can be hit by an informed trader holding a value of 2, and I lose on that trade. Weighing noise profit against informed losses gives the highest expected profit at a bid of about **1.7**.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 5.1}

Card 1 is a 4, so the contract settles at 4 unless a 2 or 3 is dealt among the two hidden cards. The settlement value can only be 2, 3 or 4.

**Fair value.** After removing the 4, 21 cards remain. Five of them are below 4 (two 2s and three 3s), and 16 are 4 or higher. Two cards are drawn from the 21, which gives C(21,2) = 210 equally likely pairs.
- Settles at 4: neither card is below 4. That is C(16,2) = 120 pairs, probability 120/210.
- Settles at 2: at least one card is a 2. That is 210 − C(19,2) = 39 pairs, probability 39/210.
- Settles at 3: no 2 but at least one 3. That is 171 − 120 = 51 pairs, probability 51/210.
- Expected value = (39·2 + 51·3 + 120·4)/210 = 711/210 ≈ **3.39**.

**Ask.** An informed trader never values the contract above 4. Any ask of 4.0 or higher can therefore only be hit by noise traders, whose valuations are fair value plus noise with standard deviation 2.3. Expected profit per quote is 0.8 × P(a noise trader buys) × (ask − 3.39):

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 4.0 | 0.19 |
| 4.5 | 0.28 |
| 5.0 | 0.31 |
| 5.5 | 0.30 |

This is close to its maximum around 5.0, so I ask 5.0.

**Bid.** At a bid of 2.0 or lower, an informed trader never sells, because its lowest possible valuation is 2. Expected profit from noise traders is 0.8 × P(a noise trader sells) × (3.39 − bid):

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 2.0 | 0.30 |
| 1.9 | 0.307 |
| 1.5 | 0.31 |

The curve is flat between about 1.5 and 1.9, so I bid 1.8.

{"bid": 1.8, "ask": 5.0}

Card 3 comes from the 20 remaining cards. The contract settles at 4 unless card 3 is below 4.

- P(card 3 = 2) = 2/20 = 0.10
- P(card 3 = 3) = 3/20 = 0.15
- P(settlement = 4) = 15/20 = 0.75

So the fair value is 0.1×2 + 0.15×3 + 0.75×4 = **3.65**.

**Ask side:** settlement can be at most 4, so an informed trader never buys at an ask of 4.0 or higher. Above that level only noise traders buy. Profit from an ask is roughly (ask − 3.65) × P(noise valuation > ask). That is highest about 0.75σ, or 1.7, above fair, so about 5.3–5.4. I'm long, so I lean slightly toward selling and pick 5.3.

**Bid side:** at a bid of 2.0 or less, an informed trader never sells, because a card worth 2 is not below 2. The noise-only optimum is again about 1.7 below fair, at 1.9–2.0. I bid 1.9 to avoid adding to my long position.

{"bid": 1.9, "ask": 5.3}

The contract settles at min(4, card 3), and its fair value is **3.65**. My best quote is a **bid of 2.0** and an **ask of 5.4**.

**Settlement value.** Twenty cards remain:
- Two cards are 2s.
- Three cards are 3s.
- Fifteen cards are 4 or higher, so the contract settles at 4 for any of them.

Expected value = (2·2 + 3·3 + 15·4)/20 = 73/20 = **3.65**.

**Ask side.**
- With an ask at 4 or above, an informed trader never buys, because the most the contract can settle at is 4.
- Against noise traders (fair value 3.65 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 2.3), expected profit per quote is 0.8 × P(valuation > ask) × (ask − 3.65).
- This is largest when the ask is about 0.75 × 2.3 ≈ 1.7 above fair value, which puts it around 5.4.

**Bid side.**
- With a bid of 2.0 or less, an informed trader never sells, because the contract can settle no lower than 2.
- Against noise traders, a bid of 2.0 has an expected profit of about 0.8 × 0.237 × 1.65 ≈ 0.31.
- A bid around 3.0 would trade more often with noise traders, but it gives up about 0.02 when the third card is a 2. Its total is only about 0.18, so the lower bid is better.

My position is +1, so either trade keeps me within the ±3 limit.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 5.4}

game.description: A custom deck of 20 cards is shuffled: 3 cards worth 3, 1 card worth 4, 1 card worth 5, 4 cards worth 7, 2 cards worth 9, 3 cards worth 10, 3 cards worth 11, 3 cards worth 15. 3 cards are dealt face down, without replacement.

info.raw:
Fair value is the expected maximum of 3 cards dealt without replacement from the 20-card deck.

**Distribution of the maximum.** There are C(20,3) = 1140 possible hands. P(max ≤ v) = C(number of cards ≤ v, 3) / 1140.

| Max | Hands | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 1 | 0.001 |
| 4 | 3 | 0.003 |
| 5 | 6 | 0.005 |
| 7 | 74 | 0.065 |

E[max] = 13658 / 1140 ≈ **11.98**.

**Ask side.** An informed trader buys only when the value is 15 (probability 0.40), and I lose 15 − ask on that trade. Noise traders buy when their valuation, 11.98 plus noise with sd 2.7, is above my ask. Expected edge per quote:
- Ask 14.0: about 0.29
- Ask 14.5: about 0.31
- Ask 15.0: about 0.32

The edge is almost flat from 14.5 to 15, so I quote 14.5.

**Bid side.** At bid 10, an informed trader sells only when the value is 9 or less. That happens with probability 0.145, and the average value then is 7.83. Expected edge per quote:

- Bid 9.5: about 0.31

Bid 10 is close to the best and keeps more noise flow, so I quote 10.

| Max value | Probability |

| 15 | 0.40 |
| 11 | 0.28 |
| 10 | 0.17 |
| 9 | 0.07 |
| 7 or less | 0.07 |

**This quote.**
- The bid of 10.5 sits below 11, so if an informed trader sells to me there, the value is 10 or lower.
- The ask of 13.5 is below 15, so I give up 1.5 if an informed trader buys when the value is 15.
- Against that, the spread captures a good share of noise traders, whose valuations spread about 2.7 either side of fair value.

{"bid": 10.5, "ask": 13.5}

Fair value is about 11.3, so I'll quote bid 10.2 and ask 12.8.

**Prior expected value.** The contract pays the maximum of 3 cards drawn from 20. There are C(20,3) = 1140 possible hands. The chance the maximum is v or less is C(number of cards ≤ v, 3) / 1140:

| Max | Probability |
|---|---|
| 3 | 1/1140 |
| 4 | 3/1140 |
| 5 | 6/1140 |
| 7 | 74/1140 |
| 9 | 81/1140 |
| 10 | 199/1140 |
| 11 | 316/1140 |
| 15 | 460/1140 |

The expected maximum is 13658 / 1140 ≈ 11.98.

**Update from the trade at quote 2.** Someone sold to me at 10.5.
- If the maximum is 10 or less, an informed trader would sell. The chance of a sale is then 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.29 ≈ 0.43. Here 0.29 is the chance a noise trader values below 10.5.
- If the maximum is above 10, only a noise trader would sell. The chance of a sale is then 0.8 × 0.29 ≈ 0.23.

Reweighting the outcomes by these chances gives a posterior expected value of about 11.3.

**Quote.** I am long one unit, so I shade both prices slightly down. I keep a spread wide enough to cover the risk of trading with an informed counterparty.

{"bid": 10.2, "ask": 12.8}

Card 1 is a 7, so the settlement is max(7, card 2, card 3), with the last two cards drawn from the 19 left in the deck.

**Fair value from the cards alone**

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 7 | 28/171 |
| 9 | 17/171 |
| 10 | 33/171 |
| 11 | 42/171 |
| 15 | 51/171 |

This gives an expected value of about 11.15.

**Adjusting for the stage-1 trades**

Counterparties sold to me twice in stage 1, at 10.5 and 10.2. Those sales are more likely if the true settlement is 10 or less. A rough Bayesian update puts the probability of a settlement of 10 or less at about 0.6 to 0.7. That pulls the public fair value down to roughly 10.2 to 10.6.

**Quote**

I am long 2 units, so I skew both sides down to make selling more likely and buying less likely. I keep the ask just below 11. An informed trader will only buy there if the settlement is 11 or 15.

{"bid": 9.0, "ask": 10.9}

Card 1 is a 7. That leaves 19 cards: eight are 7 or lower, two are 9s, three are 10s, three are 11s and three are 15s.

**Distribution of the maximum.** Cards 2 and 3 are two of those 19 cards, so there are C(19,2) = 171 possible pairs. The maximum is the largest of the 7 and those two cards.

| Max | Probability |
|---|---|
| 7 | 28/171 |
| 9 | 17/171 |
| 10 | 33/171 |
| 11 | 42/171 |
| 15 | 51/171 |

E[max] = 1906/171 ≈ 11.15.

**Adjusting for trading history.** At quote 4 nobody traded at 9 / 10.9, which pulls the estimate slightly down. The stage-1 sells may also carry a little downside information about cards 2 and 3. I put fair value at about 11.0.

**Position.** I'm long 2 and close to the +3 limit. So I lean the quotes downward to encourage selling and discourage more buying. The ask stays around fair value so that a noise buyer is likely to take it. That accepts the risk of selling to an informed trader when the value is 15.

{"bid": 9.5, "ask": 11.5}

Fair value given card 1 = 7 is about 11.15, and the last trade (a buy at 11.5) nudges it to roughly 11.3. I'm quoting bid 9.6 and ask 12.4, skewed slightly low because I'm already long 1.

**Fair value.** The settlement is the max of 7 and the two hidden cards, drawn from the 19 remaining cards. Taking 171 equally likely pairs of hidden cards:

| Settlement value | Pairs | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | 28 | 0.16 |
| 9 | 17 | 0.10 |
| 10 | 33 | 0.19 |
| 11 | 42 | 0.25 |
| 15 | 51 | 0.30 |

- The expected settlement is 1906 / 171 ≈ 11.15.
- Someone bought at 11.5, which leans slightly upward, so I put fair at about 11.3.

**Bid at 9.6.** An informed trader only sells here if the value is 9 or below, which has probability 0.26. That limits adverse selection while still catching noise sellers. The slightly low bid also makes it less likely I add to my long position.

{"bid": 9.6, "ask": 12.4}

Fair value is about 9.5. My quotes are skewed slightly away from the informed traders' likely exits.

**Prior.** With 7 and 5 revealed, the settlement value is max(7, card 3). Card 3 comes from the 18 remaining cards:

| Settlement value | Cards | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 7 | 7 | 7/18 |
| 9 | 2 | 2/18 |
| 10 | 3 | 3/18 |
| 11 | 3 | 3/18 |
| 15 | 3 | 3/18 |

The prior expected value is 175/18 ≈ 9.72.

- In stage 1, they sold to me at 10.5 and 10.2. That favours settlement values of 10 or below.
- In stage 2, they bought from me at 11.5 and 12.4. That favours 15.
- Quote 4 (bid 9, ask 10.9) had no trade. That slightly favours 9 or 10.

A rough Bayesian update gives a posterior of about 9.4. Blending that with the prior, I put fair value at about 9.5.

**Quote.** I'll quote around that value with a moderate spread:
- An informed trader holding 7 sells to me at my bid, and the posterior chance of 7 is about 35%, so I keep the bid low.

{"bid": 8.4, "ask": 10.9}

Card 1 is 7 and card 2 is 5, so the contract settles at max(7, card 3).

**Prior for card 3.** 18 cards remain: seven are 7 or lower (value 7), two are 9, three are 10, three are 11 and three are 15.
- Expected value = (7×7 + 2×9 + 3×10 + 3×11 + 3×15) / 18 = 175/18 ≈ 9.72.

**Update from quote 7.** Someone sold to me at 8.4.
- An informed trader sells at 8.4 only if the value is 7.
- A noise trader sells with probability Φ((8.4 − 9.72)/2.7) ≈ 0.31.
- So the chance of that sale is about 0.2 + 0.8×0.31 = 0.45 if the value is 7, and 0.8×0.31 = 0.25 otherwise.

| Value | Posterior probability |
|---|---|
| 7 | 0.53 |
| 9 | 0.085 |
| 10 | 0.127 |
| 11 | 0.127 |
| 15 | 0.127 |

The new fair value is about 9.08.

**Ask.** I compared expected profit at several levels:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 10.5 | ≈ 0.21 |
| 11.1 | ≈ 0.27 |
| 11.5 | ≈ 0.27 |

The curve is flat from about 11.1 to 11.5, so I'll ask 11.3.

**Bid.** A bid of 7.0 means an informed trader holding a 7 will not sell, since its valuation is not below the bid. Expected profit is about 0.37, better than 0.19 at a bid of 8.0 and 0.30 at 7.5.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 11.3}

Ask 12.0 and bid 7.0. These are the levels that maximise expected profit on this last quote.

**Settlement distribution.** The deck now holds 18 cards (one 7 and one 5 are out). The contract settles at the larger of 7 and card 3.
- It settles at 7 with probability 7/18 (card 3 is a 3, 4 or 7).
- Otherwise it settles at 9 (2/18), 10 (3/18), 11 (3/18) or 15 (3/18).
- The expected value is 175/18 ≈ 9.72. I treat this as the public fair value.

**Ask side.** Expected profit from selling at each ask:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 11.2 | ≈ 0.22 |
| 12.0 | ≈ 0.26 |
| 12.5 | ≈ 0.25 |

The best ask is around 12.0. At that level the informed loss comes only from the 15s, and noise traders still buy fairly often.

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 8.0 | ≈ 0.28 |
| 7.5 | ≈ 0.33 |
| 7.0 | ≈ 0.34 |

The best bid is 7.0. At 7.0 an informed trader never sells to me at a loss, because the settlement value is never below 7.
