- This is largest near d ≈ 1.3, giving an ask of 4.3 and an expected profit of about 0.19.

**Bid side:** the same logic applies in reverse.
- A bid at or below 2.0 means an informed trader never sells, since the least the contract can settle at is 2.
- The best bid is therefore 1.7.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
With no flips revealed, the coin is fair or always-heads with equal odds. That puts the expected number of heads at ½·3 + ½·6 = **4.5**.

**Ask side**
- About half the time the true value is 6, because the coin is always-heads.
- An informed buyer only trades if my ask is below the true value.
- So an ask at or above 6 avoids losing to informed buyers. Above that point I only give up some noise-trader volume.
- Expected profit per quote:
  - Ask 6.0: about 0.34
  - Ask 6.5: about 0.35
  - Ask 7.0: about 0.34
- I'll ask **6.5**.

**Bid side**
- If the coin is fair, the value follows Binomial(6, 0.5). Low outcomes are fairly rare.
- Expected profit per quote:
  - Bid 3.0: about 0.29
  - Bid 2.5: about 0.32
  - Bid 2.0: about 0.33
- The curve is flat between 2.0 and 2.5, so I'll bid **2.3**.

{"bid": 2.3, "ask": 6.5}

Fair value is about 4.5 before any reveals. With probability 1/2 the coin is biased and settles at 6. Otherwise settlement follows Bin(6, 0.5), with mean 3. The earlier no-trade at 2.3 / 6.5 tells us almost nothing, so I keep fair value at about 4.5.

**Ask side.** An informed buyer only buys if the value is above my ask, and the value can never exceed 6.
- At an ask of 6.0 or higher, informed traders never buy from me, so only noise traders trade there.
- Expected profit per quote is about 0.34 at 6.0, about 0.35 at 6.2 to 6.5, and only about 0.23 at 5.5.
- Expected profit is flat across 6.2 to 6.5, so I quote **6.3**.

**Bid side.** An informed seller only sells if the true value is below my bid.
- At 3.0, informed traders sell when the value is 2 or less (probability about 0.17), costing about 1.36 each time. Noise traders pay me about 0.34 per quote, so the net is about +0.29.
- At 2.5 the net is about +0.32.
- At 3.5 the net is about +0.20, because informed sellers now include value 3.

I quote the bid at about **2.7**.

{"bid": 2.7, "ask": 6.3}

The coin is now probably the biased one, so I'm quoting a low bid and a wide ask around a fair value of 5.6.

**Posterior on the coin.** Two heads are 4 times as likely under the always-heads coin (likelihood 1) as under the fair coin (likelihood 1/4). So P(biased) = 1 / (1 + 0.25) = 0.8.

**Settlement distribution.** The two revealed heads count for 2, and four flips remain.
- If the coin is biased (prob 0.8), the settlement is 6.
- If the coin is fair (prob 0.2), the settlement is 2 + Binomial(4, 0.5).
- That gives P(6) ≈ 0.8125, P(5) = 0.05, P(4) = 0.075, P(3) = 0.05 and P(2) = 0.0125.
- Fair value = 2 + 0.8·4 + 0.2·2 = 5.6.

**Ask.** The settlement can't exceed 6, so an informed trader never buys at an ask above 6. A sale therefore only happens with a noise trader, at a profit of (ask − 5.6). Expected profit is 0.8 · P(noise valuation > ask) · (ask − 5.6):
- ask 6.5: about 0.26
- ask 7.0: about 0.33
- ask 7.5: about 0.35
- ask 8.0: about 0.34

So I'll post an ask of about 7.5.

**Bid.** Noise sellers earn me (5.6 − bid) per unit. Informed sellers only sell when the settlement value is below my bid, and the low outcomes are rare. Expected profit:
- bid 3.0: about 0.33
- bid 3.5: about 0.34
- bid 4.0: about 0.33
- bid 4.5: about 0.27

So I'll post a bid of about 3.5.

{"bid": 3.5, "ask": 7.5}

The fair value is still 5.6, and I'm quoting bid 3.6, ask 7.5.

**Posterior after flips 1 and 2 both came up heads**
- If the coin is fair, two heads has likelihood 1/4. If it always lands heads, the likelihood is 1.
- So P(always-heads coin) = 1 / (1 + 1/4) = 0.8, and P(fair coin) = 0.2.

**Settlement distribution** (settlement = 2 + heads in flips 3–6)
- Always-heads coin: settles at 6 (probability 0.8).
- Fair coin: settles at 2 to 6, each multiplied by 0.2:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 2 | 0.0125 |
| 3 | 0.05 |
| 4 | 0.075 |
| 5 | 0.05 |
| 6 | 0.0125 + 0.8 = 0.8125 |

- Fair value = 0.8 × 6 + 0.2 × 4 = 5.6.
- The last buyer paid 7.5, which is above the maximum possible settlement of 6. An informed trader would never do that, so it was a noise trader. The fair value therefore stays at 5.6.

**Ask side**
- Any ask of 6 or more is never hit by informed traders.
- Expected profit = 0.8 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 5.6), with noise valuation ~ Normal(5.6, 2.6).

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 7.0 | 0.331 |
| 7.5 | 0.353 |
| 7.8 | 0.350 |
| 8.0 | 0.342 |

- The best ask is about 7.5.

**Bid side**
- Informed traders sell only when the settlement value is below my bid.
- A bid above 4 would let them sell whenever the value is 4, so the bid should stay below 4.

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 3.0 | 0.328 |
| 3.5 | 0.343 |
| 3.6 | 0.344 |
| 3.9 | 0.335 |

- The best bid is about 3.6.

My position is −1, comfortably inside the limits.

{"bid": 3.6, "ask": 7.5}

The public fair value is about 5.94, and I'm quoting a wide spread around it: bid 4.0, ask 7.9.

**Posterior on the coin.** After four heads, the chance of that sequence is 1/16 for the fair coin and 1 for the always-heads coin. Starting from 1/2 each, P(always-heads) = 16/17 and P(fair) = 1/17.

**Settlement distribution.** Settlement is 4 plus the heads in flips 5 and 6.
- It is 6 with probability 65/68.
- It is 5 with probability 2/68.
- It is 4 with probability 1/68.
- The expected value is 4 + (16/17)·2 + (1/17)·1 ≈ 5.94.

**Trading history.** The buy at 7.5 in stage 2 tells us nothing about the coin. The maximum possible settlement is 6, so an informed trader would never pay 7.5. That trade must have been noise, and the public fair value stays about 5.94.

**Ask.** The informed trader's value is at most 6, so any ask at or above 6.0 is never lifted by them. Against noise traders, I want the ask that maximises the margin above 5.94 times the chance a noise trader's valuation is higher. That peaks about 0.75 standard deviations above fair, roughly 1.95 points, so the ask is about 7.9.

**Bid.** The same calculation puts the bid about 1.95 below fair, so 4.0. The informed trader only sells if their value is strictly below my bid, and the settlement can never be below 4. So at 4.0 informed traders never hit me. A noise sale here also cuts my short position.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 7.9}

Quote **bid 4.0 / ask 7.9**. These are the same levels as quote 5.

**Posterior on the coin.** After four heads, the likelihood is 1 for the always-heads coin and 1/16 for the fair coin. So:
- P(always-heads coin) = 16/17
- P(fair coin) = 1/17

**Settlement distribution.** Settlement is 4 plus the heads in flips 5 and 6.
- Always-heads coin: settles at 6.
- Fair coin: settles at 4, 5 or 6 with probability 1/4, 1/2, 1/4.
- Overall: 6 with probability 65/68, 5 with probability 2/68, 4 with probability 1/68.
- Expected value is 101/17 ≈ 5.94.

**Ask.** At an ask of 6 or above, an informed trader never buys, because the value cannot exceed 6. So only noise traders hit the ask. Their valuations are centred on 5.94 with standard deviation 2.6.
- Expected profit on the ask is proportional to z·(1 − Φ(z)), where z is the ask's distance above fair value in standard deviations.
- That peaks at z ≈ 0.75, which gives an ask of about 5.94 + 1.95 ≈ 7.9.

**Bid.** The same calculation on the bid side puts the optimum at about 5.94 − 1.95 ≈ 4.0.
- At a bid of 4.0, an informed trader only sells if the value is strictly below 4, which is impossible. So there is no adverse selection on this side.
- Moving the bid up to 4.1 lowers the expected profit slightly.

**Position.** Being short 1 unit doesn't change the optimal quote, because profit is judged on expectation and the position limits aren't binding.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 7.9}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Before any flips are revealed, the expected settlement is 0.5 × 3 + 0.5 × 6 = 4.5. A fair coin averages 3 heads and a two-headed coin always gives 6.

**Ask side**
- If my ask is at 6 or higher, an informed trader never buys, because the value can't exceed 6.
- Expected profit per quote comes only from noise traders: 0.8 × P(noise buys) × (ask − 4.5).

| Ask | Expected profit |
|-----|-----------------|
| 6.0 | 0.34 |
| 6.5 | 0.35 |
| 7.0 | 0.34 |

I pick 6.5.

**Bid side**
- An informed trader sells only when the value is below my bid. With a low bid, that can only happen with a fair coin and very few heads, which is rare.

| Bid | Expected profit |
|-----|-----------------|
| 3.0 | 0.29 |
| 2.5 | 0.32 |
| 2.0 | 0.32 |

I pick 2.5.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 6.5}

Prior expected value is 4.5: the coin is fair with probability 1/2 (mean 3 heads) and always heads with probability 1/2 (6 heads). The settlement value is 6 with probability about 0.51; otherwise it is spread over 0 to 5.

**Ask side.** Below 6, informed buyers win whenever the true value is 6. That cost is set against profit from noise traders, whose valuations centre on 4.5 with standard deviation 2.6. Expected profit per quote is about:
- 0.23 at an ask of 5.5
- 0.34 at 6.0
- 0.35 at 6.5
- 0.34 at 7.0

The curve is flat from about 6.0 to 7.0, so the exact ask matters little.

**Bid side.** Informed sellers hurt most when the true value is 3 or below, and that is fairly likely. Expected profit per quote is about:
- 0.20 at a bid of 3.5
- 0.29 at 3.0
- 0.32 at 2.5
- 0.32 at 2.0

This is also flat, from about 2.0 to 2.5.

Last quote's 2.5 / 6.5 got no trade, which tells us little. I'll tighten slightly within the flat region, to 2.6 and 6.3, to improve the chance of a fill.

{"bid": 2.6, "ask": 6.3}

Two heads moves the odds strongly toward the always-heads coin, so I'm quoting wide on both sides.

**Fair value after two heads**
- The chance the coin is the always-heads coin is 1 ÷ (1 + 1/4) = 0.8.
- The chance it is the fair coin is 0.2.
- Expected heads = 2 + 4 × (0.8 × 1 + 0.2 × 0.5) = **5.6**.

**Settlement distribution**

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 6 | 0.8125 |
| 5 | 0.05 |
| 4 | 0.075 |
| 3 | 0.05 |
| 2 | 0.0125 |

**Ask side**
- Settlement can never exceed 6. With any ask of 6 or more, an informed trader never buys from me.
- Only noise traders buy, at a valuation of 5.6 plus noise with standard deviation 2.6.
- Let x be the ask minus 5.6. Expected profit is 0.8 × x × P(noise > x).
- This peaks around x ≈ 1.7 to 1.9, which is an ask near 7.3 to 7.5.

**Bid side**
- A bid near 3.9 earns about 0.35 per quote from noise sellers.
- Informed sellers only hit it when settlement is 3 or 2, which costs about 0.014 per quote.
- Net expected profit is about 0.335 per quote.

{"bid": 3.9, "ask": 7.3}

Fair value after two heads is about 5.6. I'm quoting bid 3.8 and ask 7.4, both about 1.8 away from it.

**Fair value**
- Before any flips, each coin type has probability 1/2.
- Two heads have likelihood 1/4 under the fair coin and 1 under the two-headed coin.
- So P(two-headed coin) = 0.5 / (0.5 + 0.125) = 0.8, and P(fair coin) = 0.2.
- Fair value = 2 + 4 × (0.8 × 1 + 0.2 × 0.5) = 2 + 4 × 0.9 = **5.6**.
- The earlier no-trade quotes add very little information, so I take the public fair value as about 5.6.

**Possible settlement values**
- 6 with probability 0.8125 (0.8 from the two-headed coin plus 0.2 × 1/16 from the fair coin).
- 5 with probability 0.05, 4 with 0.075, 3 with 0.05, and 2 with 0.0125.

**Ask side**
- The settlement value is at most 6, so an informed trader never buys at any ask of 6 or above.
- The profit therefore comes only from noise traders: 0.8 × P(noise > ask − 5.6) × (ask − 5.6).
- This is highest for an ask around 7.4 to 7.5, at about 0.35 per quote.

**Bid side**
- Noise traders give 0.8 × P(noise < bid − 5.6) × (5.6 − bid).
- An informed trader sells only when the true value is below my bid, which costs me money.
- Netting the two, the expected profit is flat at about 0.34 for bids from 3.5 to 3.9.

{"bid": 3.8, "ask": 7.4}

With 4 heads in 4 flips, I put the fair value at about **5.94** and quote a bid of **4.0** and an ask of **7.9**.

**Fair value**
- Chance of the fair coin given four heads: 0.5 × (1/16) against 0.5 × 1 for the double-headed coin, so 1/17. The double-headed coin has 16/17.
- Expected heads in flips 5 and 6: (16/17) × 2 + (1/17) × 1 = 33/17 ≈ 1.94.
- Fair value = 4 + 1.94 ≈ **5.94**.
- Settlement can only be 4, 5 or 6. The chances are about 1.5%, 2.9% and 95.6%.

**The buy at 7.4 at quote 4**
- The settlement value can never exceed 6.
- An informed counterparty would never pay 7.4, so that buyer must have been a noise trader.
- It tells us nothing about the coin.

**Quote**
- **Ask:** an informed trader never buys at any ask of 6.0 or above, so only noise traders hit it. The best edge against noise with spread 2.6 is about 0.75 × 2.6 ≈ 1.95 above fair value, which gives 7.9.
- **Bid:** the lowest possible value is 4. At a bid of 4.0 an informed trader would only sell if the value were below 4, which can't happen, so the bid can never be hit by an informed trader. It also sits about 1.95 below fair value, which is the best edge against noise traders.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 7.9}

With four heads in a row, the coin is very likely the always-heads one. Fair value is about 5.94.

**Posterior on the coin.**
- P(always-heads | four heads) = 0.5 / (0.5 + 0.5 × 1/16) = 16/17.
- The expected settlement value is 4 + (16/17)·2 + (1/17)·1 ≈ 5.94.

**Distribution of the settlement value.**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 6 | ≈ 0.956 |
| 5 | ≈ 0.029 |
| 4 | ≈ 0.015 |

**Earlier trades.** Neither earlier trade tells us anything about the coin.
- The buy at 7.4 can't have been informed, because the value is at most 6.
- The sell at 4 can't have been informed, because the value is at least 4.

So the public fair value stays at about 5.94.

**Choosing the ask.**
- Any ask at or above 6.0 means an informed trader never buys from me.
- Against noise traders, I maximise (a − 5.94)·P(Z > (a − 5.94)/2.6). The best markup is about 0.75σ ≈ 1.95, which gives an ask of about 7.9.

**Choosing the bid.**
- A bid at or below 4.0 means an informed trader never sells to me.
- The same calculation puts the best bid at 5.94 − 1.95 ≈ 4.0.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 7.9}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Expected settlement value is 0.5·3 + 0.5·6 = 4.5. The distribution is very skewed: the settlement is 6 with probability about 0.51, and otherwise it follows Binomial(6, 0.5).

**Ask side:** An informed trader only buys if the value is strictly above my ask. At an ask of 6.0 the most an informed trader can value it at is 6, so it never buys. That means an ask of 6.0 carries no adverse selection. It still earns about 0.18 per quote from noise traders, and that was the best expected profit of the asks I checked.

**Bid side:** Low bids are where informed sellers hurt me, because values of 0–3 are reasonably likely. Bids between about 2.5 and 3.0 give roughly the same expected profit, about 0.10 per quote. I'll pick 2.8.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 6.0}

The prior expected settlement is 4.5. With probability 1/2 the coin is fair, giving Binomial(6, 0.5) with mean 3. With probability 1/2 it always lands heads, giving 6.

**Updating on quote 1.** The counterparty sold at 2.8.
- An informed trader sells only if the value is 2 or less. That has prior probability 22/128 ≈ 0.17.
- A noise trader sells with probability Φ((2.8 − 4.5)/1.7) = Φ(−1) ≈ 0.16, whatever the true value.

Applying Bayes, the posterior distribution of the value is:

| Value | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 0.02 | 0.13 | 0.33 | 0.10 | 0.07 | 0.03 | 0.32 |

The posterior mean is about 3.44, which is the new public fair value.

**Ask.** About 32% of the posterior sits at 6, so any ask below 6 gets picked off by informed buyers when the value is 6. Expected profit per quote is roughly 0.111 at an ask of 6.0 and 0.107 at 5.9. I'll quote 5.9 because selling also helps unwind my long position.

**Bid.** Expected profit is about 0.128 at a bid of 1.9. It falls to about 0.03 at 2.5, where informed sellers holding values of 0–2 start to hurt.

{"bid": 1.9, "ask": 5.9}

Fair value is now about 3.2, down from a prior of 4.5. The bid is 2.0 and the ask 5.5.

**Prior.** The fair coin (P(heads) = 0.5) and the two-headed coin are equally likely. With the two-headed coin, all 6 flips are heads and the value is 6. So P(6) ≈ 0.51, and the remaining probability follows a binomial spread centred on 3. That gives a prior mean of 4.5.

**Update from quote 1 (they sold at 2.8).**
- An informed trader would only sell at 2.8 if the value is 2 or less.
- A noise trader sells about 16% of the time, since 2.8 is one standard deviation below 4.5.
- Updating on this lowers the fair value to about 3.45.

**Update from quote 2 (no trade at 1.9 / 5.9).**
- An informed trader would not trade only if the value is between 2 and 5.
- A noise trader centred on 3.45 would not trade about 74% of the time.
- Updating on this lowers the fair value to about 3.2.

**Posterior.** The distribution has two peaks: about 0.40 at a value of 2 and about 0.23 at a value of 6. The values 3, 4 and 5 together carry about 0.25, and 0 or 1 about 0.11.

**Choosing the quotes.** For each candidate price I weighed profit from noise traders against expected losses to informed traders.
- **Ask:** any price from about 5.1 to 5.9 gives roughly the same expected value, about 0.09 per quote. I picked 5.5 in the middle of that range.
- **Bid:** around 1.5 to 2.0 gives about 0.14–0.15 per quote, against about 0.10 at 2.5. At 2.0, an informed trader only sells if the value is 0 or 1, which has low probability.
- **Inventory:** a long position of +1 is no constraint, so there is no need to skew the quotes.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 5.5}

After flips 1 and 2 both came up heads, the biased coin is more likely than the fair one. The stage-1 trade and two no-trades point back toward the fair coin, so fair value is about **5.1**, with high uncertainty.

**Coin from the flips alone.** Two heads are 4 times more likely with the always-heads coin (1 vs 0.25). That gives P(biased) = 0.8.

**Adjusting for the trading history.** Each quote changes the odds by how likely the observed outcome was under each coin.
- **Quote 1 (sold at 2.8):** an informed seller only sells this low if the value is 2, which can only happen with the fair coin. Noise sellers are equally likely either way. This slightly favours the fair coin (about 1.2×).
- **Quotes 2 and 3 (no trade):** with the biased coin the value is 6. An informed trader would then have bought at asks of 5.9 and 5.5, so the no-trades favour the fair coin (about 1.7× each).
- **Result:** P(biased) is about 0.53.

**Fair value.** The two revealed heads count for 2.
- If biased, the remaining 4 flips are all heads.
- If fair, they average about 2 heads.
- So fair value ≈ 2 + 0.53 × 4 + 0.47 × 2 ≈ **5.1**.

**Settlement range.** The value is 6 with probability about 0.56. Otherwise it is mostly between 3 and 5.

**Quote.**
- **Ask 5.9:** if the value is 6, an informed buyer costs me only 0.1. Noise buyers still trade with useful frequency.
- **Bid 4.0:** an informed trader only sells to me there when the value is 3 or less, which is fairly unlikely.
- My small long position is fine to hold.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 5.9}

The contract is probably worth about 5.4, so I'll quote a bid of 4.0 and an ask of 6.0.

**Fair value**
- Two heads move the probability that the coin is two-headed from 1/2 to 0.8. Its likelihood is 1, against 1/4 for a fair coin.
- At quote 4 I quoted 4.0 / 5.9 and nobody traded. If the coin were two-headed, an informed trader would know the value is 6 and would have bought at 5.9. The lack of a trade pulls the probability down to about 0.68.
- A fair coin would leave the total spread from 2 to 6, so its expected value given the no-trade is about 4.2.
- Combined, the fair value is about 0.68 × 6 + 0.32 × 4.2 ≈ 5.43.

**Ask**
- The settlement value can never exceed 6, so selling at 6.0 can't lose money.
- An ask of 5.9 would lose 0.1 to every informed trader holding a two-headed coin.
- An ask of 6.0 still catches noise traders who value it above 6, about 37% of them, earning about 0.57 each. That works out to roughly +0.14 per quote.

**Bid**
- An informed seller only hurts me when the true value is below my bid.
- At a bid of 4.0, the only losses come from fair-coin totals of 2 or 3, which are rare. Noise sellers below 4.0 earn about 1.4 each.
- This gave the highest expected profit of the bids I checked, about +0.16, compared with +0.14 at 4.5 and about 0 at 5.0.
- My position of +1 leaves plenty of room to buy.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 6.0}

Two heads make the biased coin likely: P(biased) = 0.8, so the naive fair value is 2 + 4 × 0.9 = 5.6. The trading history pulls that down a lot:

- **Quotes 2–4:** an informed trader whose value was 6 would have bought at my asks of 5.9, 5.5 and 5.9. Nobody bought, three times.
- **Quote 5:** someone sold at 4, which is most consistent with an informed trader whose value was 2 or 3.
- **Quote 1:** someone sold at 2.8 in stage 1, which also points towards a value of 2.

Updating on all of this, the value is spread fairly evenly from 2 to 6, with an expected value of about 4.0 to 4.3. The uncertainty is large, so I quote a fairly wide spread around about 4.1. I am long 2 units, but I am risk-neutral and that is well within the limit, so I am not skewing the quote.

{"bid": 3.1, "ask": 5.1}

The tails on flips 3 and 4 rule out the always-heads coin, so the coin is fair.

**Settlement value.** Two heads are already counted. The last two flips are fair, so the settlement is 2 + Binomial(2, ½):

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 2 | 1/4 |
| 3 | 1/2 |
| 4 | 1/4 |

Fair value is 3.

**Informed traders.** An informed trader values the contract at exactly 2, 3 or 4. If my bid is at or below 2 and my ask is at or above 4, they never trade with me. With a bid of 2, a trader valuing at 2 does not sell, because 2 is not below the bid.

**Noise traders.** Their valuation is 3 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 1.7. If I quote symmetrically at 3 ± d, the expected edge is about 0.65 × 2 × d × Φ(−d/1.7):

| d | Expected edge |
|---|---|
| 1.0 | 0.36 |
| 1.2 | 0.37 |
| 1.3 | 0.37 |

The edge is flat across d = 1.2 to 1.3. Any tighter quote would let informed traders trade against me. A quote of 1.8 / 4.2 earns roughly the maximum and takes no adverse-selection losses. My long position of +2 is well inside the limits, so I don't need to skew the quote.

{"bid": 1.8, "ask": 4.2}

Flips 3 and 4 came up tails, so the coin must be the fair one. That leaves 2 heads so far, with flips 5 and 6 each heads at 0.5. Settlement is therefore 2, 3 or 4, with probabilities 0.25, 0.5 and 0.25, and fair value is 3.

**Ask side.** An informed trader can only buy profitably if the value is 4. If my ask is 4.0 or higher, they never buy, because they buy only when their valuation is strictly above my ask. So above 4.0, my only counterparties on the ask are noise traders, whose valuations are 3 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 1.7.

My expected profit from the ask is 0.65 × (ask − 3) × P(noise valuation > ask). Checking a few asks:
- At 4.0 the expected profit is about 0.181.
- At 4.3 it is about 0.188.
- At 4.4 it is about 0.187.
- At 4.5 it is about 0.184.

The maximum is around 4.3.

**Bid side.** The situation mirrors the ask around fair value 3, so the best bid is around 1.7.

My +2 position doesn't change this. Expected profit doesn't depend on inventory here, and neither side is near the ±5 limit.

{"bid": 1.7, "ask": 4.3}

The value is now pinned down, so I set each side to maximise its own expected edge on this final quote.

**Settlement distribution**
- Flips 3 and 4 came up tails, which a coin with P(heads) = 1 can never do. So the coin must be the fair one.

info.raw:
The contract's fair value before any reveal is **4.5**, and I quote **bid 2.8, ask 6.0**.

**Fair value.** The coin is fair with probability ½, giving an expected 3 heads. It always lands heads with probability ½, giving 6 heads. So the fair value is ½·3 + ½·6 = **4.5**.

**Settlement distribution.**
- It is 6 with probability ½ + ½·(1/64) ≈ 0.508.
- Otherwise it follows half of a Binomial(6, ½).
- So P(V ≤ 3) ≈ 0.33, P(V = 4) ≈ 0.12 and P(V = 5) ≈ 0.05.

**Ask side.**
- Any ask below 6 is lifted by informed traders about 51% of the time, and each of those trades loses money.
- An ask of 6.0 can never lose to an informed trader.
- Noise traders still lift it about 19% of the time, for a gain of 1.5 each time.
- Expected profit is about **+0.18** per quote, which is close to the best available.

**Bid side.**

| Bid | Expected informed loss | Expected noise gain | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3.0 | ≈0.08 | ≈0.18 | ≈0.10 |
| 2.8 | ≈0.07 | ≈0.175 | **≈0.105** |
| 2.5 | ≈0.05 | ≈0.16 | ≈0.10 |

A bid of 2.8 is about the best.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 6.0}

**Prior.** Half the time the coin is fair and the heads count is Binomial(6, 0.5), with mean 3. The other half it is double-headed and settles at 6. So the prior mean is 4.5.

**Update from the sale at 2.8.**
- An informed trader sells only if the value is 2 or less.
- A noise trader sells if 4.5 + noise < 2.8, which happens with probability about 0.16.
- After weighting by these sell probabilities, the posterior is roughly:
  - Value 6: 0.32
  - Value 2: 0.33
  - Value 1: 0.13
  - Values 0, 3, 4 and 5 make up the rest.

**Ask.** For an informed buyer to profit, the value must be above my ask. In practice that means the value is 6, with probability 0.32. An ask near 5.9–6.0 almost eliminates that loss and still earns about 2.5 per noise buy. Its expected value is about +0.11 per quote, the best of the asks I checked.

| Value | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |

| Probability | 0.08 | 0.57 | 0.19 | 0.13 | 0.03 |

| Ask | Expected profit |

| 3.9 | ≈ 0.14 |

- I'm at −1, so either trade keeps me well within the ±4 limit.

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.5 with probability 1/2, P(heads) = 1 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Before any flips are revealed, the expected settlement is 0.5×3 + 0.5×6 = 4.5. The value distribution is lopsided, though. There is about a 51% chance the settlement is exactly 6 (biased coin, or a fair coin landing six heads). The rest of the probability follows a fair-coin binomial spread over 0–5.

**Ask side:** An informed buyer gains whenever the settlement is 6 and my ask is below it. So my loss to them shrinks as the ask approaches 6. Noise traders value the contract at 4.5 plus noise with standard deviation 1.3, so they still buy fairly often around 5.8–6.0. Weighing the informed loss against the noise-trader profit, the expected profit peaks at an ask of about 5.9, worth roughly +0.11 per quote.

**Bid side:** Informed sellers only appear when the settlement is low, and low outcomes come from the fair-coin binomial. Near 4 these losses outweigh the noise-trader gains. Around 3.0 the bid is modestly profitable, at about +0.04 per quote.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 5.9}

The one trade so far, a sell at 3, pulls the fair value down to about **3.3**. I quote a bid of **2.0** and an ask of **5.5**.

**Prior.** The coin is fair with probability ½, in which case heads follow a Binomial(6, 0.5). Otherwise it always lands heads, giving 6. The prior mean is 4.5.

**Updating on the sell at 3.**
- An informed trader sells only if the value is below 3, meaning 0, 1 or 2 heads.
- A noise trader (fair value 4.5) sells only if its noise is below −1.5. That happens with probability about 0.125.
- So the chance of seeing this sell is about 0.43 if the value is 0–2, and about 0.08 otherwise.

| Heads | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Posterior probability | 0.024 | 0.143 | 0.358 | 0.090 | 0.067 | 0.027 | 0.291 |

The posterior mean, and so the public fair value, is about 3.28. The distribution is bimodal, with mass around 2 and at 6. That makes quotes near the mean costly, because informed traders hit them often.

**Choosing the quotes.** Each line is the expected gain from noise traders minus the expected loss to informed traders.
- **Ask 5.5:** noise buys gain about 0.063. Informed buys only when the value is 6, losing about 0.051. Net is about +0.01. Asks of 5.3 or lower come out roughly flat or worse, and 4.5 is clearly negative.
- **Bid 2.0:** noise sells gain about 0.135. Informed sells when the value is 0–1, losing about 0.067. Net is about +0.07. A bid of 2.5 is negative.
- I am already long 1, which is another reason not to bid higher.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 5.5}

Quote: bid 1.0, ask 6.0. Two sells at low bids (3, then 2) pulled my estimate of fair value from 4.5 down to about 2.4.

**Prior.** With probability 1/2 the coin is fair, so heads follow Binomial(6, 0.5). Otherwise every flip is heads (V = 6). The prior mean is 4.5.

**Updating on the trades.**
- **Quote 1 (sell at 3):** the chance of that sell was about 0.43 if V < 3 and about 0.08 otherwise. The posterior mean falls to about 3.28.
- **Quote 2 (sell at 2):** the chance was about 0.46 if V < 2 and about 0.11 otherwise. The posterior mean falls to about 2.42.

Current posterior:

| V | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 0.07 | 0.40 | 0.23 | 0.06 | 0.04 | 0.02 | 0.19 |

**Ask side.** The 19% mass at V = 6 means informed buyers make every reasonable ask lose money:
- Ask 3.5: about −0.04 expected
- Ask 4.5: about −0.03 expected

So I quote the ask at 6.0. No informed trader values the contract above 6, and a noise buyer that high is negligible.

**Bid side.** Expected profit by bid:
- Bid 1.5: about +0.04
- Bid 1.0: about +0.10 (best)
- Bid 0.5: about +0.08

Taking one more unit would put me at +3 long, which is acceptable.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 6.0}

Using Bayes' rule on the revealed flips and the trades so far, the fair value is about **5.4**.

**Coin after two heads.** The chance the coin is the always-heads coin is 1/(1 + 1/4) = 0.8. The chance it is the fair coin is 0.2.

**What the trades tell us.**
- **Quote 1 (sell at 3):** This is informative only about the case where the total is 2. That case needs the fair coin plus four more tails. An informed seller sells there, so a sale raises its probability. It goes from about 0.0125 to about 0.063.
- **Quotes 2 and 3:** These carry no information. The total is at least 2 now, so an informed trader would never sell at 2 or 1 or buy at 6.

**Posterior for the settlement value V:**

| V | Probability |
|---|---|
| 6 | ≈ 0.76 |
| 5 | ≈ 0.05 |
| 4 | ≈ 0.07 |
| 3 | ≈ 0.05 |
| 2 | ≈ 0.06 |

The expected value is about 5.42.

**Ask.** No informed trader buys above 6, since V can't exceed 6. So the ask only trades against noise traders. Expected profit from the ask peaks around 6.3–6.5, at about 0.14 per quote. Selling also cuts my +2 long position.

**Bid.** At 4.0, informed traders hit me only when V ≤ 3. Noise traders sell with probability of about 0.14. Expected profit is about +0.07. I shade the bid slightly lower to 3.9 because I'm already long 2.

{"bid": 3.9, "ask": 6.4}

Public fair value given flips 1–2 = heads and the trade history is about 5.4. Best quotes are bid 4.0 and ask 6.4.

1. **Coin after the reveal.** Two heads give the double-heads coin a 0.8 chance and the fair coin 0.2.

2. **Settlement value from the reveal alone:**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 6 | 0.8125 |
| 5 | 0.05 |
| 4 | 0.075 |
| 3 | 0.05 |
| 2 | 0.0125 |

3. **Stage-1 history.** Counterparties sold at my bids of 3 and 2. An informed trader sells only if the value is below the bid, so those sells raise the odds that the value is 2 by about 5.3 times.

4. **Quote 4 buy.** It said nothing about the value. The maximum possible value is 6, so no informed trader would buy at 6.4.

5. **Updated distribution:**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 6 | 0.77 |
| 5 | 0.05 |
| 4 | 0.07 |
| 3 | 0.05 |
| 2 | 0.06 |

The expected value is about **5.41**.

6. **Ask.** At any ask of 6 or above, informed traders never buy, so only noise traders hit it. The expected profit is roughly flat between 6.2 and 6.6 and highest near 6.4, at about 0.14 per quote. Selling also reduces my +1 long position.

7. **Bid.**
   - At 4.0, informed sellers appear only when the value is 2 or 3 (about 11%). Expected profit is about +0.07.
   - At 4.5 it is about +0.05.
   - At 4.9 it is about breakeven.

   Since I am already long 1, a slightly lower bid is fine, so I bid 4.0.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 6.4}

Fair value is about 5.68, so I'm quoting a bid of 4.5 and an ask of 6.7.

**Posterior after two heads.**
- Before the flips, each coin is equally likely.
- Two heads happen with chance 1 for the always-heads coin and 1/4 for the fair coin.
- So P(always-heads coin) = 1 / (1 + 1/4) = 0.8, and P(fair coin) = 0.2.
- The two flips already shown are 2 heads.
- The four unrevealed flips add an expected 4 heads with the always-heads coin and 2 with the fair coin.
- Expected heads = 2 + 0.8 × 4 + 0.2 × 2 = 5.6.
- The settlement is 6 with probability about 0.81.

**What the trading history tells us.**
- Quote 4, a buy at 6.4: the settlement can never exceed 6, so an informed trader would never buy at 6.4. That buy came from a noise trader and carries no information.
- Quote 5, no trade at 4 / 6.4: an informed trader would have sold at 4 if the settlement were 2 or 3. No trade happened, so those low outcomes become less likely.
- After that update, the public fair value is about 5.68.

**Ask.**
- Informed traders never buy at an ask of 6 or higher, so the ask only faces noise traders.
- Expected profit per quote is highest with the ask somewhere between 6.4 and 7, peaking at about 6.7.

**Bid.**
- Informed traders sell only when the settlement is below the bid, which is unlikely (2, 3 or 4).
- Weighing that loss against the gain from noise sellers, expected profit is roughly 0.10 per quote for any bid from 4.2 to 4.7. I picked 4.5.

My position is +1, well inside the limits, so both sides can be quoted.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 6.7}

The settlement value is now very likely 6, so I quote just under 5 to buy and well above 6 to sell.

**Fair value.** Four heads in a row make the always-heads coin much more likely than the fair coin.
- Probability of four heads with the fair coin is 1/16. With the always-heads coin it is 1.
- So P(always-heads coin) = 16/17 ≈ 0.94.
- Expected heads in the last two flips = 16/17 × 2 + 1/17 × 1 ≈ 1.94.
- Expected settlement is about **5.94**.
- Settlement is 6 with probability about 0.956, 5 with about 0.029, and 4 with about 0.015.
- The trading history adds no information. The buy at 6.4 came from a noise trader, since no settlement value can exceed 6.

**Ask.** An informed trader can only buy if my ask is below 6.
- At an ask of 6.0 or higher, only noise traders buy. Their valuation is centred on 5.94 with standard deviation 1.3.
- An ask of 7.0 fills about 21% of noise traders, for about 1.06 profit each.
- That is roughly the best trade-off between how often it fills and how much each fill earns.

**Bid.** An informed trader sells only if the settlement is 4 or 5, and that happens only about 4% of the time.
- A bid around 4.9–5.0 catches about 21–23% of noise traders, for about 1 of profit each.
- The expected loss to informed sellers at that level is very small.

{"bid": 4.9, "ask": 7.0}

With four heads revealed, the coin is very likely the biased one, so fair value is about 5.94. I'm quoting a bid of 5.0 and an ask of 6.9.

**Fair value**
- If the coin is fair, four heads in a row has probability 1/16.
- So P(fair coin | 4 heads) = (0.5 × 1/16) / (0.5 × 1/16 + 0.5 × 1) = 1/17.
- If the coin is biased, it settles at 6.
- If the coin is fair, the two remaining flips add an average of 1, so it settles at 5 on average.
- Expected value: (16/17) × 6 + (1/17) × 5 ≈ 5.94.

**Possible settlement values**
- 6 with probability ≈ 0.956
- 5 with probability ≈ 0.029
- 4 with probability ≈ 0.015

**Ask side**
- Any ask above 6 is safe from informed traders, because at most 6 heads are possible.
- So I only face noise traders, whose valuations are about 5.94 plus noise with standard deviation 1.3.
- Expected profit from noise buyers is greatest with the ask about 0.98 above fair value, which gives about 6.9.

**Bid side**
- Informed traders sell only when the true value is below my bid.
- At a bid of 5.0, that happens only when the value is 4, so the expected loss to informed traders is about 0.005.
- The expected gain from noise sellers is about 0.144.
- I compared this with a bid of 5.1 (≈0.134 net) and 5.9 (much worse); 5.0 does best.

My position is +1, so buying one more unit stays within the ±4 limit.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 6.9}

With 4 heads in 4 flips, the coin is very likely the biased one, so fair value is about 5.94.

**Fair value**
- If the coin is fair, 4 heads in a row has probability 1/16. If it always lands heads, the probability is 1.
- So the chance it is the always-heads coin is 16/17, and the chance it is fair is 1/17.
- Expected settlement = 4 + (16/17)·2 + (1/17)·1 ≈ **5.94**.
- Settlement is 6 with probability about 0.956, 5 with about 0.029 and 4 with about 0.015.

**Ask**
- The settlement can be at most 6. With an ask of 6 or higher, an informed trader never buys from me.
- That leaves only noise traders, whose valuations are roughly Normal(5.94, 1.3).
- I chose the ask to maximise expected profit from noise buyers, which is (ask − 5.94) × P(noise valuation > ask).
- That profit peaks at about 0.98 above fair value, so the ask is **6.9**.

**Bid**
- An informed trader sells to me only if the settlement is below my bid. With a bid of 5.0, that happens only when the settlement is 4, about 1.5% of the time.
- The expected loss from informed sellers is about 0.35 × 0.0147 × 1 ≈ 0.005.
- The expected gain from noise sellers is about 0.65 × 0.94 × P(valuation < 5.0) ≈ 0.14.
- A bid of 4.9 gives almost the same result, so the bid is **5.0**.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 6.9}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.3 with probability 2/5, P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 1/10, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 8 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The contract is worth 10 × the number of heads in 8 flips, so it can settle anywhere from 0 to 80. I chose my quote by weighing what I earn from noise traders against what I lose to informed traders.

**Fair value.** The expected chance of heads is 0.4·0.3 + 0.1·0.4 + 0.5·0.9 = 0.61. Over 8 flips that gives a fair value of about 80 × 0.61 ≈ 48.8.

**Where the value is likely to land.** The likely outcomes cluster at two ends, not around 48.8:
- With the p = 0.9 coin, settlement is about 70–80.
- With the p = 0.3 coin, settlement is about 10–40.

So an informed trader almost always knows the true value is far from 48.8. A tight quote around 49 would lose heavily to them.

**Choosing each side.** For each candidate price I compared two things:
- the gain from noise traders (spread × chance they trade);
- the loss to informed traders (how far the true value is beyond my price, weighted by its probability).

Expected profit per quote, ask side:

| Ask | Profit |
|---|---|
| 60 | ≈ +0.25 |
| 70 | ≈ +2.1 |
| 76–78 | ≈ +2.3 (peak) |

Expected profit per quote, bid side:

| Bid | Profit |
|---|---|
| 18 | ≈ +1.96 |
| 20–21 | ≈ +2.0 (peak) |
| 25 | ≈ +1.87 |

So I bid 20 and ask 77.

{"bid": 20, "ask": 77}

Fair value after the first trade is about 36, so I quote bid 10 and ask 68.

**Prior.** The average chance of heads is 0.4·0.3 + 0.1·0.4 + 0.5·0.9 = 0.61. So the expected settlement is 80 × 0.61 ≈ 48.8.

**Update from the trade at 20.**
- An informed trader sells at 20 only if the settlement is 0 or 10 (at most 1 head). The prior chance of that is about 0.113.
- A noise trader sells if its valuation is below 20. With fair value 48.8 and standard deviation 26, that chance is about 0.134.
- The posterior expected settlement is about 36. The posterior chance that the settlement is 0 or 10 is about 31%.
- The distribution has two clusters: one at 0–10, and the heads = 0.9 coin around 70–80.

**Ask.** Raising the ask cuts losses to informed buyers when the coin is the 0.9 coin. It also costs fewer noise trades.
- Ask 56: expected gain about +0.8.
- Ask 66: about +1.5.
- Ask 70: about +1.6.
- The curve is flat in this range, so I use 68.

**Bid.** Informed traders sell only when the settlement is 0 or 10.
- A bid of 10 loses to informed sellers only when the settlement is 0. It still catches noise sellers about 16% of the time, each worth about 26 profit.
- Expected gain is about +2.45, roughly the best of the bids I checked (20, 12, 10 and 9).

{"bid": 10, "ask": 68}

Fair value is about **60.6**. I'll quote **45 bid / 74 ask**, set wide around fair and leaning toward selling because I'm already long 2.

**Fair value.** Flips 1–4 show 3 heads and 1 tail. Each coin's likelihood of that is p³(1−p), weighted by its prior:
- p = 0.3: 0.0189 × 0.4 = 0.00756, so posterior ≈ 0.158
- p = 0.4: 0.0384 × 0.1 = 0.00384, so posterior ≈ 0.080
- p = 0.9: 0.0729 × 0.5 = 0.03645, so posterior ≈ 0.762

The expected P(heads) is 0.765. Four flips remain, so expected heads are 3 + 4 × 0.765 ≈ 6.06, giving a fair value of about 60.6.

The two earlier trades tell us almost nothing. Both were sells at 20 and 10, and the 3 heads already revealed guarantee a value of at least 30. So no informed trader would have sold that low, and both must have been noise traders.

**Ask side.** If the coin is the 0.9 coin (about 76% likely), the most likely final value is 70, with about a 66% chance.
- Any ask of 70 or above is never hit by an informed trader at a loss.
- Against noise traders (fair value plus noise with standard deviation 26), the expected edge keeps rising as the ask moves up to about fair + 0.75 × 26.
- Since I'm long, selling is attractive, so I set the ask a little below that optimum.

**Bid side.** An informed trader sells only when the value is below my bid, which mostly happens with the 0.3 coin (values of 30–50). Being long +2, I bid low to avoid adding to the position against informed sellers.

{"bid": 45, "ask": 74}

Fair value is about 60.6, so I'm quoting a bid of 41 and an ask of 71.

**Fair value.** The revealed flips show 3 heads in 4.
- The coin's likelihood times its prior gives:
  - p=0.3: 0.00756
  - p=0.4: 0.00384
  - p=0.9: 0.03645
- So the posterior is about 0.158, 0.080 and 0.762.
- That gives E[p] ≈ 0.765.
- Expected total heads is 3 + 4 × 0.765 ≈ 6.06, so fair value is about 60.6.

**Trading history.** The two stage-1 sells at 20 and 10 must have come from noise traders. Settlement is already at least 30, so no informed trader would sell that low.

**Possible settlement values.** The remaining 4 flips put settlement at 30, 40, 50, 60 or 70. The chance of exactly 70 is about 50%.

**Ask side.** Settlement cannot exceed 70.
- An ask of 71 means informed traders never buy from me.
- Noise traders still buy about 34% of the time, earning me about 10 each.
- That beats an ask of 68, where informed buyers would cost me about 2 per trade on the 70 outcomes.

**Bid side.** Informed traders only sell at 41 when settlement is 30 (about 4.8% chance). That loss is small. Noise traders sell about 23% of the time, earning me about 20 each. The expected edge is about +2.7, which is better than bidding 45 or 50.

**Position.** Being long 2 makes me lean slightly towards a lower bid, which fits.

{"bid": 41, "ask": 71}

Fair value is about 67.5.

**Posterior on the coin.** Five of the six revealed flips are heads.
- The likelihood of that result for each coin type is p⁵(1−p).
- Combined with the priors, this gives P(0.3) ≈ 0.022, P(0.4) ≈ 0.020 and P(0.9) ≈ 0.958.
- So the expected chance of heads is E[p] ≈ 0.877.

**Settlement distribution.** Two flips remain.
- P(2 more heads) ≈ 0.781, so settlement is 70.
- P(1 more head) ≈ 0.191, so settlement is 60.
- P(0 more heads) ≈ 0.028, so settlement is 50.
- Fair value is 50 + 10 × 1.754 ≈ 67.5.

**Ask side.**
- Settlement can never be above 70. So any ask of 70 or more is never lifted by an informed trader, and I only trade with noise traders.
- Expected profit from a noise trader is about 0.65 × P(noise > ask − 67.5) × (ask − 67.5).
- This peaks at an ask of roughly 85–90 (about 2.85 expected profit).

**Bid side.**
- Settlement can never be below 50. A bid of 50 or less is never hit by an informed trader.
- Expected profit from a noise trader peaks at a bid of about 48–50 (about 2.87 expected profit).

**Position.** I am long 1, well within the ±5 limits, so I do not need to skew the quotes.

{"bid": 49, "ask": 87}

Five of the six revealed flips are heads, so the coin is very likely the 0.9 coin, and the fair value is about 67.5. The best quote is a bid of 48 and an ask of 87.

**Which coin it is.** I weighted each coin's prior by the chance of seeing 5 heads and 1 tail:
- 0.3 coin: about 2.2%
- 0.4 coin: about 2.0%
- 0.9 coin: about 95.8%

That gives a probability of heads of about 0.877 for each of the two unrevealed flips.

**Settlement distribution.** Five heads are already in, so the contract settles at 50, 60 or 70:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 70 | about 78.1% |
| 60 | about 19.1% |
| 50 | about 2.8% |

The expected settlement is about 67.5, which is the public fair value.

**Ask.** If the ask is at or above 70, an informed trader never buys, so only noise traders hit it. Their profit is maximised where the distance above fair value, measured in standard deviations, times the chance of a trade is largest. That happens about 0.75 standard deviations above fair: 67.5 + 0.75 × 26 ≈ 87. The expected gain on this side is about 2.9.

**Bid.**
- At a bid of 50 or below, an informed trader never sells, because settlement cannot be below 50.
- The same logic puts the best bid about 0.75 standard deviations below fair: 67.5 − 19.5 ≈ 48.
- That gives an expected gain of about 2.87. A bid of 50 gives about 2.85, and 55 gives only about 2.5.

{"bid": 48, "ask": 87}

info.raw:
Fair value is about 48.8. The bias averages 0.4·0.3 + 0.1·0.4 + 0.5·0.9 = 0.61, and 8 flips × 10 × 0.61 ≈ 48.8.

Fair value given flips 1, 0, 0, 0:

**Posterior on the coin.** The revealed flips show 2 heads in 6. The likelihood of that for each coin is p²(1−p)⁴, weighted by the prior:

| Coin P(heads) | Weighted likelihood | Posterior |
|---|---|---|
| 0.3 | 0.4 × 0.021609 = 0.008644 | ≈ 0.804 |
| 0.4 | 0.1 × 0.020736 = 0.002074 | ≈ 0.193 |
| 0.9 | 0.5 × 0.000081 = 0.0000405 | ≈ 0.004 |

**Choosing the ask.**

- The expected profit from noise buyers, 0.65 × P(noise > a) × (a − 26.4), peaks at about 2.87 for an ask between 45 and 47.

**Choosing the bid.**
- With a bid of 20 or less, no informed trader will sell, because no settlement value is below 20.
- The expected profit from noise sellers peaks at about 2.87 for a bid between 6 and 8.

{"bid": 7, "ask": 46}

The posterior favours a low-bias coin, so I quote wide around a fair value of about 26.4, with the bid at 7 and the ask at 46.

**Posterior on the coin.** The revealed flips show 2 heads in 6. Each prior is weighted by how likely that result is under it:

| P(heads) | Prior | Likelihood of 2 heads in 6 | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.3 | 2/5 | 0.02161 | ≈ 0.804 |
| 0.4 | 1/10 | 0.02074 | ≈ 0.193 |
| 0.9 | 1/2 | 0.00008 | ≈ 0.004 |

The expected P(heads) is about 0.322.

**Settlement distribution.** Two heads are already counted, worth 20. Flips 7 and 8 add 0, 10 or 20 more:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 20 | ≈ 0.463 |
| 30 | ≈ 0.431 |
| 40 | ≈ 0.106 |

The fair value is about 26.4.

**Optimal quotes.** This is the last quote, so each side can be optimised on its own. Each side's expected profit combines two cases. A noise trader has valuation N(26.4, 26). An informed trader trades only when the true value is beyond my price.

- **Ask:** The informed trader only buys when the value is above my ask, so any ask of 40 or more cannot be hit by them. Above 40, I am trading off noise-trader fill probability against edge. Expected profit peaks at about 2.87 near an ask of 46.
- **Bid:** The informed trader only sells when the value is below my bid, so any bid of 20 or less is safe from them. Expected profit peaks at about 2.87 near a bid of 7.

Quoting bid 19.0, ask 30.8, slightly wide of the expected value of 24.8, since a 1-in-5 chance of facing an informed trader has to be paid for.

**Fair value**
- Expected chance of heads = 0.6 × 0.5 + 0.4 × 0.8 = 0.62.

**Ask side**

- Expected profit per quote is about 0.60–0.62 for any ask between 30 and 31.
- Quoting near 27 earns only about 0.12, because informed buying at 30, 35 and 40 costs too much.

**Bid side**
- Informed traders sell whenever the value (5–15) is below my bid.
- The low side is slightly lighter, because the mixture leans towards more heads.
- Expected profit is about 0.59 for bids from 18.5 to 19.

**Quote:** bid 19.0, ask 30.8.

{"bid": 19.0, "ask": 30.8}

Before any reveals, the chance of heads per flip averages 0.6×0.5 + 0.4×0.8 = 0.62. That gives about 4.96 expected heads, so fair value is about 24.8.

The public fair value works out to about 22.7, so I'll quote 18.4 bid and 26.2 ask, shaded slightly down because I'm long one.

**Prior.** The expected heads probability is 0.6 × 0.5 + 0.4 × 0.8 = 0.62. That gives 4.96 expected heads, so the contract is worth about 24.8 before any trading.

**Quote 1 (19 / 30.8, no trade).** An informed trader would not trade only if the value is 20, 25 or 30 (4 to 6 heads). A noise trader would not trade about 63% of the time. So this mildly favours 4 to 6 heads.

**Quote 2 (21 / 28.6, they sold at 21).** An informed trader sells only if the value is 20 or less (4 heads or fewer). A noise trader sells about 28% of the time. So the sale shifts the odds towards 4 heads or fewer.

**Trading history.** The buy at 25.8 on quote 5 shifts belief upward.

**Fair value**

- **Flip 8:** P(heads) = 0.5 + 0.3·0.2185 ≈ 0.566.
- **Settlement:** the contract settles at either 20 or 25. The expected value is 20 + 5·0.566 ≈ **22.83**.

**Quote choice**

- **Informed traders:** they only value the contract at 20 or 25. An ask at or above 25 is never lifted by an informed trader. A bid at or below 20 is never hit by one.
- **Noise traders:** they value it at 22.83 plus noise with SD 6.6. Expected profit on the ask is about 0.8·P(22.83 + noise > ask)·(ask − 22.83):
  - Ask 26 → 0.80
  - Ask 27 → 0.88
  - Ask 28 → 0.90
  - Ask 29 → 0.86
- **Best spread:** the best edge is about 5.2 from fair on each side. That gives an ask of about 28.0 and a bid of about 17.6, both safely outside the informed traders' 20–25 range.

{"bid": 17.6, "ask": 28.0}

**Fair value: about 22.8**

- Likelihood under the 0.8 coin: 0.8^4 × 0.2^3 = 0.0033.
- With priors of 0.6 and 0.4, the chance the coin is the 0.8 one is about 0.22.
- So the chance that flip 8 is heads is 0.78 × 0.5 + 0.22 × 0.8 ≈ 0.566.
- The settlement value is 20 if flip 8 is tails and 25 if it is heads.
- Fair value is 20 + 5 × 0.566 ≈ 22.83.

**Where to quote**
- An ask of 25 or more never trades with an informed counterparty, because its valuation is at most 25.
- A bid of 20 or less never trades with an informed counterparty, because its valuation is at least 20.
- Against noise traders (fair value plus noise with SD 6.6), I chose the price that maximises distance from fair value times the chance of a trade.
- On the ask side, expected value peaks around 28.
- On the bid side, it peaks around 17.6–17.7.

{"bid": 17.7, "ask": 28}

This is the last quote, my position is flat, and the settlement value can only be 20 or 25. So I set each side to maximise profit from noise traders while staying outside the range where informed traders would trade against me.

**Fair value**
- The revealed flips show 4 heads in 7. Settlement is either 20 (flip 8 tails) or 25 (flip 8 heads).
- Likelihood of the revealed flips under the fair coin: 0.5⁷ = 0.00781. With prior 0.6, that weights to 0.00469.
- Likelihood under the biased coin: 0.8⁴·0.2³ = 0.00328. With prior 0.4, that weights to 0.00131.

**Quote choice**

| Heads | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | .045 | .163 | .275 | .276 | .171 | .060 | .009 |

**Ask side.** The settlement is a whole number, so an ask of exactly 4.0 is only lifted by informed traders when the outcome is 5 or 6. That costs about 0.039 in expectation. Noise traders buy there about 13.7% of the time, paying 1.42 above fair, which is worth about 0.097. The net is about +0.058, roughly the best ask. Asks of 3.9 (+0.051) and 4.2 (+0.054) are slightly worse, and 3.1 loses money.

**Bid side.** At a bid of 1.0, informed traders only sell when the outcome is 0, costing about 0.023. Noise traders sell about 11% of the time at 1.58 below fair, worth about 0.089. The net is about +0.066. Higher bids do worse: 1.2 gives about +0.056 and 2.0 loses about 0.03.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 4.0}

Prior mean P(heads) = 0.2·0.3 + 0.3·0.4 + 0.5·0.5 = 0.43, so expected heads = 6 · 0.43 = 2.58.

**Updating on the buy at 4.** An informed trader buys at 4 only if the settlement S is 5 or more. Under the prior, P(S ≥ 5) ≈ 0.069. A noise trader buys if 2.58 + N(0, 1.3) > 4, which has probability ≈ 0.137.

**Posterior.**
- E[S | buy] = (0.5 · 0.355 + 0.0685 · 2.58) / (0.5 · 0.069 + 0.0685) ≈ 0.354 / 0.103 ≈ 3.44.
- P(S ≥ 5 | buy) ≈ 0.38.

So public fair value is now about 3.44. There is real risk the true value is 5 or 6.

**Quote.** I am short 1, so I set the ask a bit wide and centre the quote near 3.44. I quote a bid of 2.8 and an ask of 4.2.

Fair value is about 2.10. I quote bid 1.0 and ask 3.6.

**Fair value:**
- One head is already ruled out by flip 1, and five flips remain, so expected settlement ≈ 0 + 5 × 0.419 ≈ 2.10.
- The two earlier trades (a buy at 4, a sell at 2.8) point in opposite directions, so I leave the estimate at about 2.1.

**Distribution of remaining heads:** P(0)≈0.08, P(1)≈0.24, P(2)≈0.32, P(3)≈0.24, P(4)≈0.10, P(5)≈0.02.

**Choosing the quotes:** Settlement is a whole number, so informed traders only cross my price when they hit a whole-number value beyond it. I traded off adverse selection from informed traders against the edge earned from noise traders (noise standard deviation 1.3).

- **Bid:** expected profit is fairly flat between 0.8 and 1.0. At 1.0 the only informed sellers are those who know the value is 0.

| 0.5 | 0.5 | 0.5⁵ | 0.0156 | 0.215 |

This gives P(flip 6 is heads) ≈ 0.463 × 0.3 + 0.322 × 0.4 + 0.215 × 0.5 ≈ 0.375. So fair value is about 0.375.

- **Bid:** with a bid of 0 or lower, an informed trader never sells, because its valuation is at least 0. Only noise traders can hit it. At a bid of -0.6, they sell with probability about 0.23 and I earn about 0.975. That is also worth about 0.11 per quote.
- **Inside quotes are worse:** placing either side between 0 and 1 lets informed traders pick me off. For example, an ask of 0.9 is worth only about 0.07.

My position is +1, well inside the ±4 limit, so I don't need to adjust for inventory.

{"bid": -0.6, "ask": 1.3}

The contract now settles at the result of flip 6 alone, since the first five flips were all tails (0 heads so far). So it pays either 0 or 1.

**Posterior on the coin after 5 tails:**

Both sides avoid informed traders entirely and capture only noise traders.
