game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 1/5, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/10, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 5 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
Fair value after the buy at 21.5 is about **18.9**, so I'll quote a wide **10 / 28**.

**Fair value before the trade.** The prior mean P(heads) is 0.2·0.2 + 0.3·0.7 + 0.5·0.9 = 0.70. Over 5 flips that gives an expected settlement of 25 × 0.7 = 17.5.

**Update from the buy at 21.5.**
- An informed buyer only pays 21.5 if the settlement is 25 (all 5 heads). The prior chance of that is 0.346.
- A noise trader buys with probability P(Z > 4/12) ≈ 0.37.
- Combining these, the expected settlement is now about **18.9**, and P(all 5 heads) ≈ 0.47.

**Ask.** Settlement can only be a multiple of 5, and there is a 47% chance it is 25.
- Any ask below 25 is picked off by informed traders whenever all 5 flips are heads.
- Above 25, informed traders never buy, so I maximise the noise-trader edge (ask − 18.9) × P(buy).
- That edge peaks around an ask of 28, at about 1.6 per quote.

**Bid.** Informed traders sell when the settlement is below my bid.
- A bid just above 10 or 15 adds a large chunk of informed selling.
- A bid of 10 limits informed sellers to settlements of 0 or 5 (about 13% chance).
- It still catches noise sellers, for an expected value of about 1.45 per quote. It would also reduce my short position if hit.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 28}

Fair value after flip 1 = heads is about 21.2, and I'm quoting bid 17.5 / ask 25.

**Updating on the coin's bias**
- Prior probability of heads, by coin: 0.2, 0.7, 0.9, with weights 0.2, 0.3, 0.5.
- The chance of seeing heads first with each coin is 0.04, 0.21 and 0.45, for a total of 0.70.
- So the updated weights are 0.057, 0.30 and 0.643.
- The expected chance of heads on each remaining flip is 0.8.

**Fair value**
- Expected heads = 1 + 4 × 0.8 = 4.2, which gives a fair value of 21.
- The earlier buy at 21.5 hints that the true value may be higher, so I put the public fair value at about 21.2.

**Quote**
- I'm using a spread of roughly ±4 around fair value.
- I lean slightly upward because I'm short 1.

{"bid": 17.5, "ask": 25}

Fair value is about 22.8, so I'm quoting bid 15 and ask 30.

**Fair value.** I conditioned on flip 1 being heads and on what the trade history implies.
- Revealing flip 1 = 1 shifts the coin probabilities to about 0.06 (p = 0.2), 0.30 (p = 0.7) and 0.64 (p = 0.9).
- Quote 1 traded at my ask of 21.5. This makes 5 heads more likely, because an informed trader buys there only if the settlement value is 25.
- Quote 3 (17.5 / 25) did not trade. An informed trader would have sold if heads were 3 or fewer, so this makes 4 or more heads more likely.
- Combining these, expected heads ≈ 4.56, so fair value ≈ 22.8.

**Quote choice.**
- **Ask:** At 30, informed traders never lift it, since the maximum settlement is 25. Noise traders do lift it fairly often, which earns a wide edge.
- **Bid:** At 15, informed traders only sell when heads are 2 or fewer. That has a small posterior probability.
- **Skew:** I'm short 1, so the quote leans slightly toward buying back.

{"bid": 15, "ask": 30}

With flips 1 and 2 both heads, my estimate of the contract's value is about 22.6, so I quote a wide market around that: bid 14.5, ask 31.

**Coin estimate.** Two heads make the high-bias coins much more likely:
- P(p=0.2) ≈ 0.014
- P(p=0.7) ≈ 0.263
- P(p=0.9) ≈ 0.723

That gives an expected heads probability of about 0.8375.

**Value distribution.** Two heads are already in, and 3 flips remain. The settlement value is 10 plus 5 times the remaining heads:

| Remaining heads | Settlement value | Probability |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 25 | 0.617 |
| 2 | 20 | 0.293 |
| 1 | 15 | 0.075 |
| 0 | 10 | 0.015 |

The expected value is about 22.56.

**Ask side.** The contract can never settle above 25. So any ask at or above 25 can never be hit by an informed trader. With noise traders spread around 22.56 (standard deviation 12), expected profit per quote peaks for an ask around 30–32.

**Bid side.** An informed trader only sells into the bid if the value is below it. The low outcomes (15 and 10) are unlikely, so that risk is small. Expected profit is highest for a bid around 13–15.

I'm short 1, which is well within the ±3 limit, so I don't need to skew the quotes.

{"bid": 14.5, "ask": 31}

Fair value is about 22.6, so I'm quoting wide on both sides around it: bid 14, ask 31.

**Fair value.** The contract pays 5 times the total number of heads in 5 flips. Two heads are already revealed, so it settles at 10 + 5k, where k is the number of heads in the remaining 3 flips.

After two heads, the chance of each coin is:

| P(heads) | Prior | Chance after HH |
|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | 0.2 | about 0.014 |
| 0.7 | 0.3 | about 0.263 |
| 0.9 | 0.5 | about 0.723 |

That gives an expected P(heads) of about 0.8375. So fair value is 5 × (2 + 3 × 0.8375) ≈ 22.6. The no-trade on quote 5 barely moves this.

**What an informed trader could know (settlement value):**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 25 | about 0.617 |
| 20 | about 0.293 |
| 15 | about 0.075 |
| 10 | about 0.015 |

**Ask.** Any ask at 25 or above can never be hit by an informed trader. The best of the asks I tried (24 to 32) is around 30–32, worth about +1.6 per quote from noise buyers.

**Bid.** At a bid of 13–14, an informed trader sells only when the value is 10, which has about a 1.5% chance. Expected profit at 13–14 is about +1.6, and it is fairly flat in that range.

{"bid": 14, "ask": 31}

Fair value is about 24.3 after four heads, so I'm quoting 15.3 bid and 33.3 ask, roughly 9 either side.

**Fair value**
- The coin's chances are updated by the four heads seen (prior × P(heads)⁴):
  - P(heads) 0.2: 0.2 × 0.2⁴ = 0.00032
  - P(heads) 0.7: 0.3 × 0.7⁴ = 0.07203
  - P(heads) 0.9: 0.5 × 0.9⁴ = 0.32805
- These sum to 0.4004. The chance flip 5 is heads is (0.00032 × 0.2 + 0.07203 × 0.7 + 0.32805 × 0.9) / 0.4004 ≈ 0.8635.
- Settlement is 25 if flip 5 is heads and 20 if tails, so fair value ≈ 20 + 5 × 0.8635 ≈ 24.32.

**Informed traders**
- An informed trader values the contract at exactly 25 or exactly 20.
- With an ask at or above 25, an informed trader never buys from me.
- With a bid at or below 20, an informed trader never sells to me.

**Noise traders**
- The profit per noise trade is the edge x times the chance their valuation clears my price, P(Z > x/12). This is largest at about x ≈ 0.75 × 12 ≈ 9.
- That gives an ask of about 33.3, which is above 25, so it is safe from informed buyers.
- It gives a bid of about 15.3, which is below 20, so it is safe from informed sellers.
- For comparison, a bid of 20 would earn about 1.24 per quote, against about 1.63 at 15.3.
- My position limits allow either trade.

{"bid": 15.3, "ask": 33.3}

After four heads in four flips, the posterior on the coin is:

| P(heads) | Prior × p⁴ | Posterior |
|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | 0.00032 | ≈0.0008 |
| 0.7 | 0.07203 | ≈0.18 |
| 0.9 | 0.32805 | ≈0.82 |

- **Flip 5:** P(heads) ≈ 0.864.
- **Settlement:** either 20 or 25. Fair value ≈ 20 + 5 × 0.864 ≈ **24.3**.

**Informed traders:** they know the value is 20 or 25. If my ask is at least 25 and my bid at most 20, they never trade with me.

**Noise traders:** their valuations centre on 24.3 with SD 12. Expected profit from each side is about 0.8 × d × P(Z > d/12), where d is the distance from fair value. This peaks at d ≈ 9, worth about 1.6 per side.

So I quote about 9 either side of 24.3:
- **Ask 33.3:** a sale takes me to −2, which is within limits.
- **Bid 15.3:** a purchase takes me to 0.

{"bid": 15.3, "ask": 33.3}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.2 with probability 1/5, P(heads) = 0.7 with probability 3/10, P(heads) = 0.9 with probability 1/2. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 5 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at 5 times the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The contract is worth about 17.5 before anything is revealed, so I'll centre my quote there.

**Fair value**
- The expected chance of heads is 0.2·0.2 + 0.3·0.7 + 0.5·0.9 = 0.70.
- Expected heads over 5 flips is 3.5, so expected value is 5 × 3.5 = 17.5.
- The value's standard deviation is about 7.8.

**Where to put the quotes**
- Settlement can only be 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 or 25.
- An ask at 20.1 is only hit by an informed trader when the value is 25. That happens with probability about 0.35.
- A bid at 14.9 is only hit by an informed trader when the value is 10 or less. That happens with probability about 0.24.
- The 2.6 edge to fair value on each side should cover losses to informed traders, given that noise traders are 80% of arrivals.

{"bid": 14.9, "ask": 20.1}

Before any trades the fair value was 17.5 (expected heads 3.5 × 5). Someone bought at 20.1, and that buy is mild evidence the coin lands 5 heads. Updating on it moves the public fair value to about 18.8.

**Ask:** An informed trader buys only if the settlement is 25 (all 5 heads). After the buy, the chance of that is about 46%. Quoting at 25.1 means an informed buyer can never profit, and noise traders still buy fairly often well above fair.

**Bid:** An informed trader sells only on low outcomes (0 to 10). Bids in the 10–13 range earn noise-trader edge for little adverse-selection cost. I'm short 1, so I lean toward a bid that's a bit easier to hit, to bring the position back toward flat.

{"bid": 12.5, "ask": 25.1}

Fair value is about 10.3. My quote is bid 7.5, ask 14.5, set a little high because I'm short one unit.

**What flip 1 tells us.** Flip 1 is tails. The chance of tails is 0.8, 0.3 and 0.1 for the three coins. Updating the prior (1/5, 3/10, 1/2) on that gives weights of about 0.53 for p=0.2, 0.30 for p=0.7 and 0.17 for p=0.9.

**What the trading history tells us.**
- **Quote 1 (buy at 20.1):** this carries no information about the coin. Buying above 20.1 means an informed trader would need a settlement of 25, which requires all five flips to be heads. That is impossible now flip 1 is tails, so the buyer was a noise trader. A noise buy is equally likely under every coin.
- **Quote 2 (no trade at 12.5 / 25.1):** an informed trader would not trade only if the settlement is at least 15, meaning 3 or more heads in flips 2 to 5.
  - The chance of that is 0.03 for p=0.2, 0.65 for p=0.7 and 0.95 for p=0.9.
  - A noise trader would not trade about 40% of the time under every coin.
  - So the no-trade outcome favours the higher-heads coins somewhat.

**Fair value.** After both updates the coin weights are about 0.44, 0.34 and 0.22. That gives an expected heads probability of about 0.52. Four flips remain, so the expected settlement is about 5 × 2.09 ≈ 10.5. Without the history adjustment it would be about 9.3, so I use roughly 10.3.

**The quote.** The settlement can only be 0, 5, 10, 15 or 20.
- A bid of 7.5 is only hit by informed traders when the settlement is 0 or 5.
- An ask of 14.5 is only lifted by informed traders when the settlement is 15 or more.
- Against noise traders (standard deviation 12), a spread of about ±3.5 to 4 around fair value earns a reasonable edge.

{"bid": 7.5, "ask": 14.5}

Posting bid 5.0 and ask 10.9 around a fair value of about 7.9.

**Coin after flip 1 = tails.** I weighted each coin by its prior times the chance of tails.

| P(heads) | Prior | Chance of tails | Product | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | 0.2 | 0.8 | 0.16 | 0.533 |
| 0.7 | 0.3 | 0.3 | 0.09 | 0.300 |
| 0.9 | 0.5 | 0.1 | 0.05 | 0.167 |

- The expected chance of heads is 0.467.
- Four flips remain, so the expected value is 4 × 0.467 × 5 ≈ 9.33.

**What the quote-3 trade tells us.** A counterparty sold to me at 7.5.
- An informed trader sells there only if the value is 0 or 5, meaning at most 1 head in the last 4 flips.
- A noise trader sells there with probability about 0.44.
- Weighing those two cases, the fair value drops to about 7.9.

The quote-1 buy at 20.1 adds nothing now. An informed buy there needed 5 heads, which flip 1 rules out, so that trade must have been noise.

**Quote.** The value can only be 0, 5, 10, 15 or 20, with a lot of weight on 0 and 5.
- **Bid 5.0:** an informed trader sells only if the value is 0. The expected profit from noise sellers outweighs that risk.
- **Ask 10.9:** an informed trader buys only if the value is 15 or more.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 10.9}

Fair value after two tails is about **4.6**. I'm quoting wide because any profit comes from noise traders far from fair value.

**Posterior on the coin after two tails:**
- P(heads) = 0.2: posterior 0.80
- P(heads) = 0.7: posterior 0.169
- P(heads) = 0.9: posterior 0.031

This gives an expected P(heads) of about 0.306. Three flips remain, so expected heads is about 0.92. The fair value is 5 × 0.92 ≈ 4.59.

**Settlement distribution:**

| Value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.414 |
| 5 | 0.340 |
| 10 | 0.159 |
| 15 | 0.087 |

**Choosing the quotes.** For each candidate price, I compared the expected gain from noise traders (fair value plus noise with SD 12) with the expected loss to informed traders.

- **Ask:** An ask of 14 has an expected profit of about 1.6 per quote. At that price the informed trader only buys when the value is 15, and then I lose just 1.
- **Bid:** Bids above 0 get hit by informed traders when the value is 0. Bids around -3 to -5 give the best expected profit, about 1.6. A buy would also cut my short position.

{"bid": -4, "ask": 14}

Fair value is about 4.6. The quote is bid -4, ask 14.

**Posterior on the coin after two tails (TT)**

| Coin P(heads) | Prior | Likelihood of TT | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | 0.2 | 0.64 | 0.80 |
| 0.7 | 0.3 | 0.09 | 0.169 |
| 0.9 | 0.5 | 0.01 | 0.031 |

- The posterior expected P(heads) is 0.306.
- Three flips remain, so expected remaining heads are 0.919.
- Fair value is 5 × 0.919 ≈ 4.6.
- The last trade, a sale at -4, must have come from a noise trader, because no informed trader sells below 0. It therefore tells us nothing about the settlement value.

**Settlement distribution and informed buying**
- The possible values are 0, 5, 10 and 15, with probabilities 0.41, 0.34, 0.16 and 0.09.
- An informed buyer hurts the ask mainly when the value is 10 or 15.

**Choosing each side**
- The noise traders' spread is wide (standard deviation 12), so wide quotes still earn well from them.
- The expected profit on the ask peaks at around 14, giving about 1.6.
- The bid side is mirror-like: any bid at or below 0 can never be hit by an informed seller.
- The bid's expected profit peaks at around -4 to -5, also about 1.6.

**Inventory**
- The position is flat with 3 quotes left, so the ±3 limits do not restrict anything.
- Flips 3 and 4 are revealed before stage 4.

{"bid": -4, "ask": 14}

Before the last two quotes, the hidden coin bias and flip 5 still decide settlement. So the contract settles at either 10 or 15.

**Updating on the revealed flips (0, 0, 1, 1).** Each coin's likelihood is p²(1−p)².

| P(heads) | Prior | Prior × likelihood | Posterior |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.2 | 0.2 | 0.00512 | 0.229 |
| 0.7 | 0.3 | 0.01323 | 0.591 |
| 0.9 | 0.5 | 0.00405 | 0.181 |

- So P(flip 5 = heads) ≈ 0.622.
- The fair value is 10 + 5 × 0.622 ≈ 13.1.

**Choosing the quotes.** The settlement value can only be 10 or 15.
- An informed trader would sell only if the value is below my bid, so a bid of 10 or less never loses to them.
- They would buy only if the value is above my ask, so an ask of 15 or more never loses to them.
- Noise traders value the contract at about 13.1 ± 12, so they still trade often at these prices.

**Expected profit per side:**
- Bid at 10: 0.8 × 0.40 × 3.1 ≈ 0.99.
- Bid at 11: the noise gain is about 0.72, but informed sellers cost about 0.08, leaving about 0.65. That is worse than bidding 10.
- Ask at 15: 0.8 × 0.44 × 1.9 ≈ 0.66.
- Ask at 14: informed buyers lose me about 0.12, leaving about 0.21. That is worse than asking 15.

I'll shade each side by one tick to stay safely outside the informed traders' range. My position of +1 gives room to trade on either side.

{"bid": 9.9, "ask": 15.1}

Settlement can only be 10 or 15 from here. Flips 3 and 4 were heads and flips 1 and 2 were tails, so the contract has 2 heads so far. Only flip 5 is left.

**Posterior on the coin**

Each coin's weight is its prior times the chance of seeing 2 heads and 2 tails:
- p = 0.2: 0.2 × 0.0256 = 0.00512
- p = 0.7: 0.3 × 0.0441 = 0.01323
- p = 0.9: 0.5 × 0.0081 = 0.00405

These sum to 0.0224. The chance flip 5 is heads is 0.01393 / 0.0224 ≈ 0.622. Fair value is 10 + 5 × 0.622 ≈ 13.1.

**Quote design**

- **Bid:** keep it at or below 10. An informed seller only sells if the value is 10 and my bid is above 10, so this avoids losing to them.
- **Ask:** keep it at or above 15. An informed buyer only buys if the value is 15 and my ask is below 15, so this avoids losing to them.
- **Noise traders:** their valuations are 13.1 plus noise with standard deviation 12. The expected edge per side is about 0.8 × P(trade) × distance from 13.1.
  - This peaks around 0.75 standard deviations from fair value.
  - That puts the ask near 22 and the bid near 4, each worth about 1.6 in expected profit.
- **Position:** I am at +2, so a buy still fits within the +3 limit.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 22.0}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 3/5, P(heads) = 0.8 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The expected number of heads is 6 × (0.6·0.4 + 0.4·0.8) = 3.36. I centre my quotes there.

The settlement value is quite uncertain, with a standard deviation of about 1.62. The heads count varies even for a known coin, and which coin was picked moves the expected count from 2.4 to 4.8.

Informed traders (20% of arrivals) will hurt me on tight quotes. I'm using a fairly wide spread of about ±1.05 around 3.36.

{"bid": 2.3, "ask": 4.4}

Fair value is about 3.36, and I'm quoting a bid of 2.0 and an ask of 4.8.

**Fair value.** The coin's expected chance of heads is 0.6 × 0.4 + 0.4 × 0.8 = 0.56. Over 6 flips that gives 6 × 0.56 ≈ 3.36 expected heads. The no-trade at quote 1 tells us very little, so 3.36 stays the estimate.

**Settlement distribution.** The number of heads is a mix of two coin cases. It has fat tails, mostly on the high side because of the 0.8 coin.

| Heads | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | .028 | .113 | .193 | .198 | .181 | .179 | .107 |

**Choosing the quotes.** For each candidate price, the expected profit is the gain from noise traders minus the loss to informed traders.

| Side | Price | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|---|
| Ask | 4.1 | ≈ 0.12 |
| Ask | 4.4 | ≈ 0.16 |
| Ask | 4.8 | ≈ 0.18 |
| Ask | 5.0 | ≈ 0.18 |
| Bid | 2.3 | ≈ 0.16 |
| Bid | 2.0 | ≈ 0.18 |
| Bid | 1.9 | ≈ 0.18 |

Profit improves as the quotes widen and levels off at about 2.0 on the bid and 4.8 on the ask.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 4.8}

Fair value after flip 1 = 0 is about 2.36.

**Posterior on the coin**
- P(p = 0.4 | tail) = 0.36 / 0.44 ≈ 0.818.
- P(p = 0.8 | tail) = 0.08 / 0.44 ≈ 0.182.
- So the expected heads probability is about 0.473.
- The remaining 5 flips are therefore expected to give 5 × 0.473 ≈ 2.36 heads. Flip 1 adds nothing.

**Settlement distribution (key tails)**
- P(0) ≈ 0.064 and P(1) ≈ 0.213.
- P(4) ≈ 0.137 and P(5) ≈ 0.068.

**Choosing the quotes**
Each quote trades off profit from noise traders (whose valuations are spread with SD 1.6) against losses to informed traders, who know the integer outcome.

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 3.5 | ≈ 0.184 |
| 3.9 | ≈ 0.189 |
| 4.0 | ≈ 0.188 |

The best ask is about 3.9, just under the jump at 4.

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 1.4 | ≈ 0.176 |
| 1.1 | ≈ 0.199 |
| 1.0 | ≈ 0.202 |

The best bid is 1.0. At that price, an informed trader only sells to me when the settlement is 0.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 3.9}

Fair value is about 2.18. Bid 1.1, ask 3.0, skewed slightly low because I am long one unit.

1. **Coin after flip 1 = 0.** The chance of tails is 0.6 for the 0.4 coin and 0.2 for the 0.8 coin. That gives posterior weights of 0.36 and 0.08, which normalise to about 82% and 18%. Expected heads per flip is about 0.473.
2. **Before quote 3's trade.** Flip 1 counts zero heads, and 5 flips remain, so fair value is 5 × 0.473 ≈ 2.36.
3. **Update from the sale at my bid of 1.**
   - A noise trader sells below 1 with about 20% probability.
   - An informed trader sells only if the settlement is 0, which has about 6% probability.
   - Conditioning on that sale lowers fair value to about **2.18**.
4. **Quote choice.**
   - **Ask 3.0:** an informed buyer only hits it when the settlement is 4 or 5, about 21% of the time. A noise buyer hits it about 31% of the time and gives me about 0.8 of edge.
   - **Bid 1.1:** an informed seller only hits it when the settlement is 0 or 1. A noise seller gives me about 1.1 of edge.

{"bid": 1.1, "ask": 3.0}

Fair value is about 0.81 expected heads.

**Posterior on the coin.** After 4 tails, the likelihood is 0.6⁴ = 0.1296 for the p = 0.4 coin and 0.2⁴ = 0.0016 for the p = 0.8 coin. Weighting by the prior gives:

| | Prior × likelihood | Posterior |
|---|---|---|
| p = 0.4 coin | 0.6 × 0.1296 = 0.07776 | ≈ 0.992 |
| p = 0.8 coin | 0.4 × 0.0016 = 0.00064 | ≈ 0.008 |

So E[p] ≈ 0.403.

**Settlement value.** All revealed flips were tails, so settlement equals the heads in flips 5 and 6:

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | ≈ 0.357 |
| 1 | ≈ 0.479 |
| 2 | ≈ 0.164 |

The expected value is about 0.81, and noise traders value the contract at about 0.81 ± 1.6.

**Ask.** Setting the ask at 2.0 means an informed trader never buys, because settlement cannot exceed 2. Expected profit from noise traders buying is 0.8 × P(noise > 1.19) × 1.19 ≈ 0.8 × 0.23 × 1.19 ≈ 0.22. That is about the best available; an ask of 1.9 or 2.2 does slightly worse.

**Bid.** Setting the bid at or below 0 means an informed trader never sells, because settlement cannot be below 0. A bid of -0.2 earns about 0.8 × 0.264 × 1.01 ≈ 0.21 from noise traders. That beats bids above 0, where an informed trader holding a 0-value contract would sell to me.

{"bid": -0.2, "ask": 2.0}

With four tails revealed, the coin is almost certainly the 0.4 coin. That puts fair value near 0.81, and the best last quote is a bid of -0.4 and an ask of 2.0.

**Posterior on the coin after flips 1–4 all came up tails**
- 0.4 coin: 0.6 × 0.6⁴ = 0.07776
- 0.8 coin: 0.4 × 0.2⁴ = 0.00064
- So P(0.8 coin) ≈ 0.008, and expected P(heads) ≈ 0.403.

**Settlement value**
Settlement is 0 plus the heads in flips 5 and 6, so it can only be 0, 1 or 2. The probabilities are about 0.36, 0.48 and 0.16. Fair value ≈ 2 × 0.403 ≈ 0.81.

**Ask side**
Each value below is my expected profit from that side, combining noise-trader gains and informed-trader losses.
- At an ask of 2.0, an informed trader never buys, because the value is at most 2 and it only buys above the ask.
- About 23% of noise traders buy at 2.0, gaining about 1.19 each.
- Expected profit is about 0.217, which is near the best among the asks I checked.

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 1.5 | 0.168 |
| 1.9 | 0.213 |
| 2.0 | 0.217 |
| 2.2 | 0.213 |

**Bid side**
- Any bid above 0 lets an informed trader sell to me whenever the value is 0, which happens 36% of the time.
- At or below 0, informed traders never sell.
- Shading the bid lower trades less often but earns more per noise trade.

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 0.3 | 0.131 |
| 0 | 0.198 |
| -0.2 | 0.213 |
| -0.4 | 0.218 |
| -0.5 | 0.216 |

{"bid": -0.4, "ask": 2.0}

game.title: Coin of unknown bias
game.description: A coin is picked at random from a set of coins: P(heads) = 0.4 with probability 3/5, P(heads) = 0.8 with probability 2/5. The coin is not shown. It is flipped 6 times. Revealed flips show 1 for heads and 0 for tails.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of heads in all flips.

info.raw:
The settlement value has expected value 3.36 and a standard deviation of about 1.6. Because it is a whole number of heads, I set the bid and ask so the inside sits just past whole numbers. Informed traders then only trade with me on more extreme outcomes, while noise traders still trade fairly often.

**Fair value**
- Chance of heads on each flip: 0.6 × 0.4 + 0.4 × 0.8 = 0.56.
- Expected heads over 6 flips: 6 × 0.56 = 3.36.

**Uncertainty**
- If the coin is the 0.4 coin: mean 2.4, variance 1.44.
- If the coin is the 0.8 coin: mean 4.8, variance 0.96.
- Total variance: 1.248 within each coin, plus 1.38 from not knowing which coin it is. That gives about 2.63, so the standard deviation is about 1.62.

**Quote**
- At a bid of 2.4, informed traders only sell to me when the true count is 2 or fewer.
- At an ask of 4.3, informed traders only buy from me when the true count is 5 or more.
- The half-spread is about 0.95 on each side. A noise trader is still likely enough to cross it that the spread earned should outweigh losses to informed traders.

{"bid": 2.4, "ask": 4.3}

The public fair value is now about **2.74**, down from a prior of 3.36, because someone sold to me at 2.4. I quote **bid 1.8 / ask 3.5**: a spread of roughly ±0.85 around that, shaded slightly lower because I am long.

**Prior before any trade.** The expected chance of heads is 0.6·0.4 + 0.4·0.8 = 0.56. Over 6 flips that gives an expected 3.36 heads.

**What the sell at 2.4 tells us.**
- An informed trader sells only if the true count is 2 or fewer. The prior chance of that is about 0.333.
- A noise trader sells if its noise is below −0.96, which happens about 16.6% of the time.
- So a sell is about 2.5 times as likely when the count is 0–2 (0.333 vs 0.133).
- Updating on that drops the expected count to about **2.74**.

**Quote.** The value is still very uncertain, and 20% of counterparties are informed, so I keep a half-spread of about 0.85. I am long 1, so I set both sides a little low, making a sale to me slightly less likely and a sale by me slightly more likely.

{"bid": 1.8, "ask": 3.5}

Public fair value is about 3.6. I'm quoting roughly ±0.75 around it and skewing slightly lower because I'm already long one unit.

**Coin estimate after flip 1 = heads**
- Weight on the 0.4 coin: 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.24.
- Weight on the 0.8 coin: 0.4 × 0.8 = 0.32.
- So P(coin is 0.8) = 0.32 / 0.56 ≈ 0.571.
- From the coin and flip alone, the expected total is 1 + 5 × (0.429 × 0.4 + 0.571 × 0.8) ≈ 4.14.

**Adjusting for the trading history**
The fair value also reflects how trades depend on the final head count (S).
- **Quote 1, a sale at 2.4:** an informed trader sells there only if S ≤ 2. A noise trader sells about 27% of the time. This is evidence for a low S.
- **Quote 2, no trade between 1.8 and 3.5:** an informed trader does nothing only if S is 2 or 3. A noise trader does nothing about 39% of the time. This is mild evidence for S in {2, 3}.
- Combining both trades with the binomial distribution for each coin gives an expected settlement of about 3.6.

**Quote**
Bid 2.8, ask 4.3. The width protects against informed traders, and the bid sits a little further from 3.6 than the ask because of my long position.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 4.3}

Fair value is about 4.15, and I'm quoting a bid of 3.4 and an ask of 4.9 around it.

**Coin posterior after flip 1 = 1 (heads):**
- P(p = 0.4) = 0.24 / 0.56 ≈ 0.43
- P(p = 0.8) = 0.32 / 0.56 ≈ 0.57
- Expected bias is about 0.63.

**Expected settlement:** 1 head already, plus 5 × 0.63 ≈ 3.14 for the remaining flips, gives about 4.14.

**Trade history:**
- Quote 1: a counterparty sold at my bid of 2.4. That is weak evidence the settlement value is low.
- Quote 3: a counterparty bought at my ask of 4.3. That is weak evidence it is high.
- These roughly offset, so I put fair value around 4.15.

**Spread:** The settlement value still has a lot of spread, with a standard deviation of about 1.2. Informed traders know it exactly, so I keep a half-spread of about 0.75 around fair value.

{"bid": 3.4, "ask": 4.9}

The settlement is 3 heads already revealed plus the heads from flips 5 and 6. I estimate fair value at about 4.31, then set each side to maximise expected profit against the trader mix.

**Which coin is it?** The revealed flips are 1, 1, 1, 0 (3 heads, 1 tail).
- Coin with P(heads) = 0.8: likelihood 0.8³ × 0.2 = 0.1024. Times its prior 0.4 gives 0.04096.
- Coin with P(heads) = 0.4: likelihood 0.4³ × 0.6 = 0.0384. Times its prior 0.6 gives 0.02304.
- Posterior: P(0.8 coin) = 0.04096 / (0.04096 + 0.02304) = 0.64, so P(0.4 coin) = 0.36.

**Expected settlement**
- Expected heads per remaining flip = 0.64 × 0.8 + 0.36 × 0.4 = 0.656.
- Fair value = 3 + 2 × 0.656 ≈ 4.31.

**Settlement distribution** (only 3, 4 or 5 are possible):

| Settlement | Probability |
|---|---|
| 3 | 0.155 |
| 4 | 0.378 |
| 5 | 0.467 |

**Choosing the ask**
- Noise traders (80%) value the contract at about 4.31 plus noise with standard deviation 1.6.
- The informed trader (20%) buys only if the value is strictly above my ask. At an ask of 5.0 or higher, the informed trader never buys.
- Expected profit from the ask side is 0.8 × (ask − 4.31) × P(noise valuation > ask). This is about 0.21 at 5.3, peaks at about 0.217 at 5.6, and is about 0.21 at 5.8.
- I choose an ask of 5.6.

**Choosing the bid**
- At a bid of 3.0 or lower, the informed trader never sells, because the value can never be below 3.
- Expected profit is 0.8 × (4.31 − bid) × P(noise valuation < bid). This is about 0.216 at 3.0.
- At 3.1 it is about 0.218 from noise traders. But informed selling when the value is 3 costs about 0.003, leaving roughly 0.215.
- At 2.9 it is about 0.213, so I choose a bid of 3.0.

My position of +1 is well within the ±3 limit, so I don't need to skew the quote for inventory.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 5.6}

Bid 3.0 / ask 5.6.

**Fair value from the revealed flips (3 heads, 1 tail):**
- Likelihood if the coin is 0.4: 0.4³ × 0.6 = 0.0384. With prior 3/5, that gives 0.02304.
- Likelihood if the coin is 0.8: 0.8³ × 0.2 = 0.1024. With prior 2/5, that gives 0.04096.
- Posterior: P(coin is 0.8) = 0.64 and P(coin is 0.4) = 0.36.
- Expected heads per remaining flip: 0.64 × 0.8 + 0.36 × 0.4 = 0.656.
- Fair value: 3 + 2 × 0.656 ≈ 4.31.
- Settlement distribution: 3 with probability 0.155, 4 with probability 0.378, 5 with probability 0.467.

I ignored the small effect of the trading history on fair value.

**Ask:** Any ask of 5.0 or higher is safe from informed buyers, because they only buy when their value is above the ask. Expected profit from noise buyers is 0.8 × P(buy) × (ask − 4.31):

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 5.0 | 0.184 |
| 5.5 | 0.218 |
| 5.6 | 0.217 |
| 5.8 | 0.210 |

The curve is flat between 5.5 and 5.6, so I'll use 5.6.

**Bid:** A bid of 3.0 avoids losses to informed sellers, who only sell when their value is below the bid. Expected profit is about 0.216. Raising the bid to 3.3 drops it to about 0.204, because informed sellers holding 3 would then hit it. Lowering it to 2.9 gives about 0.213.

Buying one more unit takes the position to +2, which is within the limit.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 5.6}

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 10 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 10. 3 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
Prior: the red-ball count is uniform on 0–10, so the mean is 5 and the standard deviation is about 3.16. An informed trader knows the exact count, so tight quotes lose heavily to them. I compared the expected profit per quote (noise-trader gains minus informed-trader losses) for several ask levels:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 6.5 | ≈ 0.00 |
| 7.0 | ≈ 0.07 |
| 7.5 | ≈ 0.10 |
| 8.0 | ≈ 0.11 (best) |
| 8.5 | ≈ 0.10 |

The game is symmetric around 5, so the best bid is 2.0, mirroring the ask at 8.0.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 8.0}

The first trade was a buy at 8. That makes high red counts more likely, so I start by updating the public fair value.

**Updating on the buy at 8**
- Before the trade, each red count from 0 to 10 was equally likely, with a mean of 5.
- An informed trader buys at 8 only if the true count is 9 or 10.
- A noise trader's valuation is 5 plus noise with standard deviation 2.4. It buys at 8 only if the noise exceeds 3, which has probability about 0.106.
- So a buy at 8 has probability about 0.069 if the count is 0 to 8. It has probability about 0.419 if the count is 9 or 10.
- After the update, counts 9 and 10 each have probability about 0.288. Counts 0 to 8 each have about 0.047.
- The new public fair value is about **7.17**. Noise traders now value the contract around 7.17.

**Choosing the ask**
- At an ask of 10, informed traders never buy, because the count cannot exceed 10.
- Noise traders buy with probability about 0.12. Each sale earns about 2.8 over the expected value.
- Expected profit is about +0.22 per quote, close to the best of the asks I checked:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 8.5 | +0.05 |
| 9.5 | +0.20 |
| 10 | +0.22 |

**Choosing the bid**
- I compared bids by trading the gain from noise sellers against the loss to informed sellers. The informed traders sell only when the true count is below my bid.
- Expected profit is small but positive between about 4.0 and 4.5 (about +0.025 to +0.027).
- A bid of 5.5 would lose money (about -0.03).
- Buying here would also reduce my short position, which helps given the high posterior mean.

{"bid": 4.2, "ask": 10}

Public fair value is about 4.2. Draw 1 being blue alone would put the expected red count at 3.0. The stage-1 buy at 8 and the no-trade at 4.2/10 move it up to roughly 4.2.

- **Draw 1 is blue.** This weights each possible red count R in proportion to (10 − R). With a uniform prior over 0–10, the expected red count becomes 165/55 = 3.0.
- **The buy at 8 (quote 1).** An informed buyer only pays 8 if R is 9 or 10. A noise buyer, valuing near the stage-1 mean of 5, does so about 11% of the time. So R = 9 becomes about 6 times more likely than any R from 0 to 8. R = 10 is already ruled out by the blue draw.
- **No trade at 4.2 / 10 (quote 2).** An informed trader stays out only if R is between 5 and 10. Noise traders stay out about 68% of the time. So R of 5 or more becomes about 1.8 times more likely than R of 4 or less.
- **Result.** Combining these, the posterior mean is about 4.2. The spread of possible values is still wide.

Quote: I'll set a fairly wide spread around 4.2 to guard against the 35% informed flow. I'll lean it slightly upward because I'm short 1, which makes it a bit more likely I buy back.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 5.6}

The posterior fair value given all public information is about 2.9, and the distribution is skewed. I quote a low bid and a wide ask.

**Posterior fair value**
- With a uniform prior, a blue first draw gives weights proportional to (10−R), so the mean is 3.0.
- The trade history also carries information, because informed traders act on the true value:
  - Quote 1: they bought at 8, which favours R = 9 or 10.
  - Quote 2: no trade between 4.2 and 10, which favours R ≥ 5.
  - Quote 3: they sold at 3, which favours R ≤ 2.
- Combining these, the posterior puts most of its mass on R = 0, 1 or 2 (about 61%). There is a tail at R ≥ 5 (about 28%), with notable weight on R = 9.
- The posterior mean is about 2.9.

**Choosing the quotes**
- **Bid:** An informed trader only sells if R is below the bid, and below about 1 the only such case is R = 0. A bid around 0.5 has small adverse-selection cost and still catches a fair share of noise sellers. Expected edge per quote is about +0.21.
- **Ask:** The upper tail is heavy, so a tighter ask loses money to informed buyers. An ask around 5.5–6 gives the best net edge, about +0.07.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 5.6}

The public fair value comes out at about 7.2, so I'll quote a bid of 5.0 and an ask of 9.2.

**Draws alone.** Draw 1 blue and draw 2 red give a posterior on the number of red balls proportional to R(10−R). That has mean 5.0 and standard deviation about 2.2.

**Trading history.** I updated on each past trade using a simplified model of how each counterparty type would behave:
- **Quote 1, buy at 8:** this pushed weight onto R = 9 or 10, because an informed trader buys there.
- **Quote 2, no trade at 4.2 / 10:** this favoured R ≥ 5.
- **Quote 3, sell at 3:** this favoured R ≤ 2.
- **Quote 4, buy at 5.6:** this favoured R ≥ 6.

Combining all of this with the draws gives roughly:

| R | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 0–4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 41% | 12% | 16% | 18% | 4% | about 10% |

The public fair value is about 7.2, and noise traders centre their valuations there.

**Ask.** An informed trader only buys if R is above my ask. At 9.2, no informed trader would buy, since R = 10 is now impossible. Noise traders buy with probability about 0.14 and I gain about 1.9 each time. The expected edge is about +0.27.

**Bid.** At 5.0, informed traders sell only when R ≤ 4, which is about 10% of the time. That costs me about 0.09 in expectation. Noise traders sell with probability about 0.11 and I gain about 2.2 each time, worth about 0.26. The net edge is about +0.17, and this bid was close to the best of the levels I checked.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 9.2}

The two revealed draws (blue, then red) leave the expected number of red balls at 5, so I'm quoting 2.5 / 7.5, symmetric around 5.

**Fair value.** Start with each red count R from 0 to 10 equally likely. The chance of drawing blue then red is (10−R)/10 × R/9. So after updating, each R is weighted in proportion to R(10−R). These weights are symmetric around 5, so the mean is 5. The standard deviation is about 2.2.

Earlier trades give only weak and mixed signals, so I don't shift away from 5.

**Choosing the spread.** I compared ask levels by expected gain from noise traders minus expected loss to informed traders:

| Ask | Expected gain from noise traders | Expected loss to informed traders | Net per quote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6.5 | 0.26 | 0.12 | 0.14 |
| 7.5 | 0.24 | 0.05 | 0.20 |
| 7.9 | 0.21 | 0.02 | 0.19 |

An ask of 7.5 gives the best net, at about 0.20 per quote. The bid side is symmetric, so the bid is 2.5.

I'm short 1, so the most another sale can take me to is −2, which is still within the limit of −3. I quote both sides.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 7.5}

Quote: **bid 6.0, ask 9.1**. My estimate of the settlement value is about 7.5, which is uncertain because the noise-trader model behind it is rough.

**Draws alone.** With a uniform prior and draws blue, red, red, the posterior weight on R red balls is proportional to (10−R)·R·(R−1). That puts R between 2 and 9, with expected value about 6.2.

**Trading history.** The trades and no-trades also carry information, because 35% of counterparties know the true value.
- The buy at 8 in quote 1 weighs heavily toward R = 9.
- The no-trades in quotes 5 and 6 favour R between 5 and 7 if the counterparty was informed.
- Combining all six quotes with approximate noise-trader probabilities moves the estimate to about **7.5**, with roughly 40% weight on R = 9.

**Choosing the quote.**
- **Ask 9.1:** An informed buyer would need a value above 9.1, which is impossible here. Noise buyers still lift it about 15% of the time, at an expected gain of about 1.5 each.
- **Bid 6.0:** An informed seller would need R of 5 or less, which has about 7% probability. Noise sellers hit it about 19% of the time, at an expected gain of about 1.5 each.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 9.1}

Given draws of blue, red, red (2 red, 1 blue), the posterior on R is proportional to R(R−1)(10−R). The expected value works out to about 6.2.

This is the last quote, so there are no future quotes or positions to worry about. Each side can be set on its own to balance profit from noise traders against losses to informed traders, who know R exactly and only trade when R is a whole number beyond my price.

- **Ask:** around 8.5 does best. Only R=9 informed buyers hit it, and noise traders still cross often enough. Expected gain is about 0.23.
- **Bid:** around 4.0 does best. Only R≤3 informed sellers hit it, and R=4 does not sell at exactly 4. Expected gain is about 0.22.

{"bid": 4.0, "ask": 8.5}

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 10 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 10. 3 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
I priced this from the prior and the trader mix.

**Fair value now.** Nothing has been revealed. The red count is equally likely to be any of 0 to 10, so its expected value is 5.

**Trade-off.** Each counterparty is one of two kinds:
- **Informed (35%):** knows the true count and only trades when I'm mispriced, so every trade with them loses money.
- **Noise (65%):** trades at 5 plus random noise with standard deviation 2.4, so a wider spread earns more per trade but trades less often.

**Expected profit on the ask side** at a distance s above 5:

| Ask | Informed loss | Noise gain | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7 | 0.191 | 0.263 | ≈ 0.07 |
| 7.5 | 0.143 | 0.242 | ≈ 0.10 |
| 8 | 0.095 | 0.206 | ≈ 0.11 |
| 8.5 | 0.064 | 0.165 | ≈ 0.10 |

An ask of 8 gives the highest expected profit. The bid side is a mirror image, so the bid should be 2.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 8.0}

**Updating fair value:** The prior is uniform on 0 to 10 red balls, so the mean was 5. Someone sold to me at a bid of 2.

- An informed trader sells there only if the true count is below 2, meaning 0 or 1 red balls.
- A noise trader sells there with probability Φ(−3/2.4) ≈ 0.106.

So each count gets a likelihood weight:
- 0.35 + 0.65·0.106 ≈ 0.419 if the count is 0 or 1.
- 0.65·0.106 ≈ 0.069 if the count is 2 to 10.

This gives:
- P(count is 0 or 1) ≈ 0.575.
- Each other count has probability ≈ 0.047.
- Public fair value ≈ 2.84.

The posterior is lopsided. Most of the mass sits at 0 and 1, with a long tail up to 10.

**Bid side:** Any bid above 1 is costly. Informed traders hitting a bid near 1–2.5 have most likely got 0 or 1 red balls. At bid ≈ 0.3:
- Expected loss to informed traders is about −0.03.
- Expected gain from noise traders is about 0.65 × 0.145 × 2.54 ≈ +0.24.

**Ask side:** The tail up to 10 makes low asks lose money to informed buyers. Expected profit is about zero or slightly positive for asks between 5.5 and 7, and is highest near 6 (≈ +0.03). Selling there also brings my long position back toward flat.

{"bid": 0.3, "ask": 6.0}

Public fair value is about 8.1. Before any draw, the number of red balls is equally likely to be 0 to 10. I updated that on the red first draw and on both earlier trades.

- **Red first draw:** the chance of each count of red balls is proportional to the count itself. On its own this gives a fair value of 7.
- **Trade 1 (counterparty sold at 2):** this is likely if there are 0 or 1 red balls and an informed trader sold. Otherwise it needs a noise trader valuing below 2, which has probability about 0.11.
- **Trade 2 (counterparty bought at 6):** this is likely if there are 7 or more red balls and an informed trader bought. Otherwise it needs a noise trader valuing above 6, which has probability about 0.09.

Combining all three, about 90% of the probability sits on 7 to 10 red balls, and the fair value is about 8.1.

I quote a fairly wide spread around 8.1. The bid at 7.0 means informed traders only sell to me when there are 6 or fewer red balls, which now has low probability. The ask at 9.2 limits what I lose to informed buyers when there are 10 red balls. The spread still catches noise traders on both sides, since their valuations spread about 2.4 around the fair value.

{"bid": 7.0, "ask": 9.2}

Fair value now: about 7.5. This is a rough Bayesian update in which I treat the arriving counterparties' trades as signals about the number of red balls.

**Starting point after draw 1.** Draw 1 came up red, so the chance of each red count r is proportional to r. On its own that gives a mean of 7.

**What each trade told us.**
- **Quote 1:** someone sold to me at 2. That favours low red counts, r < 2.
- **Quote 2:** someone bought from me at 6. That favours high counts, r > 6.
- **Quote 3:** someone sold to me at 7. That favours r < 7 and pulls the estimate down.

**Where that leaves the estimate.** The approximate probabilities are:

| Red balls | Probability |
|---|---|
| 10 | 22% |
| 9 | 20% |
| 8 | 18% |
| 7 | 16% |
| 6 | 5% |
| 5 | 4% |
| 4 | 4% |
| 3 | 3% |
| 2 | 2% |
| 1 | 5% |

The expected value is about 7.48.

**Expected profit from each side.** For each side I weighed the gain from noise traders against the loss to informed traders.
- **Ask:** quoting about 9.4 gives the best expected profit, about +0.22. The main risk is that 10 red balls is the single most likely case.
- **Bid:** about 5.0 to 5.5 is best, at roughly +0.11. I hold a long position of +1, so I set the bid slightly lower.

{"bid": 5.2, "ask": 9.4}

Using the draws alone, two reds in two draws give a posterior on the number of red balls proportional to R(R−1). The mean of that is 8. Folding in the trading history (the sells at 2 and 7, the buy at 6, and the no-trade between 5.2 and 9.4) moves the public fair value only slightly, to about 8.3. Most of the probability is on R = 7, 8, 9 or 10.

**Bid at 6.8.** An informed counterparty sells to me only when R is 6 or less, which has about 9% posterior probability. Noise traders sell often enough at this level that the expected value is roughly +0.2.

**Ask at 9.9.** An informed counterparty buys only when R is 10, and then I lose just 0.1. Noise traders still buy fairly often at this level, so the expected value is about +0.26.

My position is +1, so either trade keeps me within the ±3 limits.

{"bid": 6.8, "ask": 9.9}

After two red draws, the expected number of red balls is **8.0**. The quote is set to make money on noise traders while limiting losses to informed traders.

**Fair value.** The starting belief is that every count of red balls from 0 to 10 is equally likely. The chance of drawing two reds when there are R red balls is R(R−1)/90. So after two reds, each R is weighted by R(R−1).
- The expected number of red balls is then Σ R²(R−1) / Σ R(R−1) = 2640 / 330 = **8.0**.
- The resulting probabilities are:

| Red balls | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 | 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 0.273 | 0.218 | 0.170 | 0.127 | 0.091 | 0.061 | 0.036 | 0.018 | 0.006 |

- The no-trade at quote 5 (bid 6.8, ask 9.9) tells us little, so I keep the fair value near 8.

**Ask.** For each candidate ask, I added the expected profit from noise traders buying and subtracted the expected loss when an informed trader buys.
- At 9.0 the net is about +0.12, and at 9.5 about +0.21.
- At 10.0 an informed trader never buys, because the value cannot be above 10. Noise traders give about 0.65 × 0.202 × 2 ≈ **+0.26**.
- At 10.2 the net is about +0.26, and at 10.5 about +0.24.
- 10.0 is the best of these.

**Bid.** I did the same calculation for the buy side.
- At 7.0 the net is about +0.07, and at 6.5 about +0.15.
- At 6.0 the net is about +0.19. Informed sellers cost about 0.074, and noise sellers bring in about 0.263.
- At 5.5 the net is also about +0.19, so the curve is flat around 6.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 10.0}

Bid 6.5 and ask 10.4. Each side has a positive expected profit, and the main reason is that no informed trader can buy above 10.

**Fair value.** After three red draws, each possible count R is weighted by C(R,3), the number of ways to draw 3 reds from R red balls. Only R = 3 to 10 is possible, and the weights sum to 330. That gives:

| R | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | .364 | .255 | .170 | .106 | .061 | .030 | .012 | .003 |

So E[R] = 2838 / 330 = 8.6.

**Ask side.** The settlement value can't exceed 10, so an ask of 10 or more loses nothing to informed traders. Only noise traders can lift it.
- At 10.4, a noise trader buys with probability about 0.227 and I gain 1.8.
- Expected value is 0.65 × 0.227 × 1.8 ≈ +0.265.
- 10.5 is about the same, and both beat 10.0 (≈0.255) and 11.0 (≈0.248).

**Bid side.**
- At 6.5, informed traders sell only when R ≤ 6. That costs about 0.35 × 0.116 ≈ 0.041.
- Noise traders sell with probability about 0.19, and each sale gains 2.1 against the 8.6 fair value.
- Net is about +0.22. That is better than a bid of 7.0 (≈0.20) or 6.0 (≈0.21).

**Position.** I'm long 1, so a fill on either side keeps me within the ±3 limit.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 10.4}

Given three red draws, the posterior is P(R) ∝ R(R−1)(R−2). That puts the fair value near 8.6, with a heavy tail toward 10.

- **Ask:** Above 10, informed traders never buy from me. Expected noise profit is 0.65 × P(noise > a − 8.6) × (a − 8.6), which peaks around 10.4–10.5 at about 0.265 per quote.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers only appear when R is below my bid, which is unlikely given the posterior. Netting their losses against noise-trader profit, the expected value peaks around 6.4–6.5 at about 0.22.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 10.5}

game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
I'm quoting about 3.5 either side of the fair value of 5, at bid 1.5 and ask 8.5.

**Fair value.** Before any draws are revealed, the number of red balls is equally likely to be anything from 0 to 10. The public fair value is therefore 5.

**Choosing the spread.** For each ask level I weighed two things:
- **Gain from noise traders:** the chance a noise trader buys (valuation is 5 plus noise with standard deviation 4.7), times the edge over 5.
- **Loss to informed traders:** the expected loss when the true count is above the ask and an informed trader buys.

| Ask | Expected profit per quote (ask side) |
|---|---|
| 6.5 | 0.31 |
| 7.0 | 0.43 |
| 7.5 | 0.51 |
| 8.0 | 0.57 |
| 8.5 | 0.60 |
| 9.0 | 0.61 |

The bid side mirrors this. Wide quotes do best because informed traders are costly when the true count is far from 5. Gains flatten out past about 8.5, so I'm not going wider than that.

{"bid": 1.5, "ask": 8.5}

Fair value is now about 4.25, and I'm quoting bid 0.8 and ask 7.8.

**Updating fair value.** Before any trade, the expected number of red balls is 5. The counterparty then sold to me at 1.5. That is more likely when the true value is low:

- **If the value is 0 or 1:** an informed trader would sell at 1.5. A noise trader sells with probability Φ(−3.5/4.7) ≈ 0.23. So the chance of this sale is 0.2 + 0.8 × 0.23 ≈ 0.38.
- **If the value is 2 to 10:** only a noise trader would sell, so the chance is about 0.8 × 0.23 ≈ 0.18.

Weighting each value by these chances moves the expected number of red balls to about **4.25**.

**Choosing the width.** I compared expected profit per quote at different half-spreads around 4.25. A wider spread earns more from each noise trade but trades less often. A narrower spread trades more often but loses more to informed traders when the true value is extreme. Expected profit rises from about 0.40 at a half-spread of 2 to about 0.58–0.59 at a half-spread of 3.5–4.

I chose a half-spread of about 3.5 and shifted the quote slightly lower because I'm already long one unit. That gives a bid of 0.8 and an ask of 7.8.

{"bid": 0.8, "ask": 7.8}

The prior is uniform on 0 to 10, so the starting fair value is 5. The two sells at my low bids pull the estimate down.

**Updating on the trades.** A sell at a bid b happens if the counterparty is informed and the true value is below b, or if a noise trader's valuation is below b.
- **Quote 1 (bid 1.5, public fair value 5):** a noise trader sells with probability Φ(−3.5/4.7) ≈ 0.23.
  - The likelihood of this sell is about 0.38 if the true value is 0 or 1, and about 0.18 otherwise.
  - This roughly doubles the weight on 0 and 1, which moves the fair value to about 4.25.
- **Quote 2 (bid 0.8, fair value 4.25):** the likelihood ratio again roughly doubles the weight on a value of 0.
- **Current posterior:**

| Red balls | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | about 0.28 |
| 1 | about 0.14 |
| each of 2 to 10 | about 0.065 |

The expected value is now about **3.6**.

**Choosing the quote.** I am long 2, so I want to lean toward selling.
- **Ask:**
  - At an ask of 6, noise traders buy about 25% of the time, earning about 2.4 each time.
  - Informed buyers, present when the value is 7 or more, cost about 0.13 in expectation.
  - The net is about +0.45, and a sale also reduces my long position.
- **Bid:**
  - At a bid of 0.5, noise traders sell about 20% of the time, earning about 3.1 each time.
  - Informed sellers, present only when the value is 0, cost very little.
  - The bid is kept low because I am already long.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 6.0}

The public fair value is about 6.4. Since I am long 2, I skew the quote slightly downward and keep the spread wide against informed traders.

**Updating on stage 1 trading (prior uniform on 0–10)**

- **Quote 1** (they sold at 1.5, public fair value 5): a noise trader sells with probability Φ(−3.5/4.7) ≈ 0.23. An informed trader sells only if k ≤ 1. So outcomes with k ≤ 1 become about twice as likely as the rest.
- **Quote 2** (they sold at 0.8, fair value about 4.25): this trade points to k = 0. After it, the fair value is about 3.6.
- **Quote 3** (no trade at 0.5 / 6): an informed trader declines only if 1 ≤ k ≤ 6. This favours k = 1..6 over k = 0 and over k = 7..10.

**Updating on draw 1 = red**

- I multiply each posterior weight by k/10, which rules out k = 0.
- The resulting public fair value is about **6.4**.
- The posterior is still widely spread, so informed traders can still hurt me badly. I keep the spread wide.

**Quote**

- I centre the quote slightly below 6.4 to lean against my long position.
- Bid 4.6, ask 7.8.

{"bid": 4.6, "ask": 7.8}

Fair value is about 5.8. I'm long 3 with only one unit of buying room left, so I'm skewing my quotes toward selling.

**Fair value from public information.**
- After draw 1 came up red, the urn's posterior is proportional to the number of red balls (R). On that alone the expected value would be 7.
- The trade history pulls this down. Each time someone sold to me, it was more likely the counterparty knew R was below my bid.
- Updating on all four quotes (three sells at my bid and one no-trade) gives a public fair value of about **5.84**.

**Inventory.**
- At +3 I can buy only one more unit before my bid is pulled.
- So I'm placing the bid low, well below fair, to limit how often I buy.
- I'm placing the ask only modestly above fair, so a sale that reduces my long position is reasonably likely.

{"bid": 3.6, "ask": 6.5}

Selling at 6.5 is a modest edge above my estimated fair value of about 5.9, and it trims inventory.

**Belief before trading.** Draw 1 was red, so each possible red count R is weighted in proportion to R. The expected red count is then Σ R² / Σ R = 385/55 = 7.

**Quote 4: sold to me at 4.6, with fair value 7.**
- A noise trader sells here with probability P(N < −2.4/4.7) ≈ 0.305.
- An informed trader sells only if R ≤ 4.
- So the chance of this sell is about 0.44 when R ≤ 4 and about 0.24 when R ≥ 5.
- Updating on that drops the expected red count to about 6.5.

**Quote 5: sold to me at 3.6, with fair value about 6.5.**
- A noise trader sells here with probability about 0.27.
- An informed trader sells only if R ≤ 3.
- Updating again drops the expected red count to about 5.9.

**Quote choice.** I'm at the +4 limit, so only the ask is allowed, and I'd like to cut inventory. An ask a bit above 5.9 earns a margin on noise buyers. It still gives a reasonable chance of selling, and it limits the loss if an informed trader knows R is high.

{"bid": null, "ask": 6.5}

After two red draws, my estimate of the number of red balls (my fair value) is about 8.

- **Effect of the two draws:** with a uniform prior, drawing two reds gives a posterior proportional to R(R−1). That gives a mean of exactly 8.
- **Effect of trading history:** the stage 1 sells at very low prices could only be informed if R were 0 or 1, which two red draws rule out, so they change nothing. The sells at 4.6 and 3.6 pull the estimate down slightly, and the buy at 6.5 pushes it up. Taken together, my estimate stays at about 7.96.

I'm long 3, so I'll centre my quotes a little below fair value to make selling more likely than buying. The spread is wide because outcomes range from 2 to 10 red balls, so informed traders could hurt me on either side.

{"bid": 6.6, "ask": 8.8}

With two reds drawn, my fair value is about 8.2, so I'll quote 6.9 bid / 9.0 ask, leaning slightly towards selling because I'm long 2.

**Fair value from the draws.** Every draw so far was red, and red = 1 in the reveals.
- Each value of R from 0 to 10 starts equally likely, so after two reds the weight on R is proportional to R(R−1).
- That gives E[R] = Σ R²(R−1) / Σ R(R−1) = 2640/330 = 8.0.

**Adjusting for the trading history.** I reweighted R by how likely each past trade was if R were true.
- The stage‑2 sells at 4.6 and 3.6 push R down a little.
- The buys at 6.5 and 8.8 push R up, more strongly.
- Net, the public fair value comes to about 8.2–8.3.

**Quote.**
- I'm long 2, so I place the quote slightly below fair to encourage selling.
- An ask of 9.0 loses only if R = 10, and then by just 1. A noise trader buys there about 43% of the time.
- A bid of 6.9 is about 1.3 below fair. That spread is reasonable given how much noise traders' valuations vary (standard deviation 4.7).

{"bid": 6.9, "ask": 9.0}

Public fair value is about 8.0, and I'm skewing slightly lower because I'm long 3 and want to sell.

**Draws.** With a uniform prior and two reds drawn, the probability of R red balls is proportional to R(R−1). That gives an expected value of R of 2640/330 = 8.0.

**Trade history.**
- At quote 7 someone bought at 8.8. An informed counterparty only does that if R ≥ 9.
- At quote 8 someone sold at 6.9. An informed counterparty only does that if R ≤ 6.
- Together these two trades mostly make R = 7–8 less likely, and their effects on the average roughly cancel. The adjusted fair value is about 8.04.

**Quote.** Being long 3 means I'd rather sell than buy, so I set the spread a little below fair value. The ask at 8.7 can only be hit by an informed trader when R is 9 or 10. The bid at 6.5 protects me from informed sellers, who appear when R ≤ 6.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 8.7}

The fair value is about 8.6. I'm long 4, so I can only post an ask, and I'd set it at about 12.

**Fair value from the draws.** The prior is uniform on R = 0…10 red balls. The chance of drawing 3 reds is proportional to R(R−1)(R−2). Weighting each R by that gives a posterior mean of 17028 / 1980 = **8.6**.

**Adjusting for the trading history.** Sells at 6.9 and 6.5 point lower, and buys at 8.8 and 6.5 point higher. These roughly cancel, so the fair value stays at about **8.56**.

**Choosing the ask.**
- An informed trader buys only if R is above my ask. Since R can be at most 10, any ask of 10 or more never sells to an informed trader at a loss.
- A noise trader's valuation is about 8.6 plus noise with standard deviation 4.7. The expected profit per quote is 0.8 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 8.6):

| Ask | P(noise buys) | Expected profit |
|---|---|---|
| 10 | 0.38 | 0.43 |
| 11 | 0.305 | 0.585 |
| 12 | 0.235 | 0.64 |
| 13 | 0.174 | 0.61 |

The best ask is about 12. Selling a unit here would let me bid again later, but that option is worth little, so I'll post an ask of 12.

{"bid": null, "ask": 12.0}

With three red draws out of three, my estimate of the red-ball count is about **8.6**, and an ask near **12.2** maximises expected profit on this quote.

**Fair value.** With a uniform prior, the chance of drawing three reds in a row is proportional to R(R−1)(R−2). That gives these probabilities for the number of red balls R:

| R | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 0.36 | 0.25 | 0.17 | 0.11 | 0.06 |

The expected value E[R] is 8.6.

**Choosing the ask.** I am long 4, so I can only sell. The settlement value can be at most 10, so with any ask of 10 or higher an informed buyer never trades and I face no adverse selection. The only question is how much edge to take from noise buyers, who value the contract at 8.6 plus noise with standard deviation 4.7.

Expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise buys) × (ask − 8.6):

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 10 | 0.43 |
| 11 | 0.59 |
| 12 | 0.64 |
| 12.5 | 0.63 |
| 13 | 0.62 |

The curve peaks at about 12.2.

{"bid": null, "ask": 12.2}

**Quote: ask 12.0, no bid** (the bid is pulled at +4).

**Fair value.** All three draws were red. Given that, the chance of each red count R is proportional to R(R−1)(R−2).
- Weights for R = 3..10 are 6, 24, 60, 120, 210, 336, 504 and 720, which sum to 1980.
- Probabilities: R=10 is 0.364, R=9 is 0.255, R=8 is 0.170 and R=7 is 0.106.
- The expected settlement value is 17028 / 1980 = **8.6**.

**Ask choice.** Any ask at or above 10 cannot be hit by an informed trader, because R is at most 10. So the expected profit is just the noise-trader term: 0.8 × P(noise > ask − 8.6) × (ask − 8.6).

| Ask | Probability a noise trader buys | Expected profit |
|---|---|---|
| 10.1 | 0.375 | 0.45 |
| 11.0 | 0.305 | 0.59 |
| 12.0 | 0.235 | 0.64 |
| 12.5 | 0.203 | 0.63 |
| 13.0 | 0.175 | 0.62 |

The curve is flat near the top, and an ask around 12 maximises expected profit.

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 10 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 10. 3 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
With no draws revealed yet, the number of red balls is equally likely to be anything from 0 to 10, so fair value is 5.

**Choosing the spread.** I compared spread widths by expected profit per side:
- **Noise traders (80%):** their valuations are spread around 5 with standard deviation 4.7. A wider spread earns more on each trade but gets fewer trades.
- **Informed traders (20%):** they only trade when the true value is beyond my quote, so each of those trades loses money.

| Distance from 5 | Ask | Expected profit per side |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | 8 | about 0.57 |
| 3.5 | 8.5 | about 0.60 |
| 4 | 9 | about 0.61 |
| 4.5 | 9.5 | about 0.60 |

A spread of 4 either side comes out best. That gives a bid of 1 and an ask of 9.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 9.0}

With nothing revealed, the number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0 to 10, so the public fair value is 5. The last quote at 1/9 drew no trade, which tells us almost nothing.

I checked the expected profit from one quote on the ask side (the bid side is symmetric):
- **Noise traders:** they arrive with probability 0.8 and value the contract at about 5 ± 4.7. Each sale to them earns the ask minus 5.
- **Informed traders:** they arrive with probability 0.2 and buy only when the true value is above my ask, so each of those sales loses money.

| Ask | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|
| 7 | ≈ 0.43 |
| 8 | ≈ 0.57 |
| 8.5 | ≈ 0.60 |
| 9 | ≈ 0.61 |
| 10 | ≈ 0.58 |

Expected profit is fairly flat between 8.5 and 9. I'm quoting 1.5 / 8.5: it gives up almost nothing against 9, and it is more likely to trade, which tells me more about where the value lies.

{"bid": 1.5, "ask": 8.5}

With nothing revealed, the red count is uniform on 0 to 10, so fair value is 5. The two no-trade quotes so far were symmetric, so they don't move it.

For a half-spread s around 5, the expected profit per side is the noise traders' gain minus the informed losses:

| s | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0.54 | 0.11 | 0.43 |
| 3 | 0.63 | 0.05 | 0.57 |
| 3.5 | 0.64 | 0.04 | 0.60 |
| 4 | 0.63 | 0.02 | 0.61 |

Net profit is roughly flat between s = 3.5 and s = 4. I'll quote s = 3.8, giving a bid of 1.2 and an ask of 8.8.

{"bid": 1.2, "ask": 8.8}

Fair value is about 7.2, so I'm quoting a bid of 6.0 and an ask of 8.6.

1. **Draw 1 only.** Revealing a red ball makes each red count R more likely in proportion to R. The expected red count becomes Σ R² / Σ R = 385/55 = 7.

2. **Buy at 8.8 in quote 3.** An informed trader would only buy there if R is 9 or 10. A noise trader buys with probability P(Z > 3.8/4.7) ≈ 0.21. So the likelihood of that buy is 0.368 for R = 9 or 10 and 0.168 otherwise. On its own this lifts the estimate to about 7.7.

3. **No trades in quotes 1 and 2.** Quote 2's ask was 8.5, so an informed trader with R = 9 or 10 would have bought. Quote 1's ask was 9, so an informed trader with R = 10 would have bought. Neither happened. This scales the weight on R = 9 by about 0.69 and on R = 10 by about 0.49, relative to the other values.

4. **Combined.** The fair value is about 7.2, with a posterior standard deviation of roughly 2.

5. **Quote.**
   - One in five counterparties knows the true value, so I keep a wide spread.
   - I'm short 1, so I lean the quote slightly upward to make buying a little more likely.

{"bid": 6.0, "ask": 8.6}

Fair value is about 7.25, and I'm quoting bid 4.2 and ask 10.2.

**Fair value**
- Before any reveal, the number of red balls R is equally likely to be 0–10.
- After draw 1 came up red, the probability of each R is proportional to R. That gives an expected value of 7.
- Quote 3: a counterparty bought at 8.8 when the public fair value was 5. That is more likely if R is 9 or 10, because an informed trader buys only then.
- Quote 4: a counterparty sold at 6 when the public fair value was about 7.74. That is more likely if R is 5 or less, because an informed trader sells only then.
- Updating on both trades leaves the posterior mean at about 7.25.
- The posterior is wide: R of 9 or 10 has about 47% probability, and R of 3 or less about 12%.

**Ask**
- With the ask at 10 or above, informed buyers no longer hurt me, since R can be at most 10.
- Noise buyers then pay roughly 3 above fair value when they trade.
- The expected edge is about 0.6–0.64 per quote across asks from 10 to 11.

**Bid**
- A bid around 3.5–4 keeps the loss to informed sellers small (they sell only if R is 3 or less).
- It still earns about 3 below fair value from noise sellers.
- The expected edge is about 0.6 per quote.

{"bid": 4.2, "ask": 10.2}

Posterior fair value is about 7.6, so I'm quoting 5.6 / 9.4 around it. The spread is wide because the posterior is heavily weighted toward 9 and 10.

**Starting point from the reveal.** The prior on the number of red balls R is uniform on 0–10. Seeing red on draw 1 makes P(R) proportional to R. That gives E[R] = 385/55 = 7.0.

**Updating on the trade history.** I treated each past quote as evidence: 20% chance an informed trader, 80% a noise trader with noise SD 4.7. The noise-trader probabilities used rough estimates of the public fair value at each quote.
- **Quote 3:** a buyer took my ask at 8.8 when fair was 5. This favours R = 9 or 10, since an informed trader buys there.
- **Quote 4:** a seller hit my bid at 6. This favours R ≤ 5.
- **Quote 5:** no trade at 4.2 / 10.2. This favours R between 5 and 10.

Combining these, the posterior mean is about 7.6. Most of the extra weight sits on R = 9 and 10.

**Choosing the quotes.**
- **Ask at 9.4:** an informed trader only buys if R = 10, which has about 27% probability, and I lose less than 1 if so. Noise traders buy about 35% of the time at roughly 1.8 edge.
- **Bid at 5.6:** an informed trader sells if R ≤ 5, about 23% probability, losing me about 1.5. Noise traders sell about a third of the time at roughly 2 edge.

Both sides should have positive expected value.

{"bid": 5.6, "ask": 9.4}

Fair value is about 7.7. I'll quote a bid of 6.3 and an ask of 9.1, which sits a little high around that value.

**Posterior from the draws.** Before any reveals, the number of red balls R is equally likely to be 0 to 10. Two red draws in a row have probability R(R−1)/90, so the posterior weight on each R is proportional to R(R−1). From the draws alone, E[R] = 8.0.

**Adjusting for the trading history.** I scored each possible R by how likely it makes the six observed outcomes. An informed counterparty trades with probability 0.2, and a noise trader's valuation is fair value plus noise with standard deviation 4.7.
- The two sells, at 6 and 5.6, are more likely when R is 5 or below.
- The stage-1 buy at 8.8 is more likely when R is 9 or 10.
- The quotes with no trade cut weight a little from R of 4 or below and from R = 10.

After these adjustments the posterior mass is roughly:

| R | 2–4 | 5 | 6–8 | 9 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | 8% | 12% | 30% | 26% | 23% |

This gives a fair value of about 7.7.

**Why the quote is skewed.** Above fair value, most of the probability sits at R = 9 and R = 10. An ask of 9.1 is only hit by an informed counterparty if R = 10, which costs about 0.9 per trade. Below fair value the mass is smaller, so a bid of 6.3 gives up a moderate amount to informed sellers. My position of +1 leaves room to trade in either direction.

{"bid": 6.3, "ask": 9.1}

Using the two red draws and the trade history, the posterior mean is about 7.9. I'm already long 1 and the chance the urn has 9 or more reds is roughly 50%, so I keep the ask above 9. That way only an informed buyer with 10 reds can take it. I set the bid low enough to limit losses to informed sellers.

{"bid": 6.4, "ask": 9.2}

The draws alone put fair value at about **8**, and the trading history pulls that slightly lower, to about **7.8**. I'm quoting **6.5 / 9.0** around that.

**Fair value from the draws**
- Both revealed draws are red.
- The prior on the red count R is uniform on 0 to 10. The chance of drawing two reds is R(R−1)/90, so the posterior is proportional to R(R−1).
- That gives E[R] = Σ R²(R−1) / Σ R(R−1) = 2640 / 330 = **8**.
- The posterior standard deviation is about 1.9. That is a sizeable risk from informed traders, so I need a reasonably wide spread.

**What the trading history adds**
- In stage 2, counterparties sold to me at 6 and at 5.6. Fair value then was about 7, and noise traders sell below 6 fairly often. These sales still lean slightly towards a lower true value.
- In stage 3, nobody traded at 6.3/9.1 or at 6.4/9.2. That leans slightly towards a value somewhere between 7 and 9.
- Overall I take fair value to be about **7.8**.

**The quote**
- I set a spread of roughly ±1.3 around 7.8 and shade the ask down slightly because I'm already long one unit.

{"bid": 6.5, "ask": 9.0}

By Bayes' rule, the public fair value is about **8.6**, so I'll quote wide around it: **bid 5.4, ask 11.8**.

**Fair value from the draws.** The prior is uniform over 0 to 10 red balls. After 3 red draws out of 3, the posterior for R red balls is proportional to R(R−1)(R−2). That gives E[R] = 3 + 7·(4/5) = **8.6**.

**Effect of the trading history.** I re-weighted the posterior by how likely each past trade or no-trade was under each R. Each was treated as 20% informed and 80% noise with standard deviation 4.7. Wins for each R:
- Values of 9 or 10 are favoured by the early buy at 8.8.
- Values of 9 or below are favoured by the sells at 6 and 5.6.
- Values of 7 to 9 are favoured by the two no-trades.
- Values of 6 or below are favoured by the sell at 6.5.

These effects roughly cancel, and the fair value stays at about **8.6**. The posterior is concentrated on R = 9, with R = 10 at about 17% and R ≤ 5 at about 4%.

**Quote placement.**
- **Ask side:** R can never exceed 10, so an ask above 10 can never be hit by an informed trader. The ask only needs to balance noise-trader fill probability against edge. For normal noise, the optimum is about 0.75σ above fair value, so roughly 12.
- **Bid side:** an informed trader only sells below the bid if R ≤ 5, which has about 4% probability. So a bid around 3.5 below fair value is close to optimal there too.
- **Inventory:** I am risk-neutral and the position limits are not binding at +2. So I don't need to skew the quote; I lean very slightly toward selling.

{"bid": 5.4, "ask": 11.8}

Bid 5.0 and ask 12.0, both well outside my estimate of fair value (about 8.3), with the bid shaded a little lower because I'm already long 2.

**Fair value from the reveals alone.** All three draws were red. Starting from a uniform prior, the chance of R red balls is proportional to C(R,3). That gives R = 10 at 0.36, R = 9 at 0.25 and R = 8 at 0.17, with an expected value of 8.6.

**Adjusting for the trading history.** I weighted each R by how likely the observed trades were, using a 0.2 chance of an informed trader.
- The sells at my bids (6, 5.6 and 6.5) point toward lower R.
- The no-trade quotes in stage 3 (bids 6.3 and 6.4, asks 9.1 and 9.2) favour R between 7 and 9.
- This brings my fair-value estimate down to about **8.3**.

**Quote sizing.** Each side is set to maximise noise-trader edge minus losses to informed traders.
- **Ask:** an informed trader never pays more than 10, so an ask above 10 carries no risk from informed traders. A noise trader's valuation is about 8.3 ± 4.7. Expected edge is about 0.61 at an ask of 11, peaks near 0.64 at 12, and is back to 0.60 at 13.
- **Bid:** an informed trader sells only if R is below my bid. At a bid of about 5 that has a probability of roughly 0.04 and costs little each time. Expected noise edge is about 0.6, and it is flat between bids of 4.5 and 5.5.

{"bid": 5.0, "ask": 12.0}

With draws 1, 2 and 3 all red, I set the fair value at about 8.6. This is the last quote, so I'm pricing it purely on expected profit for this one trade.

**Fair value.** The chance of drawing three reds given R red balls is proportional to R(R−1)(R−2). With a uniform prior, that gives this posterior on R:

| R | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 | 5 | 4 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| P | 0.364 | 0.255 | 0.170 | 0.106 | 0.061 | 0.030 | 0.012 | 0.003 |

The mean is 17028 / 1980 ≈ 8.6. Three of the four earlier trades were customers selling to me, which might push the public fair value a little lower. I ignore that here.

**Ask.**
- Settlement can't exceed 10, so any ask above 10 is never hit by an informed trader.
- The noise payoff, 0.8 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 8.6), is roughly:
  - 0.52 at an ask of 10.5
  - 0.62 at 11.5
  - 0.64 at 12
  - 0.63 at 12.5
- I quote 12.

**Bid.**
- The informed loss is 0.2 × the expected amount by which the bid exceeds settlement. This is small, because low settlement values are unlikely.
- Expected profit net of that loss is roughly:
  - 0.44 at a bid of 7
  - 0.59 at 6
  - 0.62 at 5.5
  - 0.635 at 5
- I quote 5.2, near the top of that range.

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 10 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 10. 3 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
Before any reveal the red count is uniform on 0 to 10, so fair value is 5 and the spread of true values is wide (standard deviation about 3.2). I picked the spread by weighing the gain from noise traders against the loss to informed traders on each side.

For a quote d away from fair value (ask = 5 + d), the expected profit per quote is:
- **Noise traders:** 0.8 × P(noise > d) × d, with noise having standard deviation 2.4.
- **Informed traders:** minus 0.2 × the average of (V − ask) over true values V above the ask.
