Before any draws are revealed, the red count is equally likely to be 0 through 10, so fair value is 5. I'll quote symmetrically around 5 and choose the half-spread h that maximises expected profit on this quote.

**Trade-off for each half-spread h:**
- **Noise traders** (probability 0.65) trade when their valuation falls outside 5 ± h, and I earn h on each such trade.
- **Informed traders** (probability 0.35) trade only when the true count lies beyond my quote, and I lose the difference.

| h | Gain from noise traders | Loss to informed traders | Net expected profit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.0 | 0.53 | 0.38 | 0.14 |
| 2.5 | 0.48 | 0.29 | 0.20 |
| **3.0** | **0.41** | **0.19** | **0.22** |
| 3.5 | 0.33 | 0.13 | 0.20 |
| 4.0 | 0.25 | 0.06 | 0.19 |

A half-spread of 3 gives the highest expected profit, so I quote bid 2 and ask 8.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 8.0}

Fair value is 5. The red count is uniform on 0 to 10, and a no-trade at a symmetric 2/8 quote leaves the mean unchanged. I priced each side of the quote at a distance d from 5:
- **Noise traders:** I earn d on each fill. Fills come with probability 0.65 × P(noise > d), with noise standard deviation 2.4.
- **Informed traders:** I lose on fills when the true value is beyond my quote.

| d | Quote side | Expected profit per side |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | 7 | about 0.07 |
| 2.5 | 7.5 | about 0.10 |
| 3 | 8 | about 0.11 (best) |
| 3.5 | 8.5 | about 0.10 |

So I keep the quote at 2 / 8.

{"bid": 2, "ask": 8}

With no reveals yet and no trades, fair value is still 5, so I quote symmetrically at 2.5 / 7.5.

- **Fair value:** The prior on red balls is uniform over 0 to 10, so its mean is 5. The two earlier no-trade quotes at 2/8 make middle values a little more likely. They don't shift the centre because the update is symmetric.
- **Choosing the width:** A narrower spread earns more from noise traders but loses more to informed traders. A half-spread of about 2.5 to 3 roughly maximises expected profit.
  - **Half-spread 2:** gains about 0.53 per quote from noise traders, loses about 0.28 to informed traders, net about 0.25.
  - **Half-spread 2.5:** gains about 0.49, loses about 0.19, net about 0.29.
  - **Half-spread 3:** gains about 0.41, loses about 0.10, net about 0.30.
- **Pick:** I chose 2.5 over 3 because the two options are close. The tighter quote also trades more often while there is time left to adjust.

{"bid": 2.5, "ask": 7.5}

Given that draw 1 was red, the posterior is P(R = r) ∝ r. That gives a fair value of E[R] = 385/55 = 7, with a standard deviation of about 2.45. The three earlier quotes produced no trades, so the history tells us little.

I compared, for each side, the expected loss to informed traders against the expected profit from noise traders.

**Ask side:**
| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 8.5 | +0.135 |
| 9.0 | +0.199 |
| 9.2 | +0.206 |
| 9.5 | +0.210 |

Profit is nearly flat between 9.2 and 9.5, so I chose 9.3.

**Bid side:**
| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 5.0 | +0.136 |
| 4.5 | +0.147 |
| 4.0 | +0.142 |

4.5 is the best bid.

{"bid": 4.5, "ask": 9.3}

Bid 3.0, ask 8.0: a wide spread around a fair value I estimate at about 5.4.

**Fair value before the quote 4 trade.** With draw 1 red, the chance of each red-ball count R is proportional to R. That gives E[R] = 385/55 = 7.

**Effect of the sale at 4.5.** I treated noise traders as centred on the fair value of 7.
- A noise trader sells at 4.5 with probability about 0.15.
- An informed trader sells only if R ≤ 4.
- Updating on that sale gives P(R ≤ 4) ≈ 0.51, and my fair value falls to about 5.4.
- If the public fair value does not reflect this trade and stays near 7, noise traders lean towards buying. That would make a high ask even more attractive.

**Ask.** Informed traders only buy if R ≥ 8 or 9, and are most often wrong-footing me when R is 9 or 10. Noise traders, with a standard deviation of 2.4, often value above 8 and pay a large edge over fair value. My estimated net edge rises as the ask moves up through about 7.5–8.5. I chose 8.0 because I am long 1 and want some chance of selling.

**Bid.** At 3.0, informed sellers only come when R ≤ 2. Noise sellers give an edge of about 2.4 when they trade. The estimated net edge is about +0.17 per quote, the best of the bid levels I compared.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 8.0}

Fair value is now about 5.3.

- **Draw 1 was red.** That makes P(R = r) proportional to r, so the expected number of red balls is 385/55 = 7.
- **The sell at my 4.5 bid (quote 4).** Informed traders sell there only if R ≤ 4, while noise traders sell there only about 15% of the time. This pulls the estimate down to about 5.4.
- **No trade at 3/8 (quote 5).** This is consistent with R between 3 and 8. It moves the estimate slightly further, to about 5.3.

The distribution of possible values is still wide, so I keep a fairly wide spread. Because I am already long one unit, I set the quote slightly low.

{"bid": 3.4, "ask": 7.0}

With one red and one blue drawn, the posterior on the number of red balls is centred on 5 with a standard deviation of about 2.2. The two trades so far roughly cancel out, so I'm quoting symmetrically around 5.

**Posterior on red balls, R.** The chance of drawing red then blue is R/10 × (10−R)/9, so P(R) ∝ R(10−R).
- The weights for R = 0 to 10 are 0, 9, 16, 21, 24, 25, 24, 21, 16, 9, 0, summing to 165.
- The weights are symmetric around 5, so the mean is 5.
- The variance is 792/165 = 4.8, giving a standard deviation of about 2.2.

**Trading history.**
- At quote 4 (after draw 1 = red, when fair value was about 7), someone sold to me at 4.5. That points towards a low value.
- At quote 6, someone bought from me at 7. That points towards a high value.
- These two signals roughly offset, so I take public fair value to be about 5.

**Quote.** I'll quote symmetrically around 5. The spread is wide enough to protect against informed traders, whose valuations spread across the posterior, while still catching noise traders, whose valuations are about 5 ± 2.4.

{"bid": 3.6, "ask": 6.4}

The posterior mean of the red-ball count is 5, so I'm quoting 3.1 / 6.9 around it.

**Posterior.** One red and one blue have been drawn, so the posterior weight on R red balls is proportional to R(10−R).
- This is symmetric around 5, so the mean is 5.
- The standard deviation is about 2.2.
- Recent trading leaves fair value near 5: I sold at 7 and bought at 4.5, which roughly cancel, and the symmetric 3.6/6.4 quote got no trade.

**Choosing the quotes.** Settlement is a whole number, so I put each quote just inside an integer.
- **Ask 6.9:** an informed trader buys only if R is 7 or more. That costs about 0.08 per quote on average.
- **Edge from noise traders:** a 1.9 gap from fair value earns about 0.26 per quote from them.
- **Net:** about +0.18 per side.
- **Wider option:** a 7.9 ask gives a similar net (+0.19) but trades much less often, so I prefer 6.9.
- **Bid 3.1:** this is the mirror of the ask, by symmetry around 5.

{"bid": 3.1, "ask": 6.9}

With one red and one blue drawn, I estimate fair value at about 4.9 and quote bid 2.9, ask 7.0.

**Posterior after the draws.** The prior on the number of red balls R is uniform on 0 to 10. The chance of drawing red then blue is R/10 × (10−R)/9, so the posterior is proportional to R(10−R) for R = 1 to 9:

| R | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weight (out of 165) | 9 | 16 | 21 | 24 | 25 | 24 | 21 | 16 | 9 |

- The mean is 5 and the standard deviation is about 2.2.
- The sale at my bid of 3.1 in quote 8 tilts things slightly lower. An informed seller (R ≤ 3) is a bit more likely than a noise seller, so I put fair value near 4.9.

**Choosing the ask.** Expected profit per quote is the gain from noise trades minus the loss from informed trades:

| Ask | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6.1 | 0.23 | 0.16 | 0.07 |
| 6.9 | 0.27 | 0.08 | 0.18 |
| 7.0 | 0.26 | 0.07 | 0.19 |
| 7.5 | 0.24 | 0.05 | 0.20 |

The curve is flat from about 7.0 to 7.5. The bid side is symmetric, so the best bid sits around 2.5 to 3.0.

**Adjusting for position.** I am long 1 and fair value leans slightly low, so I shade both sides down a little.

{"bid": 2.9, "ask": 7.0}

Three balls have been drawn: 1 red and 2 blue. With a uniform prior on the number of red balls, the remaining 7 balls each have a Beta(2,3) chance of being red, with mean 0.4. So the expected settlement is 1 + 7 × 0.4 = **3.8**. Possible values run from 1 to 8 red balls.

I compared expected profit per quote for different prices. Noise traders are centred on 3.8 with SD 2.4. Informed traders, 35% of arrivals, know the true count.

- **Ask:** an ask near 6.0 is best, earning about 0.22 per quote. Below about 5 the informed buyers (true count 5 or more) wipe out the edge.
- **Bid:** a bid between 1.5 and 2.0 is best, earning about 0.23. A bid just under 3 leaves too much exposure to informed sellers when the true count is 1 or 2.

I'm long 2 units, so I lean the ask slightly lower to make selling a little more likely.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 5.9}

The fair value after the three revealed draws is about **3.8**, so I'll quote a bid of 1.8 and an ask of 6.0.

**Fair value.** The prior on the number of red balls is uniform over 0–10. We have seen 1 red and 2 blue, so the posterior weight on r red balls is r·(10−r)(9−r)/2:

| Red balls | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weight | 36 | 56 | 63 | 60 | 50 | 36 | 21 | 8 |

The weights total 330, and the posterior mean is 1254 / 330 = **3.8**.

**Choosing the quotes.** For each side, I weighed two effects:
- the gain from noise traders, whose valuations are 3.8 plus Normal noise with sd 2.4;
- the loss to informed traders, who know the true count (between 1 and 8).

| Bid | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net per quote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.9 | 0.207 | 0.126 | ≈ 0.08 |
| 2.5 | 0.249 | 0.087 | ≈ 0.16 |
| 2.0 | 0.265 | 0.038 | ≈ 0.23 |
| 1.5 | 0.253 | 0.019 | ≈ 0.23 |

The bid is best between 1.5 and 2.0, so I'll use 1.8.

| Ask | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net per quote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5.5 | 0.264 | 0.074 | ≈ 0.19 |
| 6.0 | 0.257 | 0.039 | ≈ 0.22 |

The ask is best at about 6.0.

My position is +2, so there is no constraint on either side. Being long, I'd mildly prefer to sell, but the ask's expected value is nearly flat around 6.0, so I'll keep it there.

{"bid": 1.8, "ask": 6.0}

This is the last quote, so I priced it purely on expected profit at settlement.

**Fair value.** The draws so far are 1 red and 2 blue. With a uniform prior on the number of red balls R, the posterior is proportional to R(10−R)(9−R):

| R | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weight (out of 660) | 72 | 112 | 126 | 120 | 100 | 72 | 42 | 16 |

That gives E[R] = 2508 / 660 = 3.8. I took the public fair value to be 3.8.

**Ask.**
- Noise traders buy with probability P(noise > a − 3.8), and I earn a − 3.8 each time.
- Informed traders buy only when R > a, costing me E[(R − a)+].
- Net expected profit:
  - at a = 5.5: about 0.19
  - at a = 6.0: about 0.22, roughly the peak
  - at a = 6.5: about 0.20
- I'll ask **6.0**.

**Bid.**
- Noise traders sell with probability P(noise < b − 3.8), and I earn 3.8 − b.
- Informed traders sell only when R < b, which here means R = 1.
- Net expected profit:
  - at b = 2.0: about 0.227
  - at b = 1.5 to 1.6: about 0.234, the peak
- I'll bid **1.6**.

My position is +2, so buying one more unit stays within the limit.

{"bid": 1.6, "ask": 6.0}

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 11 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 11. 4 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
The prior mean is 55, because the number of red balls is uniform on 0 to 11 and the contract pays 10 per red ball.

**Ask side.** The expected profit at ask a is:

0.5 × E[(a − V)·1{V > a}] + 0.5 × P(noise > a − 55) × (a − 55)

The first term is the informed traders and is negative. The second term is the noise traders. Evaluating a few asks:

| Ask | Informed term | Noise term | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 85 | −3.75 | +5.88 | +1.07 |
| 95 | −1.67 | +5.06 | +1.70 |
| 100 | −0.83 | +4.47 | +1.82 |
| 101 | −0.75 | +4.34 | +1.80 |

The net peaks at an ask of about 100.

**Bid side.** The setup is symmetric around 55, so the best bid is about 10.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 100}

With no draws revealed yet, the number of red balls is equally likely to be anything from 0 to 11, so the public fair value is 10 × 5.5 = **55**. The last quote at 10/100 didn't trade, which tells us almost nothing, so fair value stays at 55.

I chose the spread by trading off two things on each side:
- **Noise traders** value the contract at 55 plus Normal noise with standard deviation 35. They are profitable to trade with, and a wider spread earns more per trade but trades less often.
- **Informed traders** know the true value, which is equally likely to be any of 0, 10, …, 110. They only trade when the value lies beyond my price, so every trade with them loses money.

Expected profit per side, by distance from 55:

| Distance from 55 | Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|---|
| 35 | 90 | about 1.5 |
| 40 | 95 | about 1.7 |
| 45 | 100 | about 1.8 (best) |
| 50 | 105 | about 1.7 |

The bid side is symmetric, so the best quote is about 45 either side of 55: 10 / 100.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 100}

With two blue draws revealed, the expected number of red balls is 2.25, so the public fair value is about 22.5.

**Posterior.** With a uniform prior, P(R) is proportional to (11−R)(10−R). That gives P(V=0) ≈ 25%, P(10) ≈ 20%, P(20) ≈ 16%, P(30) ≈ 13%, with a thin tail up to 90.

**Ask.** Each ask trades off profit from noise buyers against losses to informed buyers when the true value is above the ask. The expected profit per quote is:

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 39 | ≈ 0.9 |
| 49 | ≈ 2.1 |
| 59 | ≈ 2.3 |
| 69 | ≈ 2.0 |

The best ask is about 59.

**Bid.** A bid of 0 is never hit by an informed seller, because the value cannot fall below 0. Noise sellers below 0 give about 22.5 × 0.26 ≈ 5.9 in expectation, so about 2.9 per quote. Any bid above 0 starts losing to informed sellers when the value is 0, which has a 25% chance. The expected profit drops at a bid of 1 and turns negative by a bid of 19.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 59}

After two blue draws, the expected settlement value is about **19.8**. I'm quoting bid 0 and ask 51.

**Fair value.**
- The prior on the number of red balls R is uniform over 0 to 11.
- After two blue draws, the posterior weight on R is proportional to (11−R)(10−R). That gives E[R] = 2.25, so the fair value is 22.5.
- At the last quote (bid 0, ask 59) nobody traded. An informed trader would have bought if R ≥ 6, so the lack of a trade lowers those states' weight.
- After that update, E[R] ≈ 1.98, so the fair value is about 19.8.

**Ask.** The value can only be a multiple of 10. I compared expected profit for asks just above each multiple of 10. Each figure is gains from noise traders minus losses to informed traders.

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 31 | 0.3 |
| 41 | 2.1 |
| 51 | 2.6 |
| 61 | 2.3 |

An ask of 51 does best.

**Bid.**
- At a bid of 0, an informed trader never sells, because the value cannot be below 0.
- Noise traders sell to me with probability about 0.29, at about 20 below fair value. That makes 0 the best bid, at about 2.8 expected profit.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 51}

Bid 0, ask 60.

**Fair value is about 22.** The prior on red balls is uniform over 0–11. Three blue draws give each red count a likelihood proportional to C(11−R, 3). The buy at my ask of 51 in stage 2 is also informative. Before draw 3 the public fair value was about 22.5, so an informed trader buys at 51 when R ≥ 6, and a noise trader buys about 21% of the time. That multiplies the weight of R ≥ 6 by about 0.60 and the weight of R ≤ 5 by about 0.10.

The resulting posterior is about 29% for R=0, 21% for R=1 and 15% for R=2, falling off from there. There is a tail of about 10% at R=6 (value 60) and about 5% for R=7 or 8 (values 70–80). The expected value is about 2.21 red balls, so fair value is about 22.

**Bid at 0.** An informed trader never sells below 0, so a bid of 0 cannot lose. A noise trader sells there with probability about 0.27, and I gain about 22 when that happens. A buy would also reduce my short. Higher bids lose more to informed sellers when R=0 than they gain from extra noise trades.

**Ask at 60.** I checked the expected profit of each ask against the posterior tail. Asks in the 59–61 range score best, at about +2.3 per quote. Lower asks such as 50 or 55 lose more to informed buyers at R ≥ 6 than they gain from noise buyers.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 60}

After three blue draws, my estimate of the settlement value is about 16, and I quote bid 0, ask 49.

**Updated estimate.** Three draws, all blue. Given that, the chance of each red count R is proportional to C(11−R, 3), for R = 0 to 8.
- These weights are 165, 120, 84, 56, 35, 20, 10, 4 and 1.
- The expected red count is 792/495 = 1.6, so the fair value is about 16.
- No one bought at 60 last quote, which nudges this slightly lower.
- R = 0 (value 0) has probability 1/3.

**Ask.** Informed traders buy only when the value is above my ask. At an ask of about 49, they buy only if R ≥ 5, which has probability about 7%.
- Noise traders (valuation around 16, spread 35) still buy about 17% of the time at a profit of about 33.
- Expected profit per quote is about 2.6, the best of the asks I checked.

**Bid.** With a bid of 0, informed traders never sell, since the value can't be below 0.
- Noise traders sell about 32% of the time at a profit of about 16.
- Expected profit per quote is about 2.6, higher than any positive bid, because a positive bid lets informed traders sell when R = 0.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 49}

The contract is underpriced well below the old quotes, so I'll post a bid of 0 and an ask of 41. These are the prices that maximise expected profit against the mix of informed and noise traders.

**Fair value now.** With the number of red balls R equally likely to be 0 to 11, the chance of 4 blue draws in a row is proportional to C(11−R, 4). That makes the posterior proportional to 330, 210, 126, 70, 35, 15, 5, 1 for R = 0 to 7, which sum to 792.
- E[R] = 924 / 792 ≈ 1.167, so the public fair value is about 11.7.
- P(R = 0) ≈ 0.42, so there is a 42% chance the contract settles at 0.

**Bid.** At a bid of 0, an informed trader never sells, because the value cannot be below 0. A noise trader sells to me about 37% of the time at roughly 11.7 below fair value. Any bid above 0 lets informed traders with a value of 0 sell to me. On balance a bid of 0 is best, worth about +2.2.

**Ask.** I traded off the margin earned from noise buyers against losses to informed buyers when the true value is above my ask:

| Ask | Expected value |
|-----|----------------|
| 30 | +2.2 |
| 35 | +2.6 |
| 40 | +2.8 |
| 45 | +2.7 |

The peak is around 40–42.

**Position.** I am short 1, so selling one more unit takes me to −2, which is within the limit.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 41}

With four blue draws revealed, the expected settlement value is about 11.67.

**Posterior.** With a uniform prior on R, the chance of seeing 4 blue in 4 draws is proportional to C(11−R, 4). This gives:

| Settlement value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.417 |
| 10 | 0.265 |
| 20 | 0.159 |
| 30 | 0.088 |
| 40 | 0.044 |
| 50 | 0.019 |
| 60 | 0.006 |
| 70 | 0.001 |

The expected value E[10R] is 924/792 × 10, which is about 11.67. This is the public fair value. Noise traders value the contract at 11.67 plus noise with standard deviation 35.

**Ask side.** The expected profit is ½·E[(a−V)·1{V>a}] + ½·(a−11.67)·P(N > a−11.67).

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 35 | 2.59 |
| 40 | 2.78 |
| 42 | 2.78 |
| 45 | 2.73 |

The best ask is about 41.

**Bid side.** I am short 1, so buying is allowed. Any bid of 1 or more loses to informed sellers when V = 0, which has probability 0.42.

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 1 | 1.82 |
| 0 | 2.16 |
| −10 | 2.90 |
| −15 | 2.99 |

The rules only forbid a bid above the ask, so I read a negative bid as allowed. The profit curve is flat between −10 and −15, so I choose a modestly negative bid.

{"bid": -10, "ask": 41}

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 10 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 10. 3 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
The prior has red balls uniform on 0 to 10, so the fair value is 5 with a standard deviation of about 3.16. I picked the half-spread s around 5 by trading off profit from noise traders against losses to informed traders on each side. The table shows the per-side expected profit for the ask side; the bid side is symmetric.

| s | Informed loss (0.35 weight) | Noise gain (0.65 weight) | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.0 | 0.191 | 0.263 | 0.072 |
| 2.5 | 0.143 | 0.242 | 0.099 |
| 3.0 | 0.095 | 0.206 | 0.111 |
| 3.5 | 0.064 | 0.165 | 0.101 |

The net is highest at s = 3, so I quote 2 / 8.

{"bid": 2.0, "ask": 8.0}

Updated fair value is about 2.84; I'll bid 0.5 and ask 6.0.

**Updating on the first trade.** The prior on red balls is uniform over 0–10, with mean 5. Someone sold at my bid of 2.
- An informed trader sells at 2 only if the true count is below 2, so only when it is 0 or 1.
- A noise trader values the contract at 5 plus noise with standard deviation 2.4. They sell below 2 with probability about 0.106.
- So the chance of that sell was 0.35 + 0.65 × 0.106 ≈ 0.42 for a count of 0 or 1. For any count from 2 to 10 it was about 0.069.
- After the update, counts of 0 and 1 each have about 28.7% probability. Each count from 2 to 10 has about 4.7%.
- The expected count is now about **2.84**.

**Choosing the ask.** I compared the expected gain from noise buyers with the expected loss to informed buyers at each ask:

| Ask | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 4 | about −0.11 |
| 5 | about +0.01 |
| 6 | about +0.03 |
| 7 | about +0.01 |

An ask of 6 is best.

**Choosing the bid.** The same comparison for the bid:

| Bid | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 1.5 | about +0.05 |
| 1.0 | about +0.16 |
| 0.5 | about +0.20 |

A bid of 0.5 is best. I am long one unit, but buying another unit this cheaply still has positive expected value.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 6.0}

The public fair value is about 2.7, and I'm quoting bid 0.5 and ask 5.5 around it.

**Belief after quote 1.** The prior on red balls (R) is uniform on 0 to 10, so the starting mean is 5. A counterparty sold at my bid of 2.
- An informed trader would only sell there if R is 0 or 1.
- A noise trader with valuation 5 + N(0, 2.4) would sell there with probability about 0.11.
- So R = 0 and R = 1 each became about 6 times more likely than the other values.

**Belief after quote 2.** Nobody traded at bid 0.5, ask 6.
- An informed trader would pass only if R is between 1 and 6.
- That makes R from 1 to 6 somewhat more likely, and R = 0 or R from 7 to 10 somewhat less likely.

**Posterior now.**
- R = 0: about 0.21
- R = 1: about 0.36
- R = 2 to 6: about 0.06 each
- R = 7 to 10: about 0.034 each
- Mean (public fair value): about 2.7

**Choosing the quote.** For each price, I set the expected profit from noise traders against the expected loss to informed traders.
- **Ask:** the expected edge per quote was about +0.03 at 4.5, +0.07 at 5.5 and +0.05 at 6.5. So 5.5 is best.
- **Bid:** the expected edge was about +0.23 at 0.3, +0.22 at 0.5, +0.20 at 0.9 and +0.07 at 1.5. A low bid is best, because an informed trader sells at 0.5 only if R = 0.
- I chose 0.5 because it is essentially tied with 0.3 for the best edge.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 5.5}

Posterior mean ≈ 1.6. Draw 1 being blue gives weights ∝ (10−R), which alone puts the mean at 3. The sell at 2 and the no-trade quotes then push weight onto R ≤ 1. My posterior is about 52% on R=1 and 19% on R=0.

- **Bid:** 0 is about the best expected-profit bid. It loses nothing to an informed seller, since the value can't go below 0, and it still catches noise sellers.
- **Ask:** around 3.9–4 is optimal. It balances noise buyers against informed buyers when R is 5 or more. I shade it slightly to 3.9 because I'm already long.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 3.9}

Posterior fair value is about 1.35. Draw 1 being blue and the trade history together push most of the weight onto R=1 (about 56%) and R=0 (about 20%).

**Reveal.** A blue first draw makes R ∝ (10−R). On its own that gives a mean of 3.

**Trade history.** I updated the posterior on each past quote, assuming an informed trader 35% of the time and a noise trader (public fair value plus N(0, 2.4)) otherwise:
- **Quote 1:** someone sold at 2. That is strong evidence that R is 0 or 1.
- **Quotes 2 and 3:** no trade between 0.5 and about 6. This removes some weight from R=0 and from high values of R.
- **Quote 4:** no trade between 0 and 3.9. This cuts weight on R≥4.

**Quote choice.**
- **Bid 0.3:** an informed trader only sells here if R=0, which loses me just 0.3 per unit. Noise traders sell often, with about 1 point of edge per trade.
- **Ask 2.4:** an informed trader only buys if R≥3, about 15% probability. Noise traders buy about 32% of the time, with about 1 point of edge.
- **Position:** I am long 1, so I set the ask slightly closer to fair to make a sale a little more likely.

{"bid": 0.3, "ask": 2.4}

The draw and the trading history put the expected red count near 1.2, so I quote a tight spread around it: bid 0.5, ask 2.0.

**Draw only.** Drawing a blue ball makes each red count R proportional to (10 − R). On its own that gives an expected value of exactly 3.

**Adding the trading history.** This step uses my own estimates of what public fair value was at each quote.
- **Quote 1:** someone sold at 2 while the prior fair value was 5. That points towards an informed seller who knows R is 0 or 1.
- **Quotes 2 and 3:** no trade at bid 0.5 makes R = 0 less likely, because an informed trader with R = 0 would have sold there.
- **Quote 4:** no trade at ask 3.9 makes R of 4 or more less likely.
- **Quote 5:** no trade between 0.3 and 2.4 is fairly strong evidence. Only informed traders with R = 1 or 2 stay out, and a noise trader stays out only about 21–32% of the time.

**Posterior.**

| R | Probability |
|---|---|
| 1 | about 73% |
| 2 | about 11% |
| 0 | about 10% |
| 3 or more | a small tail |

The mean is about 1.2. Public fair value is probably between 1.2 and 1.7.

**Quote.**
- **Ask 2.0:** an informed trader with R = 2 does not buy, since its valuation is not above 2. Only R of 3 or more buys, and those are now unlikely.
- **Bid 0.5:** only an informed trader with R = 0 sells to me here, and that costs just 0.5 per unit.
- **Noise traders:** both sides capture spread from them around the fair value.
- **Position:** being long 1 is fine with this slight downward skew.

{"bid": 0.5, "ask": 2.0}

With two blue draws revealed, my fair value is about 1.9, and I'm quoting a wide spread of 0.3 / 4.0 around it.

**Fair value.** The prior on the number of red balls R is uniform from 0 to 10. Seeing two blue draws has likelihood proportional to (10−R)(9−R).
- Posterior weights for R = 0…8 are 90, 72, 56, 42, 30, 20, 12, 6, 2. R = 9 and R = 10 are ruled out.
- The weights sum to 330, so the posterior mean is 660 / 330 = 2.0.
- The sell at 2 in quote 1 nudges fair value down slightly, so I use about 1.9.

**Ask side.** An informed buyer comes when R is 4 or more, which has probability 0.21. When that happens, the average R is about 5.0.
- At an ask of 3.5, the expected edge per quote is about +0.15.
- An ask between 3.9 and 4.5 gives about +0.18, the best of those I tried.

**Bid side.** The only informed sell risk is R = 0, which has probability 0.27.
- Bids between 0.0 and 0.3 give an expected edge of about +0.24 to +0.26 per quote.
- I set the bid at 0.3. Being long one unit, I want to skew the bid low rather than add to the position.

{"bid": 0.3, "ask": 4.0}

The posterior centres on about 0.9 red balls, so I'll quote a bid of 0.0 and an ask of 2.6.

**Posterior from the draws.** The prior is uniform on R = 0 to 10. Two blue draws give each R a weight of (10−R)(9−R). On the draws alone, the expected count is 660 / 330 = 2.0.

**Update from the trading history.** Several quotes tell us something:
- Quote 1 (stage 1): someone sold at 2. An informed seller would do that only if R is 0 or 1.
- Quotes 2 to 6: no trades. An informed trader would have traded on those quotes if R were 0 or high (roughly 3 or more). The silence favours R of 1 or 2.
- Quote 7: someone sold at 0.3. An informed seller would do that only if R = 0.

Combining these with the draw weights gives:

| R | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 or more |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | ≈ 23% | ≈ 65% | ≈ 8% | ≈ 4% |

The expected value is about 0.93.

**Choosing the quote.**
- **Bid 0.0:** an informed trader never sells here, because R cannot be below 0. A noise trader sells with about 35% probability, at an edge of about 0.9.
- **Ask about 2.6:** an informed trader buys only if R is 3 or more, which is about 4% likely. A noise trader buys with about 25% probability, at an edge of about 1.6. Around 2.5 to 3 the expected profit is roughly flat, and selling also trims my long position of +2.

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 2.6}

Quote bid 0 and ask 2.8. My estimate of the contract's value is about 0.8, below the 2.0 the urn alone implies, because the trading history points to a low count.

**Value from the urn alone.** After two blue draws, each possible red count R is weighted by (10−R)(9−R). This puts most weight on low counts:
- R = 0 has weight 90 out of 330.
- R = 1 has weight 72.
- R = 2 has weight 56.
- The weights keep falling, and R = 9 and R = 10 are ruled out.

The average red count under these weights is exactly 2.0.

**Updating on the trades.**
- **Quote 7 (sale at my 0.3 bid):** An informed trader would only sell at 0.3 if R = 0. So the sale makes R = 0 about three times as likely relative to other counts.
- **Quote 8 (no trade at 0 / 2.6):** An informed trader would not trade there if R is 0, 1 or 2. So the lack of a trade shifts weight further toward low counts.
- **Result:** About 62% of the weight is now on R = 0, and the expected count is about 0.83. The noise traders also centre on roughly this value, since they use all public information.

**Ask side.** I am long 2 and want to sell. For each ask I weighed the profit from noise buyers against the expected loss to informed buyers:

| Ask | Net expected value |
|---|---|
| 1.5 | +0.05 |
| 2.1 | +0.17 |
| 2.6 | +0.21 |
| 3.1 | +0.21 |

The value is flat between about 2.6 and 3.1, so I pick 2.8.

**Bid side.** At a bid of 0, an informed trader never sells, because a count of 0 is not below 0. Noise traders still sell there about 36% of the time, which is worth about +0.20 per quote. Raising the bid to 0.1 lets the informed trader sell whenever R = 0, which lowers the value to about +0.16. So 0 is the better bid.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 2.8}

With three blue draws, the expected settlement value is 1.4. The best quote I found is a bid of 0.0 and an ask of 3.5.

**Fair value.** The chance of seeing three blues given R red balls is proportional to C(10−R, 3). That gives weights for R = 0…7 of 120, 84, 56, 35, 20, 10, 4 and 1, out of a total of 330. The posterior mean is 462/330 = 1.4, and P(R = 0) is about 0.36.

**Bid.** Any bid above 0 is hit by an informed trader whenever R = 0, which happens about 36% of the time. At exactly 0, an informed trader never sells, because their valuation can't be below 0.

| Bid | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.3 | 0.231 | 0.038 | 0.193 |
| 0.1 | 0.249 | 0.013 | 0.236 |
| 0.0 | 0.255 | 0 | 0.255 |

**Ask.** An informed trader buys whenever R is above my ask.

| Ask | Noise gain | Informed loss | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.0 | 0.156 | 0.134 | 0.02 |
| 3.0 | 0.262 | 0.059 | 0.20 |
| 3.4 | 0.263 | 0.045 | 0.218 |
| 3.5 | 0.261 | 0.041 | 0.22 |
| 3.9 | 0.242 | 0.026 | 0.216 |

Ask 3.5 is the best of these. My position is +1, so a sale there would also take me flat.

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 3.5}

With three blue draws and the trading history, I estimate the settlement value at about 1.3. It is most likely 1 or 2 red balls.

**Probability of each red-ball count:**
- Before trading is counted, three blues give weights of 720, 504, 336, 210, 120, 60, 24 and 6 for 0 to 7 red balls. That gives a mean of 1.4.
- The trades and no-trades then shift the probabilities. The sell at 2 in quote 1 and the no-trades on tight quotes in stage 2 favour 1 or 2 red. The buys at 2.8 and 3.5 add some weight to 3 or more.
- My rough estimate is: 0 red about 9%, 1 red about 54%, 2 red about 36%, 3 or more about 2%. The mean is about 1.31.

**Choice of quotes:**
- **Bid 1.0:** An informed trader holding 1 values the contract at exactly 1, so it will not sell to me. Only the about 9% case of 0 red can sell to me at a loss of 1. Noise traders sell often, and each sale gains about 0.3.
- **Ask 2.0:** An informed trader holding 2 values the contract at exactly 2, so it will not buy. Only the about 2% case of 3 or more red can buy at a loss. Noise traders buy about 38% of the time, and each sale gains about 0.7.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 2.0}

With all three draws blue, the posterior mean from the draws alone is 1.4.

**Draws-only posterior.** After three blue draws, the weights for R = 0…7 are 720, 504, 336, 210, 120, 60, 24, 6. These sum to 1980, and the mean is 2772 / 1980 = 1.4.

**Adjusting for trading history.** I made a rough correction for the trades, with fair values approximated at each quote:
- **Trades that point low:** the sales at 2 (quote 1) and 0.3 (quote 7) favour very low R.
- **Trades that point high:** the buys at 2.8, 3.5 and 2 favour R ≥ 3.
- **No-trades:** these push weight away from both extremes, particularly R = 0 and R ≥ 4. Most of the weight ends up on R = 1.

This gives a fair value of roughly 1.1 to 1.4, centred near 1.3.

**Quote.** I'm short 1, and this is the last quote, so I'll put a fairly symmetric spread around that range.

{"bid": 0.6, "ask": 2.1}

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 11 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 11. 4 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at 10 times the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
The contract settles at 10 × (number of red balls). Red balls are equally likely to be 0 to 11, so before any draws are revealed the fair value is **55**, with a standard deviation of about 34.5.

**Approach.** I compared the expected profit of different ask prices. Each ask trades off two things:
- **Informed counterparty (probability 0.5):** it knows the true value, so it only buys from me when the settlement value is above my ask. I lose (value − ask) on each such trade.
- **Noise trader (probability 0.5):** it buys when 55 plus Normal noise (standard deviation 35) is above my ask. I gain (ask − 55) on each such trade.

**Expected profit per quote for different asks:**

| Ask | Expected loss to informed | Expected gain from noise | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 75 | −3.33 | +2.84 | −0.49 |
| 85 | −1.88 | +2.94 | +1.06 |
| 95 | −0.83 | +2.53 | +1.70 |
| 100 | −0.42 | +2.23 | **+1.82** |
| 105 | −0.21 | +1.92 | +1.71 |

An ask of 100 gives the highest expected profit. The setup is symmetric around 55, so the best bid is 10.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 100}

The prior mean is 55, because the number of red balls is uniform over 0 to 11 and the contract pays 10 per red ball. The first quote, 10/100, got no trade. That lowers the chance that the value is at either extreme (0 or 110), but the update is symmetric, so the public fair value stays at 55.

To choose the width of each side, I compared what I earn from noise traders with what I lose to informed traders at different distances from 55, using that updated belief:

| Distance from 55 | Ask | Expected profit per side |
|---|---|---|
| 25 | 80 | about 1.0 |
| 35 | 90 | about 1.9 |
| 44 | 99 | about 2.0 |
| 45 | 100 | about 2.0 |
| 50 | 105 | about 1.8 |

The best width is about 44–45 on each side. So I quote about 44 on each side of 55, the same spread as before tightened by one tick.

{"bid": 11, "ask": 99}

Two blue draws shift the estimate down to a public fair value of about **22.5**. I'm quoting **bid 0, ask 60**, which is wide and skewed upward to fit that skewed estimate.

**Fair value after two blue draws.** The chance of drawing two blues when the urn holds R red balls is proportional to (11−R)(10−R). Combined with the uniform prior, R now runs from 0 to 9 with weights 110, 90, 72, 56, 42, 30, 20, 12, 6, 2, out of a total of 440. That gives an expected R of 2.25, so the fair value is 22.5. The value is heavily skewed: there is a 25% chance it settles at 0, and only about 9% that it settles above 50.

**Bid side.** I checked each bid by its expected profit against both kinds of counterparty.
- An informed seller only sells if the true value is strictly below my bid. At bid 0 that never happens, because the value cannot be below 0.
- A noise trader still sells about 26% of the time, at an average edge of about 22.5. That is an expected profit of roughly +2.9 per quote.
- Raising the bid toward 10 lets informed sellers with value 0 hit me. That costs more than the extra noise trades earn.

**Ask side.** I scanned ask levels the same way:

| Ask | Expected profit per quote |
|---|---|
| 40 | about 1.1 |
| 50 | about 2.2 |
| 55 | about 2.3 |
| 60 | about 2.3 |

At 60 the upper tail is thin, so informed buyers rarely profit against me. Noise buyers still lift the offer about 14% of the time, with a large edge.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 60}

Two blue draws make red balls less likely. The posterior weight on R red balls is proportional to (11−R)(10−R). That gives E[R] = 2.25, so the fair value is 22.5. The no-trade at quote 3 only slightly trims the chance of high values (R ≥ 7).

**Bid at 0.** If the value is 0 (probability ≈ 0.25), an informed trader's valuation of 0 is not below my bid, so it won't sell. Noise traders still sell often enough at that price to keep the edge, about 2.9 per quote. Raising the bid to 10 lets informed traders sell whenever the value is 0, and the edge falls to about 1.0.

**Ask around 52.** I compared expected profit for asks from 40 to 55. Profit from noise buyers stays roughly flat over that range. Losses to informed buyers, who only buy when R ≥ 6, keep falling as the ask rises. An ask near 52 comes out best, at about 2.5–2.6 per quote.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 52}

Three blue draws in a row make red balls unlikely. That shifts the fair value down to about 16, and I quote around that with wide spreads.

**Posterior after three blue draws.** With a uniform prior on R (red balls, 0 to 11), the chance of three blues is proportional to (11−R)(10−R)(9−R). The normalised posterior is:

| R | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.333 |
| 1 | 0.242 |
| 2 | 0.170 |
| 3 | 0.113 |
| 4 | 0.071 |
| 5 | 0.040 |
| 6 | 0.020 |
| 7 | 0.008 |
| 8 | 0.002 |

- The expected number of red balls is 1.6, so the public fair value is about 16.
- The four quotes so far had no trades, which tells us almost nothing new.

**Ask.** I compared the noise-trader profit against the expected loss to informed traders at several ask levels:

| Ask | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 30 | about +1.1 |
| 39 | about +2.3 |
| 45 to 49 | about +2.6 (the peak) |

The curve is flat between 45 and 49, so I quote 47.

**Bid.** The settlement value can never be below 0. A bid at or below 0 is therefore never hit by an informed trader with a value I'd lose on, and only noise sellers trade with me.

| Bid | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 0 | about +2.6 |
| −5 | about +2.9 |
| −10 | about +3.0 |

The rules only rule out a bid above the ask, so a negative bid should be valid. The gain from going lower is small, so I choose a moderate −5.

{"bid": -5, "ask": 47}

The fair value is 16. I'm quoting a bid of -10 and an ask of 48, chosen to maximise expected profit for this quote.

**Posterior after three blue draws.** The chance of drawing three blues is proportional to C(11−R, 3) for each possible red count R. That gives these weights:

| R | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weight | 165 | 120 | 84 | 56 | 35 | 20 | 10 | 4 | 1 |

The weights sum to 495, and E[R] = 792 / 495 = 1.6. So the fair value is 16. The settlement value is 0 with probability 1/3, and has about a 14% chance of being 40 or more.

**Ask side.**
- An informed buyer only lifts my ask when the value is above it.
- For any ask between 40 and 49, that means the value is 40 or more. Those cases have probability 0.141 and average about 48.
- Noise traders value the contract at 16 plus noise with standard deviation 35.
- Expected profit at each candidate ask:

| Ask | Informed | Noise | Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| 45 | −0.22 | +2.95 | 2.73 |
| 48 | −0.01 | +2.88 | 2.87 |
| 49 | −0.25 | +2.85 | 2.60 |

- 48 gives the most, so I ask 48.

**Bid side.**
- The value can never be negative, so an informed trader never sells to me at a bid of 0 or below.
- That leaves only noise sellers. With bid b, my expected profit is 0.5 × P(noise valuation < b) × (16 − b).
- That works out to about 2.59 at b = 0, 2.97 at b = −10 and 2.91 at b = −15.
- −10 gives the most, so I bid −10.

{"bid": -10, "ask": 48}

After four blue draws, fair value is about **11.7**. I'm quoting bid -15 and ask 40, which puts my expected profit on this quote at about 5.8.

**Posterior.** The probability of r red balls is proportional to C(11−r, 4), for r = 0 to 7. The weights are 330, 210, 126, 70, 35, 15, 5 and 1, which sum to 792. That gives:

| Settlement value | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.417 |
| 10 | 0.265 |
| 20 | 0.159 |
| 30 | 0.088 |
| 40 | 0.044 |
| 50 | 0.019 |
| 60 | 0.006 |
| 70 | 0.001 |

The expected number of red balls is 924/792 ≈ 1.167, so fair value is about 11.67.

**Bid.** Any bid above 0 lets informed traders holding a zero-value contract sell to me. That costs more than the extra noise flow brings in: a bid of 5 earns only about 0.4. With a bid at or below 0, informed traders never sell, so only noise flow matters. I compared bids by the margin below fair value times the chance a noise trader sells:

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| -10 | 2.90 |
| -15 | 2.97 |
| -20 | 2.90 |

So I bid -15.

**Ask.** A higher ask earns more per noise trade but fills less often. A lower ask lets informed traders buy when the value is 40 or more. Because buyers need a value strictly above the ask, an ask of 40 is not lifted when the value is exactly 40.

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 35 | 2.58 |
| 40 | 2.78 |
| 45 | 2.73 |

So I offer at 40.

{"bid": -15, "ask": 40}

The settlement value is 10 × R, where R is the number of red balls. The fair value is the expected settlement value given everything seen so far.

**Posterior after four blue draws.**
- The chance of drawing 4 blue balls when the urn holds R red balls is C(11−R, 4) / C(11, 4).
- For R = 0 to 7, the weights are 330, 210, 126, 70, 35, 15, 5 and 1. They sum to 792.
- The expected R is 924 / 792 ≈ 1.17, so the fair value before the last trade was about 11.7.

**Update for the buy at 40 on quote 7.**
- An informed counterparty buys at 40 only if R ≥ 5.
- A noise trader buys at 40 with probability P(Z > 28.3/35) ≈ 0.21.
- Updating on that buy gives an expected R of about 1.64, so the public fair value is now about 16.4.
- The posterior probabilities for R = 0 to 7 are roughly 0.37, 0.235, 0.14, 0.08, 0.04, 0.10, 0.03 and 0.007.

**Choosing the bid.**
- With a bid at or below 0, an informed counterparty never sells to me, so the only effect is profit from noise traders.
- The expected profit from noise traders, 0.5 · P(noise < b) · (16.4 − b), is highest at about 2.97 for b near −10.

**Choosing the ask.**
- With the ask at 50, an informed counterparty buys only if the value is 60 or 70. That costs about 0.23 in expectation.
- Noise traders buy with probability about 0.17 at a margin of 33.6, worth about 2.83.
- The net is about +2.6, the best of the asks I checked (40, 49, 50 and 55).

My position is −1, so both sides are allowed.

{"bid": -10, "ask": 50}

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 9 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 9. 2 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
The fair value is 4.5. That is the mean of red balls uniform on 0 to 9. Half the counterparties are informed and know the true count. So tight quotes lose money to them. I checked the expected profit per quote at several ask levels. Each figure averages the informed traders' losses against the noise traders' profits.

| Ask | Net expected profit |
|---|---|
| 6.5 | about 0.02 |
| 7.5 | about 0.125 |
| 8.0 | about 0.149 |
| 8.2 | about 0.147 |
| 8.5 | about 0.143 |

An ask of 8.0 gives the highest expected profit. By symmetry, the best bid is 1.0.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 8.0}

The fair value is still 4.5, because the prior is uniform on 0 to 9 and the symmetric quote last time drew no trade.

**Ask side.** I checked the expected profit at a few asks:

| Ask | Loss to informed traders | Profit from noise traders | Net per quote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 7.5 | 0.20 | 0.45 | ≈0.125 |
| 8.0 | 0.10 | 0.40 | ≈0.149 |
| 8.5 | 0.05 | 0.34 | ≈0.143 |

- The informed loss is the expected amount by which the true value exceeds the ask.
- Noise profit is the chance a noise trader buys times the gap between the ask and 4.5.
- Net is half the noise profit minus half the informed loss, since each type arrives with probability 0.5.

The best ask is about 8.0.

**Bid side.** By symmetry around 4.5, the best bid is about 1.0.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 8.0}

Fair value after the reveal and the trades is about 1.6, so I'm posting bid 0.0 and ask 4.8.

**Belief update.**
- **Draw 1 is blue.** This makes R red balls more likely the fewer there are: the prior weight on R becomes proportional to (9 − R). Alone, that gives an expected value of 2.67.
- **Quote 1 (bid 1, ask 8), no trade.** An informed trader would not trade at any R from 1 to 8. Assuming noise traders centred on 4.5, about 77% of them would also not trade.
- **Quote 2, someone sold at 1.** An informed trader sells only if R = 0. A noise trader values below 1 only about 11% of the time.
- **Combined posterior.** P(R = 0) is about 0.52, and the rest is spread over R = 1 to 8 in proportion to (9 − R). The expected value is about 1.6.

**Choosing the quotes.**
- **Bid.** A bid at 0 loses nothing to informed traders, because they only sell when the true value is below the bid. It still buys from noise traders valuing below 0, about 29% of them. Expected edge is about +0.23. Raising the bid towards 1 lets informed traders sell to me when R = 0, which makes the quote worse.
- **Ask.** The expected profit from the ask peaks at around 4.5 to 5, at roughly +0.13. That is the point where gains from noise buyers best outweigh losses to informed buyers when R ≥ 5. Being long 1 unit, I'm content to sell.

{"bid": 0.0, "ask": 4.8}

My estimate of the fair value is about 1.2. Quoting a bid of 0 and an ask of 4.0 has the best expected profit.

**Updating on the history.** The prior is uniform over R = 0–9 red balls.

- **Quote 1** (no trade at 1/8): mass at R = 0 and R = 9 goes down, since an informed trader would have traded there.
- **Quote 2** (they sold at 1): this is strong evidence for R = 0. Only an informed trader holding R = 0 sells below 1; a noise trader does so only about 11% of the time.
- **Draw 1 = blue:** each R is multiplied by a likelihood proportional to (9 − R).
- **Quote 3** (no trade at 0/4.8): an informed trader would have bought if R were 5 or more, so those values are down-weighted.

The resulting posterior is roughly:

| R | Probability |
|---|---|
| 0 | 0.56 |
| 1 | 0.12 |
| 2 | 0.10 |
| 3 | 0.09 |
| 4 | 0.07 |
| 5 | 0.02 |
| 6 | 0.016 |
| 7 | 0.011 |
| 8 | 0.005 |

The fair value E[R] is about 1.2.

**Bid.** An informed trader holding R = 0 values the contract at 0, so it will not sell at a bid of 0. A noise trader sells about 34% of the time, and I gain about 1.2 each time. A bid of 0 is clearly profitable.

**Ask.** I scanned asks from 2.5 to 4.5. The expected edge from noise buyers, minus losses to informed buyers, peaks at about 4.0, worth roughly +0.18 per quote. Selling there also cuts my long position.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 4.0}

Two blue draws make a low red count likely. The trading so far, especially the sell at a bid of 1 in quote 2, points further toward R = 0. My estimate of the settlement value is about 0.8, with roughly a 66% chance that R = 0.

**Bid at 0.** Settlement can never be below 0, so buying at 0 cannot lose money. An informed trader never sells at 0, so only noise traders would hit it.

**Ask at 3.5.** An informed buyer only takes it when R ≥ 4, which has about a 6% chance. Noise traders will sometimes pay well above my value estimate. Selling also reduces my long position. Of the asks I compared, 3.5 had the highest expected profit at about 0.21 per quote.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 3.5}

Expected settlement value is about 0.6, most likely 0, so I bid 0 and ask 3.0.

**Posterior after two blue draws.** The prior is uniform on R = 0..9. The weight for each R is (9−R)(8−R), normalised. That gives a mean of 1.75, with R = 8 and R = 9 ruled out.

**Updating on the trade history.** The fair value should also reflect the trades. I weighted each R by the chance of each observed outcome, assuming each counterparty was informed half the time:
- **Quote 2 (sold to me at 1):** an informed seller only sells below 1, which means R = 0. A noise trader sells there only about 11% of the time. This pushes heavy weight onto R = 0.
- **Quote 3 (no trade at 0 / 4.8):** an informed trader stays out only if R ≤ 4, which cuts the higher values.
- **Quote 5 (no trade at 0 / 3.5):** an informed trader stays out only if R ≤ 3, which cuts them further.
- **Quote 4 (sold to me at 0):** no informed trader sells below 0, so this was noise and tells us nothing.

The result is P(R = 0) ≈ 0.69 and an expected settlement value of about 0.6.

**Choosing the quotes.** I am long 2, so selling is the more valuable side.
- **Ask:** I compared the gain from selling to noise traders above my ask against the loss from informed buyers when R exceeds it.
  - Ask 2.0: net ≈ 0.17.
  - Ask 3.0: net ≈ 0.46.
  - Ask 3.5: net ≈ 0.45.
  
  An ask around 3.0 is about the best.
- **Bid:** at 0, informed traders never sell to me, since R cannot be below 0. Noise traders sell about 42% of the time at roughly 0.6 below fair value. Raising the bid to 0.1 lets informed sellers in when R = 0, which costs more than it gains. So the bid stays at 0.

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 9 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 9. 2 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
game.contract: The contract settles at the number of red balls originally in the urn.

info.raw:
The contract settles at the number of red balls, which is equally likely to be any of 0 to 9. That makes the fair value 4.5 before anything is revealed.

**Ask side (quoting at 4.5 + d):**
- An informed trader buys only when the true value is above my ask, and then I lose money.
- A noise trader buys when its noise exceeds d. Its noise is Normal with standard deviation 2.9, and I earn d on each such trade.
- At an ask of 6.5, the expected profit per quote is about +0.02. At 7.5 it is about +0.125.
- At an ask of 8.0, I only lose to an informed trader when the value is 9. That costs about 0.05. Noise traders buy about 11.4% of the time, which earns about 0.20.
- Net expected profit at 8.0 is about +0.15. That is the peak; 7.9 and 8.1 give about the same.

**Bid side:** The problem is symmetric around 4.5, so the best bid is about 1.0.

{"bid": 1.0, "ask": 8.0}

With nothing revealed yet, fair value is 4.5, and a wide symmetric quote of 1.1 / 7.9 looks best.

**Fair value.** The prior on red balls is uniform on 0–9, so the mean is 4.5. Quote 1 (bid 1, ask 8) got no trade. An informed counterparty would have sold at 1 if the value were 0 and bought at 8 if it were 9. So the no-trade lowers the weight on 0 and 9 equally:
- Values 0 and 9 each get relative weight about 0.385.
- Values 1–8 each get relative weight about 0.885.

The posterior is still symmetric, so fair value stays at 4.5.

**Choosing the half-spread.** A wide quote keeps some profit from noise traders, whose valuations have a standard deviation of 2.9. It also exposes me only to informed traders holding extreme values. Expected profit per side for different asks:

| Ask | Expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| 6.5 | ≈ +0.07 |
| 7.5 | ≈ +0.16 |
| 7.9 | ≈ +0.17 |
| 8.0 | ≈ +0.17 |
| 8.5 | ≈ +0.16 |

The best range is about 3.4–3.5 either side of 4.5. I'll quote 1.1 / 7.9, which is slightly tighter than quote 1 and gives a little more chance of a trade that reveals information.

{"bid": 1.1, "ask": 7.9}

Because the first draw was red, the posterior on R is weighted toward more red balls. The two earlier no-trades also tell me something: they make R values outside the old quotes (R≤1 or R≥8) less likely. Combining both gives a public fair value of about 5.6, with most of the probability on R between 3 and 8.

- **Ask:** Informed buyers only trade with me when R is above my ask. Checking a range of ask prices, expected profit is highest at about 8.1–8.5. At those levels an informed buy mostly happens only when R=9, while noise buyers still trade often enough to pay.
- **Bid:** By the same reasoning on the downside, expected profit is highest at a bid of about 2.5–2.9. Informed sellers rarely have R that low, and noise sellers still lift the bid at a useful rate.

{"bid": 2.8, "ask": 8.2}

Quote bid 3.0 and ask 8.0: each side sits on a whole number of red balls, so the informed trader only trades against me when the true count lies beyond the quote.

**Posterior after draw 1 = red:** a red first draw makes each count r more likely in proportion to r, so P(r) ∝ r.

**No-trade updates:** each quote that drew no trade changes the odds.
- An informed trader would not have traded if r was inside my bid–ask range.
- A noise trader's chance of not trading is roughly the same whatever r is.
- So counts inside each past range keep more weight. The most likely values are 3 to 8, and the extremes (1, 2, 9) are much less likely.

Combining these, the posterior mean is about **5.67**. Roughly 13.7% of the probability is on r ≥ 8, and roughly 3% is on r ≤ 2.

**Edge per side:** ask 8.0 is never hit by an informed trader at r = 8. A noise trader buys at 8.0 about 21% of the time, earning about 2.33. Bid 3.0 is never hit by an informed trader at r = 3. A noise trader sells at 3.0 about 18% of the time, earning about 2.67. Expected profit is about +0.23 on each side, the best of the levels I checked.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 8.0}

Since both draws were red, I update the prior on R using weights proportional to R(R−1). That gives a posterior mean of **7.25**. The settlement value is skewed: P(9)=0.30, P(8)=0.23, P(7)=0.175, P(6)=0.125, with smaller chances down to 2.

For each side I weighed two effects:
- **Informed traders:** they only trade when it hurts me. On the ask they buy only if the true value is above my price; on the bid they sell only if it is below.
- **Noise traders:** they value the contract at 7.25 plus noise with SD 2.9. Each trade with them earns me roughly the gap between my price and 7.25.

**Ask side:** At any ask of 9 or more, informed buyers never profit, since 9 is the maximum value. Expected profit from noise buyers peaks at about **+0.25** for an ask around 9.0–9.5.

**Bid side:** Expected profit is about **+0.19** for a bid anywhere from 4.5 to 4.9, and it is fairly flat across that range.

I'll quote a bid of 4.7 and an ask of 9.4.

{"bid": 4.7, "ask": 9.4}

With two reds drawn, my fair value for the urn's red count is about **6.1**, and the best final quote is **bid 3.0, ask 9.0**.

**Posterior after the two red draws.** The chance of drawing two reds given R red balls is proportional to R(R−1). That puts weight on R = 2…9 of 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, 42, 56, 72, which sum to 240. On the draws alone, E[R] = 1740/240 = 7.25.

**Update for the sale at my bid of 4.7.**
- An informed trader sells at 4.7 only if R ≤ 4.
- A noise trader sells with probability Φ((4.7 − 7.25)/2.9) ≈ 0.19.
- So the chance of a sale is 0.5 + 0.095 = 0.595 if R ≤ 4, and 0.095 otherwise.
- Reweighting by these chances gives a posterior mean of about **6.11**.
- The probabilities are P(R ≤ 4) ≈ 0.36, P(R = 8) ≈ 0.16 and P(R = 9) ≈ 0.21.

**Choosing the quote.** This is the last quote, so I set each side to maximise its own expected profit. Being long one unit doesn't change that, since I only care about expected profit.
- **Ask:** at 9.0, an informed buyer never profits from me, because R can be at most 9. A noise trader buys about 16% of the time, earning me about 2.89 each time. Expected profit is about 0.23, the best I found.
- **Bid:** at 3.0, I lose only when an informed trader sells with R = 2, which costs about 0.02. A noise trader sells about 14% of the time, earning me about 3.11 each time. Expected profit is about 0.20, the best I found.

{"bid": 3.0, "ask": 9.0}

info.raw:
Fair value is 50, the expected number of red balls (5) times 10. I picked the spread half-width by trading off two effects. Noise traders pay me the spread. Informed traders, who arrive 20% of the time, hit me only when the true value lies beyond my quote. The settlement value is uniform on 0, 10, …, 100 and noise has a standard deviation of 47.

Expected profit per side at each half-width:

| Half-width | Expected profit per side |
|---|---|
| 20 | ≈ 4.3 |
| 30 | ≈ 5.7 |
| 35 | ≈ 6.0 |
| 40 | ≈ 6.1 |
| 45 | ≈ 6.0 |

The peak is around a half-width of 40, so I quote 10 / 90.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 90}

Fair value after the sell at 10 is about 44.8; I'm quoting wide (bid 5, ask 87) because that maximises expected profit per quote.

**Updated fair value.** The prior on the settlement value V is uniform on 0, 10, …, 100, with mean 50. An informed trader sells at a bid of 10 only if V = 0. A noise trader sells with probability P(50 + N(0,47) < 10), which is about 0.197.

- The chance of that sell is about 0.358 when V = 0 and about 0.158 for every other V.
- Updating on the observed sell gives V = 0 a posterior weight of about 0.185. Every other value gets about 0.0815.
- The posterior mean, which is now the public fair value, is about **44.8**.

**Choosing the quotes.** For each candidate price I weighed the profit from noise traders against expected losses to informed traders.

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 70 | about 5.0 |
| 75 | about 5.55 |
| 80 | about 5.9 |
| 85 | about 6.06 |
| 90 | about 6.08 |

The ask curve is flat between 85 and 90, so I picked 87.

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 10 | about 6.0 |
| 5 | about 6.15 |
| 0 | about 6.1 |

Bid 5 gives the highest expected profit.

{"bid": 5, "ask": 87}

Two blue draws make the posterior weight on R proportional to (10−R)(9−R), so the expected red count is 2. Public fair value is about 20, and the trade history roughly cancels out.

**Ask side.** I weighed noise-trader profit against losses to informed traders, using noise standard deviation 47 and informed probability 0.2.

| Ask | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 40 | 4.9 |
| 50 | 6.1 |
| 55 | 6.3 (best) |
| 60 | 6.2 |

**Bid side.** The value can't go below 0, so an informed trader never sells to me at a bid of 0. A bid of 0 gives about 5.4 expected, all from noise traders. A bid of 5 gives about 4.2, because informed traders sell when R = 0. Bidding below 0 would score slightly higher on paper, but I've kept the bid at 0 since the contract can never settle below 0.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 55}

After two blue draws the fair value is about 20, so I'm quoting the same 0 / 55 as last quote.

**Fair value.** The prior on the number of red balls R is uniform over 0 to 10. After two blue draws, each R is weighted by the chance of drawing two blues, (10−R)(9−R):

| R | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weight | 90 | 72 | 56 | 42 | 30 | 20 | 12 | 6 | 2 |

The weights total 330, and R = 9 or 10 has zero weight. The posterior mean of R is 660 / 330 = 2, so fair value is about 20. The earlier trades carry little information, so I leave this unchanged.

**Ask.** Noise traders are spread around 20 with a standard deviation of 47. Informed traders buy only when the settlement value is above my ask. The expected edge per quote on the ask side is:

| Ask | Expected edge |
|---|---|
| 40 | about 4.9 |
| 50 | about 6.1 |
| 55 | about 6.26 |
| 60 | about 6.24 |

The edge is flat between 55 and 60, so I keep the ask at 55.

**Bid.** At a bid of 0, an informed trader never sells to me, because the value can't be below 0. Noise traders still sell often, giving an edge of about 5.4. Raising the bid gives up too much edge on noise trades and loses to informed traders when R = 0, which has a 27% chance. So the bid stays at 0.

{"bid": 0, "ask": 55}

Posterior fair value is about 40, and I'll quote bid 10 / ask 72 around it.

**Fair value.** With a uniform prior on the number of red balls R, the chance of seeing blue, blue, red is proportional to R(10−R)(9−R). That posterior gives an expected R of 3.8, so a fair value of 38. Last quote's buy at 68 shifts weight slightly toward R ≥ 7, which lifts fair value to about 40–41.

**Bid side.** At a bid of 10, an informed seller only appears if R = 0 or 1. At R = 1 the value equals 10, so I lose nothing. Noise traders, whose valuations are about N(41, 47), sell to me there about 25% of the time, with an edge of roughly 31. Expected profit is about 6.3, the best of the bids I checked.

**Ask side.** An ask of 71–72 is only hit by an informed buyer when R = 8, worth 80, which is rare. Noise traders still lift it about 21% of the time, with an edge of about 30. Expected profit is about 6.2. Since I'm short 2, I lean slightly higher on the ask.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 72}

Given 1 red in 4 draws and a uniform prior on the number of red balls, the expected number of red balls is 3.0, so fair value is about 30.

I am short 3, so I can only bid. A buy at bid b earns:
- **Noise traders:** they sell with probability Φ((b−30)/47), and I gain 30−b each time.
- **Informed traders:** they only sell if the true value is below my bid. The lowest possible value is 10, so any bid of 10 or less carries no informed loss.

| Bid | Expected profit |
|---|---|
| 20 | ≈ 3.0 |
| 10 | ≈ 5.4 |
| 0 | ≈ 6.3 |
| −5 | ≈ 6.4 |

The best value is around −5, but 0 is almost as good and avoids a negative price, so I bid 0.

{"bid": 0, "ask": null}

Final quote: bid 0, no ask. My ask is pulled because I'm already at -3.

**Fair value is 30.** After 4 draws (1 red, 3 blue), the chance that the urn holds R red balls is proportional to R × C(10−R, 3):

| R | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weight | 84 | 112 | 105 | 80 | 50 | 24 | 7 |

These weights sum to 462, and the weighted average of R is 1386/462 = 3. So the expected settlement value is 30.

**Choosing the bid.** A counterparty who sells to me at bid b earns me on average 30 − b if it is a noise trader. Noise traders sell when 30 + N(0, 47) < b.

- At any bid of 10 or below, informed traders essentially never sell to me, because the settlement value is at least 10 (one red ball has been drawn).
- Expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise trader sells) × (30 − b):
  - b = 10 gives about 5.4
  - b = 0 gives about 6.3
  - b = −5 gives about 6.4, which is the theoretical maximum
- I'm using 0 rather than a negative bid. It gives up less than 0.1 in expected value and avoids any risk of the quote being rejected as invalid.

info.raw:
Fair value is 50, the mean red count of 5 times 10. The settlement value can be any of 0, 10, ..., 100, each with probability 1/11.

I compared expected profit per side for different half-spreads s, set against what informed traders would cost me:
- **s = 20:** about 4.3
- **s = 30:** about 5.7
- **s = 40:** about 6.1
- **s = 50:** about 5.8

A half-spread of about 40 does best, so I quote a bid of 10 and an ask of 90.

{"bid": 10, "ask": 90}

Fair value is 50. The prior on red balls is uniform over 0–10, so the settlement value is uniform over 0, 10, …, 100. The no-trade at 10/90 tells us nothing in either direction, so 50 still stands.

For each side, I traded off what noise traders pay against what informed traders take.
- **Noise gain:** 0.8 × P(noise > s) × s, where noise has standard deviation 47.
- **Informed loss:** 0.2 × the expected amount by which the true value lands beyond the quote.

| Half-spread s | Informed loss | Noise gain | Net per side |
|---|---|---|---|
| 30 | 0.55 | 6.28 | 5.74 |
| 35 | 0.36 | 6.38 | 6.02 |
| 38 | 0.25 | 6.35 | 6.10 |
| 40 | 0.18 | 6.31 | 6.13 |
| 45 | 0.09 | 6.09 | 6.00 |

The best value is near s = 40, and the curve is flat between about 38 and 40. Last quote I used 40 (10/90) and got no trade. I'll tighten slightly to s = 38, which gives up almost nothing in expected value and makes a trade a bit more likely.

{"bid": 12, "ask": 88}

After two red draws, the public fair value is **80**. The posterior on red balls R is proportional to R(R−1). That gives E[R] = (3025 − 385)/330 = 8, so the fair value is 10 × 8 = 80. The posterior standard deviation is about 19 in contract units.

The earlier sale at 12 in stage 1 must have come from a noise trader. An informed seller at 12 would mean R = 0 or 1, and both are now ruled out.

**Choosing the quotes.** For each price I compared the expected gain from noise traders with the expected loss to informed traders.
- **Ask:** The settlement value can be at most 100, so an informed trader never buys above 100. Above that level only noise traders trade, and the expected gain keeps rising until roughly 110–115. I set the ask at 112.
- **Bid:** Informed sellers cost little once the bid is below about 50. The expected gain peaks at about 6.3 per quote for bids between 40 and 45. I set the bid at 45.

My position of +1 leaves room to buy without reaching the +3 limit.

{"bid": 45, "ask": 112}

Fair value is about 86 after three red draws in a row. I'm quoting wide around it, at 50 / 120.

**Fair value**
- The prior on the number of red balls R is uniform over 0..10.
- Three reds in three draws gives a posterior proportional to R(R−1)(R−2), for R = 3..10.
- That makes E[R] = 17028 / 1980 = 8.6, so fair value is about 86.
- The most likely settlements are 100 (36% probability), 90 (25%) and 80 (17%).
- The history adds little information, so I'm leaving 86 unadjusted.

**Ask side**
- The settlement can't exceed 100, so an ask above 100 is never lifted by an informed trader.
- Above 100, only noise traders (fair value plus noise with standard deviation 47) can buy.
- Expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise trader buys) × (ask − 86). This peaks around an ask of 120, at about 6.4 per quote.

**Bid side**
- I traded off the edge from noise sellers against the expected loss to informed sellers when the true value is below my bid.
- A bid of 50 gives about 6.4 per quote, slightly better than 55 (about 6.2) or 60 (about 5.9).

{"bid": 50, "ask": 120}

Fair value is about **86**.

**Posterior.** The prior on the number of red balls R is uniform over 0 to 10. After three red draws, the posterior weight on each R is proportional to R(R−1)(R−2).
- Posterior mean: E[R] = 3 + 7·(4/5) = 8.6, so fair value = 86.
- Possible settlement values are 30 to 100.
- The chance the value is exactly 100 is 720/1980 ≈ 36%.

**History adds nothing.**
- The buys at 112 and 120 must have been noise traders, because no informed trader pays more than 100.
- The early sell at 12 could only have been informed if the value were 0 or 10, and the draws have ruled that out.

**Choosing the quotes.** I'm risk-neutral and short 1, so selling one more unit (to −2) is fine.
- **Ask:** an informed trader rarely beats an ask above 100. The noise-trader edge, roughly 0.8·P(N>a)·(a−86), peaks at about 6.3 when the ask is around 120 to 125.
- **Bid:** expected profit is roughly 0.8·P(N<b)·(86−b) minus small losses to informed sellers. It peaks at about 6.4 when the bid is around 50 to 55.

{"bid": 52, "ask": 120}

Fair value is **90**, the expected settlement after four red draws out of four. I'm quoting a wide spread around it: **bid 55, ask 125**.

**Posterior on the number of red balls (R).** Start from a uniform prior and weight each R by the chance of drawing 4 reds, which is proportional to R(R−1)(R−2)(R−3).

| R | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | 9 | 10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Weight | 24 | 120 | 360 | 840 | 1680 | 3024 | 5040 |

This gives E[R] = 9, so fair value = 90. The chance that R = 10 (settlement 100) is about 45%.

**Ask.** Settlement can't exceed 100. So with any ask of 100 or more, an informed trader never buys and adverse selection is zero on that side. Against noise traders (90 plus noise with SD 47), expected profit is 0.8 × P(buy) × (ask − 90). This peaks at about 6.4 per quote for an ask around 125.

**Bid.** Settlement below 60 has only about 1.3% probability, so an informed seller costs almost nothing at a low bid. Expected profit from noise sellers peaks at about 6.4 per quote for a bid around 55. The expected loss to informed sellers there is only about 0.02.

**Position.** I'm short 1, so trading either side keeps me within the ±3 limit.

{"bid": 55, "ask": 125}

With four red draws out of four, fair value is about 90, so I'm quoting a wide spread around it: bid 55, ask 124.

**Fair value.** The chance of drawing 4 red out of 4, given R red balls in the urn, is proportional to R(R−1)(R−2)(R−3). Weighting each possible R by that gives the posterior below.

| R | 10 | 9 | 8 | 7 | 6 or fewer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Probability | ≈45% | ≈27% | ≈15% | ≈8% | ≈5% |

The expected value is E[R] = 9, so the contract is worth about 90. The trading history may pull this slightly lower, but not by much.

**Ask side.**
- An informed trader values the contract at 100 at most, so any ask above 100 is never hit by them. Only noise traders, centred around 90, would buy.
- Expected profit is 0.8 × P(noise valuation > ask) × (ask − 90).
- This is about 5.5 at an ask of 110 and about 6.3 at both 120 and 130. The maximum is roughly 124.

**Bid side.**
- Noise traders sell often enough below 90 that a low bid still earns about 6.2 to 6.4 for any bid from 50 to 60.
- Informed traders would only sell to me at a bid of 55 if R is 5 or fewer, which has about 1% probability. Their expected loss to me is negligible.
- A bid around 55 is roughly optimal.

game.title: Urn of unknown mix
game.description: An urn holds 8 balls, each red or blue. The number of red balls is equally likely to be any of 0, 1, ..., 8. 2 balls are drawn without replacement. Revealed draws show 1 for red and 0 for blue.
